claim: It is fair for insurers and lenders to use credit scores and risk models.
argument:
To understand why credit scores and risk models are fundamentally fair, one must first confront the alternative: what happens when we do not use them?

Before the advent of standardized credit scores and algorithmic risk modeling, lending and underwriting were deeply personal, subjective, and arbitrary. A borrower’s likelihood of getting a mortgage or a business loan often came down to whether a local loan officer liked their handshake, recognized their family name, or felt comfortable with their background. That system was a breeding ground for cronyism, nepotism, and overt discrimination. Standardized risk models did not invent disparity; they stripped away human prejudice and replaced it with measurable, verifiable behavior. Mathematics has no malice, no social bias, and no personal favor.

At its core, fairness in finance is not about guaranteeing the exact same price or outcome to every individual; it is about ensuring that individuals are judged by relevant, objective criteria, and that one person is not forced to bear the cost of another’s risk. 

Consider how insurance works. It is fundamentally a risk pool. When an insurer prices a policy, it is estimating the likelihood that the policyholder will file a claim. Decades of actuarial data from the Federal Trade Commission and state insurance commissioners have repeatedly affirmed a simple reality: credit-based insurance scores are exceptionally powerful, statistically sound predictors of future risk. Individuals who manage their financial obligations with consistent care also tend to exercise greater caution behind the wheel, maintain their homes more diligently, and avoid reckless behaviors. 

If insurers are forbidden from using these predictive models, risk does not simply vanish into thin air. Instead, the costs are averaged across the entire pool. In practice, this means that a working-class individual who scrupulously pays their bills on time and maintains a pristine driving record is forced to pay higher premiums to subsidize someone with a history of financial carelessness and higher claim rates. There is nothing equitable about asking the financially prudent to underwrite the costs of the statistically reckless. 

The same principle applies to lending. When lenders use credit models to accurately assess the probability of default, they are able to expand credit to millions of people who previously would have been locked out. A risk model allows a lender to say "yes" to an applicant with no family wealth or personal connections, solely on the strength of their demonstrated track record. Moreover, because risk-based pricing allows institutions to manage default exposure with surgical precision, interest rates for lower-risk borrowers are dramatically lower than they would be in a system forced to price against the unknown.

Crucially, credit scores provide what static demographic markers never could: individual agency. A credit score is not a caste system; it is a dynamic, living record of choices over time. It can be built, repaired, and leveraged. It empowers the consumer by giving them a transparent, actionable pathway to lower their own costs of living. 

To eliminate objective risk models would not make society fairer. It would merely reintroduce opacity, force the responsible to pay for the irresponsible, and resurrect the arbitrary gatekeeping of the past. Credit scores and risk models are fair precisely because they insist that in the realm of shared financial risk, empirical reality and personal accountability must matter more than wishful thinking.

claim: Lifespan extension would exacerbate inequities and should not be pursued
argument:
The history of medical innovation tells a consistent, cautionary story: breakthrough treatments do not democratize; they stratify. From basic access to clean water and insulin to cutting-edge cancer immunotherapies, the benefits of biological science have always accrued first, most comprehensively, and often exclusively to the wealthy. To believe that radical lifespan extension will somehow break this iron law of distribution is not optimism—it is willful blindness. Pursuing technologies to drastically lengthen human life will transform our current, already destabilizing socio-economic divisions into a permanent, biological caste system. 

Inequality today is, at the very least, bounded by mortality. The wealthiest individual and the most destitute laborer operate within the same fundamental temporal constraints. Death serves as humanity’s final, inescapable equalizer, ensuring that fortunes must eventually be dispersed, monopolies on power broken, and leadership passed to new generations with fresh perspectives.

Remove that natural horizon, and the mechanisms that sustain an open society collapse.

Consider the compounding nature of capital. Wealth generates wealth exponentially over time; compounding interest is the most powerful financial force on Earth. If an elite class gains the biological privilege of living for two centuries while the rest of humanity continues to live for seven or eight decades, economic concentration will reach levels unprecedented in human history. The ultra-rich will not merely own the means of production—they will own the timeline upon which dynasties are built. Generational turnover, which historically breaks up concentrated estates through inheritance taxes, generational dilution, and the simple chaos of time, will cease to function. 

The consequences for political life are even more dire. Political institutions in modern democracies are already gridlocked by gerontocracies reluctant to yield influence. Radical longevity among the powerful would cement authoritarian or oligarchic rule. Leaders, judges, and entrenched political actors could hold office for a century or more, entirely choking off the emergence of younger voices, civil rights advancements, and ideological evolution. Progress relies heavily on generational replacement; as the physicist Max Planck famously observed, science advances one funeral at a time. The same holds true for social morality. If the architects of segregated, extractive, or oppressive systems lived indefinitely, those systems would simply never end.

Advocates of lifespan extension counter that costs will eventually fall, as they did with personal computers or smartphones. But this analogy fails under scrutiny. Consumer electronics rely on massive economies of scale and marginal manufacturing costs approaching zero. Advanced biogerontology—cellular reprogramming, telomere restoration, organ replacement, and epigenetic rejuvenation—involves intensely personalized, continuous, and resource-heavy medical interventions. In a world that cannot even guarantee affordable insulin to citizens in the wealthiest nations on Earth, the idea that complex life-extension therapies will be universally distributed is a fantasy. Public health systems would be crushed under the fiscal burden, forcing societies to make explicit moral choices about whose longevity is worth subsidizing. 

When life itself becomes a purchasable commodity, inequality ceases to be a social condition and becomes an ontological fact. The rich will not merely have more money; they will inhabit a different plane of existence, looking down upon shorter-lived populations not just with economic superiority, but with the profound biological paternalism that the long-lived have always reserved for the ephemeral.

Scientific inquiry is not an unalloyed good that must be pursued irrespective of its social reality. True human progress does not mean perfecting the biological immortality of the privileged few while billions struggle with the basic necessities of life, clean air, and dignity. It means using our resources to compress morbidity, alleviate preventable suffering, and ensure that every person can live a full, healthy, natural span. To prioritize the engineering of longer lives before solving the distribution of a fair life is to build an aristocracy written directly into our DNA. We must have the wisdom to refuse to build it.

claim: Limits should be placed on acceptable human risk levels for initial Mars colonization missions
argument:
The romantic myth of the frontier has always demanded blood. From the Oregon Trail to early Antarctic expeditions, history celebrates those who pushed into the unknown heedless of the mortal odds, accepting catastrophe as the inevitable tariff of human progress. It is tempting, even intoxicating, to apply this same swashbuckling ethos to the sands of Mars—to argue that the stakes of becoming a multi-planetary species are so high, and the volunteers so willing, that society should tolerate virtually any level of human risk to plant the flag.

Yet this perspective fundamentally mistakes recklessness for ambition. Placing strict, non-negotiable limits on acceptable human risk during the initial colonization of Mars is not a symptom of bureaucratic cowardice; it is the single most critical safeguard for the survival of the enterprise itself.

The primary flaw in the "risk everything" doctrine is its blindness to historical reality: catastrophes do not accelerate space exploration; they paralyze it. When Apollo 1 burned on the launchpad in 1967, the American lunar program did not bravely surge forward on grit alone—it was grounded for nearly two years while systems were redesigned from scratch. When *Challenger* and *Columbia* disintegrated, the space shuttle fleet was halted for years at a time, bleeding billions of dollars and shattering public and political support. Space exploration does not exist in an ideological vacuum; it operates at the mercy of public trust, political capital, and sustained funding. 

If the inaugural mission to Mars is treated as a high-stakes gamble where fifty-percent mortality is deemed acceptable, the first predictable tragedy will not produce noble martyrs. It will produce a global moral and political backlash capable of shutting down deep-space human exploration for a generation. A crew slowly suffocating due to life-support degradation, succumbing to radiation-induced organ failure, or starving because of agricultural collapse in high-definition video would be the death knell of the interplanetary dream. To protect the mission, we must protect the narrative viability of human spaceflight, and that requires surviving the attempt.

Furthermore, the classic libertarian defense—that fully informed volunteers have the sovereign right to sign their own death warrants in the name of science—collapses under scrutiny. The environment of Mars is unprecedented in its total hostility: cosmic radiation, pervasive perchlorates in the regolith, microgravity-induced neuro-ocular syndrome, and psychological degradation born of unprecedented isolation. In an operational environment where the physiological and psychological stressors are still largely unknown, genuine "informed consent" is a mathematical impossibility. More urgently, a habitat on Mars is not an open frontier where an individual can wander off to fail on their own terms. It is an intensely interdependent, fragile artificial biosphere. The catastrophic illness or cognitive decline of a single crew member endangers the life-support systems, labor pool, and survival of everyone else. Risk on Mars is inherently collective; it cannot be individualized.

Most importantly, establishing strict regulatory ceilings on risk does not hinder innovation—it drives it. Engineering history consistently demonstrates that the most revolutionary breakthroughs occur under the pressure of severe constraints. If mission planners are permitted to treat human life as an expendable margin of error, they will inevitably cut corners on environmental controls, radiation shielding, redundant life-support systems, and automated abort capabilities in the race to be first. Conversely, mandating a rigorous standard of survivability forces the development of the robust, closed-loop technologies truly required for *permanent* habitation. 

Crossing the Atlantic was survivable because the air was breathable and water fell from the sky; Mars offers no such baseline mercy. If our goal is merely a suicide sprint to generate headlines, we can afford to be reckless. But if our goal is to build an enduring civilization beyond Earth, we cannot afford to fail. Hard limits on risk are not the brakes on human destiny—they are the track that ensures the train reaches its destination.

claim: Penguins of all existing species are biologically incapable of self-powered flight.
argument:
To understand why every living penguin species is biologically barred from aerial flight, one must look past the superficial fact that they possess feathers and wings, and instead examine the uncompromising laws of biomechanics. Flight is not merely a behavioral choice that an animal can attempt with sufficient willpower; it is an unforgiving mathematical equation balancing body mass, wing surface area, skeletal density, and muscular output. For penguins, every single variable in that equation has been systematically rewritten by evolution for an entirely different medium: water.

Consider, first, the skeleton. Aerial birds rely on extreme weight reduction. Their bones are pneumatic—honeycombed with air sacs—to allow them to achieve a thrust-to-weight ratio that permits takeoff. Penguins possess the exact opposite. Over tens of millions of years, their bones evolved to become dense, heavy, and solid. This is not an incidental trait; it is a critical physiological requirement. Solid bones act as natural ballast, counteracting positive buoyancy so that penguins can dive hundreds of meters into the ocean without exhausting themselves fighting to submerge. A gentoo or emperor penguin attempting to launch into the air carries a skeletal payload that makes aerodynamic lift physically impossible.

Second, examine the wings. Generating aerodynamic lift requires broad, flexible, cambered surfaces with individual flight feathers that can rotate and part to reduce drag on the upstroke. Penguin wings have completely forfeited this flexibility. Their wing joints are largely fused and rigid, transformed into stiff, bladelike paddles. The long, slotted flight feathers seen in eagles or gulls have been replaced by short, dense, scale-like structures designed exclusively to create a seamless, waterproof seal. While this structure functions flawlessly as a propeller in water—a fluid roughly 800 times denser than air—it cannot generate the dynamic airfoils required to produce lift in the thin medium of the atmosphere. The wing area is simply far too small, and the shape far too rigid, to support their heavy, blubber-insulated bodies.

This is not a matter of speculation; it is confirmed by bioenergetics. Landmark studies on alcids—diving seabirds like the guillemot, which can both fly in the air and dive underwater—have demonstrated the hard energetic wall that governs this evolutionary tradeoff. Research measuring the energy expenditure of these dual-purpose birds revealed that as their wing biomechanics became more efficient for diving, the energetic cost of air flight skyrocketed to the highest ever recorded in flying animals. Biomechanically, there is a distinct threshold where optimizing for deep, efficient diving makes air travel thermodynamically unsustainable. Penguins did not merely approach this boundary; they crossed it entirely, abandoning aerial locomotion in exchange for peerless aquatic mastery.

From the diminutive Little Blue penguin of New Zealand to the massive Emperor of Antarctica, all extant penguin species share this identical, deeply canalized body plan: solid ballast bones, fused flippers incapable of aerodynamic reshaping, massive pectoral muscles locked into an aquatic stroke plane, and a high-density body mass that drastically outstrips their wing surface area. 

Penguins do, in fact, fly—with breathtaking speed, agility, and precision. But they do so exclusively through the dense medium of the sea. To imagine that any living penguin could take to the sky is to ignore the fundamental laws of fluid dynamics: the very adaptations that make them the greatest avian divers on Earth render self-powered aerial flight an absolute biological impossibility.

claim: No limits should be placed on acceptable human risk for initial Mars colonization missions
argument:
Every profound expansion of the human horizon has required a complete departure from the calculus of safety. When Polynesian voyagers set out into the open Pacific with no guarantee of landfall, when Magellan’s fleet sailed with an eighty percent mortality rate, and when Shackleton’s crew ventured into the Antarctic ice, they did not operate under an institutional ceiling of "acceptable risk." Had modern bureaucratic risk thresholds been applied to the age of maritime exploration, the ships would never have left the harbor. The human species would have remained permanently anchored to its cradle.

Mars cannot be settled through the lens of terrestrial occupational safety. An interplanetary mission involves hostile physical realities—deep-space radiation, prolonged microgravity, aerodynamic entry into a rarefied atmosphere, and the unrelenting harshness of an unbreathable, frozen world—that cannot be fully simulated or safeguarded in advance. To mandate an arbitrary ceiling on risk, such as the low-percentage loss-of-crew metrics enforced by modern space agencies, does not make colonization safer; it makes it impossible. A zero-tolerance or capped-risk standard is functionally an indefinite moratorium on human expansion.

Crucially, the decision to venture into the unknown rests upon the foundational principle of human moral agency: informed consent. The men and women who will volunteer for the first missions to Mars will not be conscripts or naive adventurers. They will be world-class scientists, engineers, and aviators who understand the physics, the mathematics, and the lethality of the endeavor better than any ethics board on Earth. To tell a fully informed, sovereign individual that they are forbidden from offering their life to a transcendent human endeavor infantilizes the pioneer. Society routinely respects an individual’s right to accept uncapped risk in other domains—from extreme mountaineering and deep-sea diving to military service in defense of one’s nation. Denying that same autonomy to those who wish to extend the boundary of human civilization is an unprincipled double standard driven by institutional liability, not moral virtue.

Furthermore, the ethical calculus of planetary colonization is not individual; it is civilizational. Humanity exists in a state of perpetual existential fragility, vulnerable to bioweapons, nuclear conflict, ecological collapse, and asteroid impacts. Establishing a self-sustaining outpost on a second world is the only permanent hedge against the total annihilation of human consciousness. When weighed against the survival of human history, art, science, and lineage, the prospective loss of an initial crew—however tragic—is fundamentally immaterial. The risk of inaction is infinite. 

Great frontiers do not yield to caution. They yield to resolve, sacrifice, and the willingness to pay whatever price the cosmos demands. If we place artificial limits on the peril our pioneers are permitted to face, we will guarantee safety at the cost of destiny. The only acceptable limit on risk for the initial colonization of Mars is the limit that the explorers themselves freely choose to accept.

claim: People receiving welfare benefits should be tracked to prevent fraud/abuse.
argument:
A social safety net is only as strong as the public trust that supports it. When a society agrees to tax its working citizens to support those facing hardship, it enters into a dual moral contract: to treat the vulnerable with compassion, and to treat the taxpayer with respect. Implementing robust, transparent tracking mechanisms to verify eligibility and monitor welfare disbursements is not an act of cruelty; it is the single most effective way to protect that social contract.

Skeptics often worry that tracking welfare benefits creates an intrusive, dehumanizing surveillance state that treats poverty as a crime. This concern comes from a good place, but it misunderstands both the scale of modern entitlement spending and the nature of contemporary data oversight. We do not need armed inspectors at people’s doors; we need modern, rigorous digital verification. Every day, legitimate organizations use transaction tracking, data cross-matching, and identity verification to prevent theft and ensure resources reach their intended destination. Applying these basic auditing principles to public assistance is standard fiduciary responsibility.

Consider the true victim of welfare fraud: it is almost never the wealthy taxpayer, who absorbs systemic waste as a marginal line item. The true victim is the person living on the edge of survival. Public resources are fundamentally finite. Every dollar lost to identity theft, duplicate claims, unreported income, or black-market benefit trafficking is a dollar that cannot be used to raise benefit caps, expand childcare subsidies, or support an unhoused family. Fraud shrinks the pool of aid, driving political backlash that often results in across-the-board budget cuts. By contrast, an ironclad tracking system strips away the political ammunition used by those who wish to dismantle welfare programs entirely. When a program can prove, with verifiable data, that it operates cleanly, it gains broad, bipartisan durability.

Furthermore, we readily accept tracking in virtually every other domain involving public funds. University students receiving federal grants are tracked for academic progress and enrollment status. Defense contractors and small businesses receiving federal loans face strict, non-negotiable accounting standards to ensure the public gets what it paid for. Demanding accountability for public assistance is not a punitive measure directed at low-income individuals; it is the universal standard for any entity receiving public money. To exempt welfare from rigorous tracking is to hold social programs to a lower standard of stewardship, which only invites cynicism and neglect.

Finally, modern tracking can be designed to empower recipients rather than marginalize them. Smarter data-sharing between agencies reduces the bureaucratic burden on families, eliminating the need to repeatedly submit paper forms, wait in physical lines, or navigate contradictory rules. An efficient system tracks the flow of aid automatically, spotting anomalies—like syndicated fraud rings or stolen benefit cards—instantly, protecting recipients from predatory exploitation.

Welfare is an investment in human dignity and social stability. But dignity cannot survive without trust, and trust cannot survive without verification. Responsible tracking does not punish poverty; it safeguards compassion by ensuring that every public dollar fulfills its intended, life-changing purpose.

claim: Prescription drug ads should be allowed on television
argument:
It is easy to understand why prescription drug commercials invite cynicism. The rapid-fire recitations of alarming side effects set against idyllic footage of people walking on the beach have made them an easy target for parody and frustration. But looking past the aesthetic annoyances reveals a critical, often overlooked reality: direct-to-consumer advertising democratizes medical knowledge, transforms passive patients into active health advocates, and routinely saves lives by driving underdiagnosed people into the doctor’s office.

For most of modern history, medicine operated under a model of strict paternalism. Patients were expected to passively accept whatever treatment their physician suggested, without the tools, language, or awareness to question options or explore alternatives. Direct-to-consumer advertising broke that information monopoly. By bringing medical science out of specialized journals and into the living room, these advertisements educate the public on the existence of new mechanisms of action, novel therapeutic classes, and advances in managing chronic conditions that general practitioners—who must keep up with thousands of diseases—may not yet have integrated into standard practice.

More importantly, these advertisements act as a catalyst for diagnosis. Millions of people live with treatable symptoms—from chronic insomnia and clinical depression to rheumatoid arthritis and diabetic neuropathy—believing their suffering is merely an inevitable consequence of aging, stress, or personal failing. A television commercial provides a vocabulary for their distress. It tells a viewer that their chronic fatigue might be an autoimmune response, or that their persistent joint pain is not something they simply have to "live with." 

Skeptics often worry that these ads lead to the overprescribing of expensive, unnecessary drugs. Yet the data tells a far more nuanced and reassuring story. An advertisement cannot write a prescription; only a licensed medical professional can. When an informed patient approaches their physician to ask about a drug they saw on television, it initiates a clinical dialogue that might never have occurred otherwise. Multiple studies, including surveys conducted by the FDA, have found that while physicians frequently decline to prescribe the specific brand-name drug a patient asked about, the visit itself regularly leads to the diagnosis of a previously untreated condition, often treated with lifestyle changes or low-cost generics. The commercial served its most vital public health purpose: it brought a sick person into care.

Television advertising has also played an undeniable role in destigmatizing conditions that were once shrouded in shame. Normalizing treatments for mental health disorders, sexual dysfunction, addiction, and bowel diseases on mainstream broadcast networks chips away at social taboos. When an illness is discussed openly during prime-time programming, it sends a powerful message to those suffering in silence that they are neither alone nor broken, and that help exists.

To call for a ban on these advertisements is, at its core, a paternalistic impulse. It operates on the condescending premise that everyday citizens are too gullible, impulsive, or unintelligent to be trusted with information about their own healthcare options. We trust adults to evaluate political candidates, take on mortgages, and make complex decisions about diet and wellness, yet critics argue they must be shielded from knowing what pharmaceuticals exist to treat human illness.

The solution to imperfect advertising is not censorship and ignorance; it is transparency, strict oversight, and clear disclosure of risks—standards that the FDA already enforces rigorously. Patients deserve agency, knowledge, and a seat at the table in their own care. Allowing prescription drug advertising on television ensures that the power to initiate life-changing medical conversations remains where it belongs: in the hands of the patient.

claim: Prescription drug ads should not be allowed on television
argument:
If you travel anywhere in the developed world outside of the United States and New Zealand, you will notice a striking absence on television: no soft-focus commercials featuring silver-haired couples walking on beaches, no upbeat acoustic guitar tracks abruptly paired with a breathless list of catastrophic side effects, and no cheerful directives to “ask your doctor” about a drug you cannot pronounce. 

This absence is not an accident of culture; it is a deliberate, codified safeguard. The rest of the world recognizes an uncomfortable truth that the American broadcast system continues to ignore: prescription medicine cannot function simultaneously as a public health necessity and a consumer retail product.

The primary argument in defense of direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical advertising is empowerment—that it educates patients and encourages them to seek care for untreated conditions. But a commercial is fundamentally incapable of medical education. The medium itself is designed for persuasion, not nuance. Within a sixty-second window, pharmaceutical companies deploy sophisticated behavioral psychology, emotional imagery, and lifestyle branding to engineer demand for a chemical compound. The mandatory recitation of risks—rattled off in a monotonous blur while actors smile over birthday cakes—is not genuine disclosure; it is a calculated attempt to normalize life-threatening side effects as mere background noise. 

This dynamic fundamentally corrodes the doctor-patient relationship. In modern medicine, the physician’s role is to evaluate a patient’s unique physiology, weigh complex clinical trade-offs, and recommend the safest, most cost-effective path forward. Direct-to-consumer advertising subverts this dynamic, transforming the patient into a consumer demanding a specific brand. 

In a healthcare environment where primary care visits are often squeezed into fifteen-minute windows, a doctor faces an unfair dilemma when a patient demands an advertised drug. Dissecting why a heavily marketed, expensive therapy is unnecessary—or inferior to an unadvertised generic or lifestyle change—takes time, emotional energy, and risks alienating the patient. Acquiescing and writing the script takes thirty seconds. Studies consistently confirm that patients who request advertised drugs are significantly more likely to receive them, regardless of clinical suitability. The physician is effectively demoted from an expert diagnostician to an administrative barrier between a consumer and an ad campaign.

The economic fallout of this system burdens everyone. Pharmaceutical companies do not spend billions of dollars on television ad buys out of civic duty; they do it because it generates an extraordinary return on investment by pushing the newest, most expensive, patent-protected drugs over cheaper, equally effective alternatives. These massive marketing budgets do not vanish into the ether—they are baked into the exorbitant cost of prescription drugs and passed along through rising insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs for every taxpayer and patient in the country.

No one is arguing that patients should be kept in the dark about their health. But there is a profound difference between accessible public health education and corporate profit-driven persuasion. True patient empowerment comes from unbiased research, accessible clinical guidance, and robust public health initiatives—not from multi-million-dollar marketing campaigns broadcast between game shows and evening news. 

Prescription drugs are, by legal and medical definition, substances too dangerous to be chosen without an expert intermediary. To market them on television like breakfast cereal or automobiles is an ethical contradiction that drives up costs, compromises clinical judgment, and treats human illness as an advertising demographic. It is time to align with the rest of the world and remove the pharmacy from commercial television.

claim: Raising the minimum wage to $15 would hurt small businesses and jobs.
argument:
The instinct to raise the minimum wage to $15 is rooted in a fundamentally compassionate desire: to ensure that everyone who works can afford a decent standard of living. But good economic policy must be judged by its results rather than its intentions. When examined not through the lens of corporate giants with billions in cash reserves, but through the everyday reality of Main Street businesses, a rigid, blanket $15 minimum wage reveals itself as a blunt instrument that threatens the very workers and local enterprises it aims to protect.

Consider the vast structural difference between a multinational corporation and an independent small business. When a company like Amazon or Target raises wages, it absorbs the cost through immense economies of scale, sophisticated supply chain efficiencies, and deep capital reserves. Often, large retailers actively lobby for higher federal wage floors precisely because they know it creates an insurmountable barrier to entry for their smaller competitors.

For an independent diner, a neighborhood hardware store, or a local dry cleaner, the math is entirely different. Most small businesses operate on razor-thin profit margins, typically between 3% and 7%. Labor is almost always their largest variable expense. When payroll costs jump by 40%, 60%, or even 100% in areas where the previous wage was near the federal baseline of $7.25, that money cannot simply be pulled from an executive bonus pool. 

To survive, a small business owner has only a few levers to pull, and each carries unintended, damaging consequences:

First, they must raise prices. Unlike tech platforms or global retailers, small businesses serve immediate, price-sensitive communities. If the local bakery doubles the cost of a coffee and pastry, customers cut back, revenue falls, and the business’s viability deteriorates.

Second, they must cut costs—starting with labor. This rarely takes the form of a dramatic mass layoff; instead, it happens quietly. It means cutting an employee’s schedule from 35 hours to 24 hours, eliminating overtime, freezing new hires, and requiring the remaining staff to absorb more work. When hours are reduced, a worker with a higher hourly rate often takes home the exact same paycheck—or even less—while carrying more stress. 

Third, and most permanent, it accelerates the replacement of entry-level labor with automation. Self-service kiosks, automated inventory systems, and digital ordering platforms suddenly become cheaper than paying a human worker $15 an hour. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated in its nonpartisan analysis of a federal $15 minimum wage that while millions would see earnings rise, approximately 1.4 million jobs would be permanently eliminated—disproportionately impacting younger, less experienced, and less educated workers.

Finally, a national $15 mandate ignores the fundamental geographic diversity of the American economy. While $15 an hour might be manageable—or even standard—in high-cost urban centers like San Francisco, Seattle, or New York, it is economically devastating in rural Ohio, Mississippi, or upstate New York, where the cost of living and median wages are significantly lower. A federal standard forces low-cost regions into an economic model built for affluent coastal metros, drying up employment opportunities in the areas that need investment the most.

True, durable wage growth does not come from government mandates that outpace productivity; it comes from competitive markets, skills training, and an economic environment where small businesses can flourish and compete for talent. Forcing a uniform $15 wage floor risks trading thousands of real, accessible jobs for an idealized policy goal, leaving Main Street hollowed out and younger workers locked out of the critical first rung of the economic ladder.

claim: Prescription drug importation should be allowed to increase access and lower costs.
argument:
Consider an ordinary blister pack of Eliquis, a common blood thinner. If you purchase it at a pharmacy in Detroit, it costs roughly $550 a month out of pocket. Drive ten minutes across the Ambassador Bridge into Windsor, Ontario, and that identical package, manufactured by the exact same pharmaceutical giant in the exact same facility, costs around $80. 

The pill is not chemically distinct. The blister foil is not different. The only difference is an invisible border—and a legal framework that forces American patients to subsidize the highest profit margins in the world while denying them the basic consumer right to shop elsewhere.

The most persistent objection to prescription drug importation is safety. Skeptics, often echoing pharmaceutical industry talking points, argue that opening borders would invite a flood of counterfeit, adulterated, or improperly stored medications. But this argument fundamentally misunderstands modern drug manufacturing. The domestic pharmaceutical market is already thoroughly globalized. Over 70 percent of the active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) used in American drugs, and roughly half of all finished medications, are manufactured abroad—primarily in India, Europe, and China—and inspected by the FDA. 

To claim that an American cannot safely purchase a drug packaged for Canada, the United Kingdom, or the European Union is to suggest that the regulatory bodies of those nations—Health Canada, the European Medicines Agency, the UK’s MHRA—are dangerously negligent. In truth, their standards for purity, efficacy, and supply-chain integrity are effectively equal to, and often collaborate directly with, the FDA. When a framework allows importation exclusively from heavily regulated, high-standard peer nations, the risk of counterfeit medication is functionally no higher than picking up a prescription at your local neighborhood pharmacy.

What remains, then, is not a question of safety, but of pure market economics. The current ban on personal and wholesale drug importation is an egregious form of state-sanctioned protectionism. It grants pharmaceutical companies a captive domestic audience. In standard market capitalism, when a company inflates prices far beyond production costs, competitors or distributors step in to arbitrage the difference, driving prices down to an equilibrium. By prohibiting importation, the law creates an artificial moat around the United States, effectively criminalizing the free market to protect localized monopoly pricing.

The consequences of this artificial barrier are measured not merely in dollars, but in human suffering. One in four Americans reports skipping doses, splitting pills, or leaving prescriptions unfilled because they cannot afford them. People ration insulin until they slip into diabetic ketoacidosis; cancer patients drain retirement savings to afford maintenance therapies that are sold at a fraction of the cost an hour’s flight away. 

Allowing regulated drug importation is not a radical or untested gamble. It is a proven mechanism. Within the European Union, "parallel trade"—the legal movement of pharmaceuticals between member states to take advantage of price discrepancies—has functioned safely for decades, consistently applying downward pressure on prices without compromising public health.

American patients have funded the research, subsidized the tax breaks, and carried the global burden of pharmaceutical profits for generations. Stripping away the ban on drug importation from peer nations simply introduces the very thing that drives value anywhere else in the economy: competition. It is time to dismantle an artificial blockade that protects corporate balance sheets at the direct expense of American lives.

claim: Recreational drone pilots should be registered and tested
argument:
For decades, remote-controlled aviation meant a balsa-wood glider or a foam airplane flown within line of sight at an empty park. Today, anyone with a few hundred dollars and a smartphone can walk into an electronics store and walk out with an advanced, multi-rotor aircraft capable of climbing thousands of feet, traveling miles away at highway speeds, and carrying substantial payloads. 

The moment a drone leaves the ground, it ceases to be a toy. It enters the national airspace—a complex, shared public infrastructure where the margin for error is measured in human lives.

Skeptics often view registration and testing as bureaucratic overreach designed to stifle a harmless hobby. But consider what is actually at stake. When a recreational drone enters restricted airspace, it is not merely trespassing; it is jeopardizing safety. Drones have grounded aerial firefighting operations during raging wildfires because air-tanker pilots cannot risk a mid-air collision. They have forced international airports to halt departures and arrivals, stranding thousands. Most critically, a multi-pound drone ingested into the engine of a commercial jetliner, or striking the rotor of a low-flying emergency medical helicopter, can result in catastrophic structural failure. In aviation, physics does not distinguish between a commercial payload and a hobbyist's camera.

We do not allow people to drive cars on public roads without demonstrating a basic understanding of traffic laws, nor do we allow individuals to operate motorboats on crowded waterways without fundamental safety education. Why should the third dimension—where there are no guardrails, no painted lanes, and gravity multiplies every hazard—be treated with less care?

Testing does not require a multi-thousand-dollar pilot’s license. A basic, accessible knowledge test simply ensures that an operator understands the fundamentals: maximum altitude ceilings, no-fly zones around airports and critical infrastructure, line-of-sight requirements, and right-of-way rules for manned aircraft. It eliminates the dangerous plea of ignorance. 

Registration, meanwhile, provides the essential foundation of all public safety: accountability. An unmarked aircraft operating anonymously in the sky creates an environment of total impunity. Registration ties a machine to a person, transforming the operator from an invisible spectator into a responsible custodian of the airspace.

Paradoxically, reasonable regulation is the only thing that will protect the future of the hobby itself. If recreational flight remains an unregulated free-for-all, the outcome is predictable: a single horrific disaster—a mid-air collision with a passenger aircraft or a catastrophic crash into a crowded stadium—will provoke an outraged public and a swift, draconian government crackdown that bans consumer drones entirely. 

Testing builds competence; registration builds accountability. Together, they are not barriers to freedom, but the very safeguards that will keep the skies open for everyone.

claim: Recreational drone pilots should not require registration and testing
argument:
For nearly a century, millions of enthusiasts built and flew remote-controlled aircraft—balsa-wood gliders, miniature gas-powered biplanes, and model helicopters—without a single federal registry, mandatory government exam, or bureaucratic database. The skies did not fall. Catastrophic mid-air collisions did not materialize. Communities governed themselves through local flying clubs, common sense, and the shared etiquette of the hobby. 

Today’s impulse to mandate registration and standardized testing for recreational drone pilots is a classic case of regulatory overreach driven by novelty bias, not demonstrable risk. By treating casual hobbyists like commercial aviators, we have constructed a burdensome regime of security theater that does nothing to enhance public safety while actively strangling innovation and youth engagement in aerospace.

Consider the reality of what a recreational drone actually is. The vast majority are small, lightweight devices made of lightweight plastic and foam, equipped with automatic hover capabilities, return-to-home fail-safes, and geofencing technology. To suggest that a teenager flying a camera drone in an open park requires a federal registration number and a government-sanctioned aeronautical knowledge test assumes a level of inherent danger that simply does not exist. A high-speed baseball, a golf ball, or a falling tree branch carries equal or greater kinetic energy than the typical recreational quadcopter, yet we do not require registration to buy a bat or a nine-iron.

Proponents argue that testing and registration foster accountability and prevent airspace disasters. But this misunderstands how human behavior works. Bureaucracy does not deter malice or gross negligence; it only inconveniences the law-abiding. A reckless individual intent on flying a drone near an airport or over a stadium will not be stopped by a digital multiple-choice exam or an FAA tracking number. Meanwhile, the legal framework to punish dangerous behavior already exists. Trespassing, reckless endangerment, invasion of privacy, and interfering with aircraft are all serious crimes with severe, pre-existing legal penalties. We regulate the *harm*, not the hobby. 

Worse, mandatory red tape creates a damaging chilling effect on the very pipeline that feeds our future technological workforce. For generations, model aviation has been the gateway drug to STEM careers: the spark that turned curious children into aerospace engineers, computer scientists, and commercial pilots. When we place barriers between a young person and their first flying machine—whether it is a government database, parental consent forms for federal registration, or mandatory aeronautical exams—we transform what should be a spontaneous moment of discovery into an intimidating administrative chore. We teach aspiring inventors that experimentation is something that requires prior permission from the state.

Public safety is paramount, but true safety is achieved through proportionate, risk-based rules. Commercial operators, who fly heavier payloads over crowded urban areas for profit, naturally require oversight. But for the weekend hobbyist, the current system is an answer in search of a problem. Decentralized community standards, built-in manufacturer safety software, and existing criminal statutes already provide all the protection the public needs. 

It is time to strip away the unnecessary red tape. Abolishing mandatory testing and registration for recreational drone pilots would not compromise our airspace; it would simply restore proportionality, trust ordinary citizens, and allow the next generation of aviators to take flight unencumbered.

claim: Requiring all police officers to wear body cameras should not be mandated
argument:
The push to mandate body-worn cameras for every police officer in the country is fueled by an understandable, noble impulse: the desire for transparency, accountability, and objective truth in an era of fraught community-police relations. On its face, the camera appears to be an unassailable solution—a neutral mechanical eye that protects the public from abuse and protects officers from false accusations. 

Yet, when we move past the appealing simplicity of the sales pitch, the reality of a universal, one-size-fits-all mandate collapses under the weight of severe constitutional, financial, and structural consequences. Mandating body cameras for all officers is not merely an imperfect fix; it is a profound policy miscalculation that trades civil liberties and vital community resources for the illusion of accountability.

First and most critically, a universal mandate creates a pervasive surveillance apparatus directed not at the state, but at the private citizen. Police officers do not spend their days exclusively patrolling public sidewalks; they enter private residences during domestic disputes, respond to horrific medical emergencies, encounter victims of sexual assault in shock, and intervene in acute mental health crises. Under a blanket mandate, the state’s lens is forced into living rooms, bedrooms, and the most humiliating, vulnerable moments of ordinary people’s lives. Because this footage frequently becomes subject to public records requests, the privacy rights of victims, juveniles, and bystanders are systematically compromised. Vulnerable citizens, fearing that their trauma will be permanently digitized and potentially leaked, become hesitant to call 911 in the first place.

Second, the universal mandate is an extraordinary financial windfall for private tech monopolies at the direct expense of meaningful public safety investments. The most significant cost of body cameras is not the hardware pinned to an officer’s chest; it is the staggering, perpetual cost of cloud storage, proprietary software licenses, evidence management, and the legions of personnel required to review and redact thousands of hours of video for public release. For small towns and cash-strapped urban departments alike, these multi-million-dollar contracts create massive budgetary black holes. Every dollar funneled to surveillance conglomerates like Axon is a dollar stripped away from evidence-based violence interruption programs, non-armed mental health response units, intensive de-escalation training, and deep systemic oversight. We are starving genuine reform to feed a digital archive.

Third, video does not offer the objective truth that the public has been promised. An optical lens possesses intrinsic technical limitations: a narrow field of view, no depth perception, low-light distortion, and the inability to capture tactile threats or peripheral events that an officer or citizen actually experienced. Studies in cognitive science have repeatedly shown that two people watching the exact same body-camera footage will arrive at radically different conclusions based on their preexisting biases. By elevating video footage as the supreme arbiter of justice, we cultivate a dangerous "video-or-it-didn't-happen" culture that discounts human testimony, while simultaneously creating a false sense of certainty out of fragmented, two-dimensional recordings.

Finally, a rigid mandate damages the very community relationships that effective policing relies upon. The foundation of community-oriented policing is human trust, discretion, and informal communication. When every interaction is mandated to be recorded, an officer’s ability to exercise leniency—such as letting a troubled teenager off with a stern warning rather than entering them into the criminal justice system—is severely chilled by fear of administrative micro-management. Furthermore, informants, victims, and neighborhood residents who wish to share sensitive information off-the-record will simply walk away if they see a red recording light blinking on an officer’s chest. The camera interposes a cold, bureaucratic barrier between the officer and the neighborhood, transforming public servants into robotic agents of evidence collection.

Accountability is a cultural, legal, and institutional challenge; it cannot be outsourced to a camera lens. By treating body cameras as a universal panacea rather than a situational tool to be deployed thoughtfully and selectively, we surrender civil privacy, enrich surveillance contractors, and divert resources from the structural reforms our communities desperately need. Blanket mandates should be rejected in favor of local, tailored policies that prioritize human trust over digital surveillance.

claim: Self-driving cars will increase safety and should replace human drivers.
argument:
Every year, roughly 1.3 million people die in automobile crashes worldwide. In the United States alone, traffic fatalities consistently hover around 40,000 annually—the equivalent of a fully loaded commercial airliner falling out of the sky every single day of the year. 

If any other consumer technology, from commercial aviation to smart home appliances, produced a casualty rate remotely approaching this, the public would demand an immediate, nationwide shutdown. Yet because we have lived with the automobile for over a century, we have normalized an ongoing public health catastrophe. We treat these deaths not as systemic failures, but as the unavoidable cost of mobility.

They are not unavoidable. They are the direct consequence of human biology.

The overwhelming majority of serious motor vehicle crashes—roughly 94 percent, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration—are caused by human error. We drink, we text, we fall asleep, we succumb to road rage, and we glance away from the road for two seconds to adjust the air conditioning. Even at our absolute best, our reaction time is constrained by the speed of biological neural impulses—roughly a tenth of a second at peak alertness. At highway speeds, that delay means traveling dozens of feet before a foot even touches the brake pedal.

To ask whether autonomous vehicles are perfect is to ask the wrong question. Perfection is not on the ballot; the alternative is human drivers, who are catastrophic. The real question is whether autonomous systems are fundamentally capable of doing the job better. The answer is unequivocally yes.

An autonomous vehicle does not drive drunk. It does not check a notification, look into the rearview mirror to discipline a child, or speed through a yellow light because it is running late for a meeting. Its perception is not limited to two forward-facing eyes with a blind spot over each shoulder; it utilizes a 360-degree, overlapping array of LiDAR, radar, and high-resolution cameras that perceive depth, velocity, and distance hundreds of times per second. It can detect a pedestrian stepping out from behind a parked van in pitch-black darkness, predict the trajectory, and apply the brakes long before a human brain could register a shadow.

Skeptics often fixate on rare, high-profile accidents involving autonomous test vehicles, concluding that the technology is untrustworthy. But this reaction reveals a profound psychological bias: we instinctively prefer a familiar danger over an unfamiliar one, and we fear the illusion of losing control far more than we fear statistical reality. When a human kills a family because of a text message, it barely makes the local evening news—it is a routine tragedy. When a self-driving car misidentifies an obstacle, it generates international headlines. Yet empirical data from millions of commercial autonomous miles already demonstrates that autonomous systems generate dramatically fewer injury-causing crashes per mile than human-piloted vehicles operating in the same environments.

Furthermore, autonomous vehicles possess an evolutionary advantage that humans never will: collective memory. 

When a human driver spends forty years behind the wheel and avoids an accident through sheer luck or instinct, that knowledge dies with them. Every sixteen-year-old begins from scratch, making the exact same lethal mistakes as previous generations. Autonomous vehicles, by contrast, operate on a shared, continuously updating fleet intelligence. When one vehicle encounters a novel hazard—a bizarre construction zone, unusual glare, or an erratic cyclist—the data is analyzed, a solution is coded into the software, and overnight, every vehicle in the entire fleet instantly learns how to handle that situation. Safety does not reset with each new car; it compounds infinitely.

We have seen this transition before. We once entrusted the safety of elevators to human operators, convinced that a mechanical lever operated by a living person was safer than an automated button. Today, the idea of requiring a human operator to move a box between floors seems absurd. We automated the system, eliminated human error, and elevator travel became one of the safest modes of transportation on earth.

Driving will follow the exact same trajectory. We are not being asked to surrender our freedom; we are being offered liberation from the leading cause of preventable, violent death for young people in the modern world. In a generation, our children will look back at old footage of highways packed with tired, distracted humans hurtling two-ton metal cages past one another at seventy miles per hour, inches apart, separated only by painted yellow lines. They will view it not with nostalgia, but with horror—and wonder why it took us so long to stop the carnage.

claim: Smartphones/social media should be banned for kids under 16
argument:
Every generation of parents faces a new technology they are told to fear, from the printing press to comic books to television. It is tempting, therefore, to dismiss the alarm over smartphones and social media as just another cycle of moral panic. 

That dismissal, however, rests on a fundamental category error. Television was passive. Comic books did not follow children into their bedrooms at 2:00 a.m. Neither employed thousands of the world’s most sophisticated behavioral engineers using machine-learning algorithms to optimize for one specific metric: the continuous extraction of human attention.

We are currently running an uncontrolled psychological experiment on an entire generation, and the results are already in. Beginning around 2012—the precise moment when smartphones became ubiquitous and social media shifted to algorithmic feeds—rates of adolescent depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicide began a historic, unprecedented ascent across the developed world. This is not a correlation waiting for an alternative explanation; it is a direct biological consequence of replacing the physical, play-based childhood with a screen-based childhood defined by perpetual social comparison, sleep deprivation, and fragmented attention.

The most common objection to a legal age minimum of 16 is that this should be left to "parental responsibility." But this argument ignores the brutal reality of the collective action problem. When an entire peer group lives on Instagram and TikTok, a parent who says "no" is not simply restricting screen time; they are effectively exiling their child from their social ecosystem. Parents are trapped in an arms race: surrender your child’s mental health to the algorithm, or surrender their social belonging. Individual households cannot fight multi-trillion-dollar corporations designed to addict their children. A legal baseline solves this coordination failure instantly, giving parents the collective cover to do what most desperately want to do anyway.

Skeptics also argue that kids need phones for logistics and physical safety—calling for a ride, checking in after practice. But we must distinguish between communication and algorithmic capture. A sixteen-year-old cutoff does not mean a child cannot have a basic phone capable of voice calls, SMS, and GPS. What it eliminates is the hyper-stimulating, algorithmic portal in their pocket. Safety requires communication; it does not require an infinite scroll engineered to keep a twelve-year-old awake until dawn.

Finally, consider our legal precedents. We do not allow fourteen-year-olds to purchase cigarettes, drink alcohol, enter casinos, or drive cars. We do not do this because we want to arbitrarily restrict their freedom, but because we recognize that the human brain’s prefrontal cortex—the center of impulse control, long-term planning, and risk assessment—is not fully developed until the mid-twenties. It is irrational to acknowledge that a child lacks the neurological maturity to gamble with money, yet allow them free rein to gamble with their self-worth, mental stability, and dopamine pathways against algorithms more powerful than any casino game on Earth.

Restricting smartphones and social media until 16 is not an authoritarian overreach; it is a long-overdue child labor law for the attention economy. By establishing a firm, society-wide boundary, we are not sheltering our children from the modern world—we are giving them the developmental runway they need to survive it.
