claim: Apples are a type of fruit.
argument:
If you doubt that apples are a type of fruit, you are not really doubting apples—you are doubting what the word “fruit” means. And once you look at the definition, the case is closed.

Botanically, a fruit is the seed-bearing structure that develops from the ovary of a flowering plant. That is not a matter of opinion; it is basic plant anatomy. An apple begins as a flower. After pollination, the ovary at the base of that flower swells, its tissues thicken and become fleshy, and inside it form the seeds. The result—the apple—is exactly what botany calls a fruit. More precisely, it is a pome: a specific type of fruit in which the ovary develops into the core and surrounding floral tissue becomes the edible flesh. A pome is not an alternative to fruit; it is a subtype of fruit. So apples are not merely “like” fruit or “used as” fruit. They are fruit by definition.

Now consider ordinary language. Walk into any grocery store, open any cookbook, read any nutrition guide, or ask any child what an apple is. It is a fruit. It is sweet, fleshy, seed-bearing, and eaten as a fruit. It appears in fruit bowls, fruit salads, fruit pies, and fruit juices. No one says “apple vegetable” or “apple grain” or “apple nut.” The word “fruit” is the only everyday category that fits.

You might object that some foods—like tomatoes—are botanically fruits but culinarily vegetables. That is true, and it shows that categories can overlap. But it does not help the skeptic here, because apples are fruit in both senses. Botanically, they are pomes. Culinarily, they are fruits. Nutritionally, they are fruits. There is no competing category waiting to claim them. If apples are not fruit, what are they? A vegetable? Vegetables are typically roots, stems, leaves, or flowers—not seed-bearing ovaries. A nut? Nuts are hard-shelled fruits or seeds, not fleshy pomes. A seed? An apple contains seeds; it is not itself a seed. Every alternative collapses.

So the conclusion is unavoidable. The apple develops from a flower, contains seeds, is classified by botanists as a pome, is treated as a fruit in kitchens and markets, and has no coherent place in any other category. Apples are a type of fruit—not by convention alone, but by structure, function, and universal usage. To deny it, you would have to reject botany, common language, and common sense at the same time. The only reasonable position is the obvious one: apples are fruit.

claim: By definition, one liter in the metric system equals 1,000 milliliters.
argument:
You don’t have to trust scientists, meters, or beakers to know this. You only have to understand what the words mean. “Milli-” is not a vague suggestion; it is a metric prefix fixed by international agreement to mean one thousandth, or \(10^{-3}\). A milliliter, therefore, is literally a thousandth of a liter. If something is a thousandth of a liter, then a liter contains exactly one thousand of them. That is not a measurement result; it is the definition restated.

If you resist, consider what you’d be denying. To say \(1 \text{ L} \neq 1000 \text{ mL}\), you’d have to say “milli-” sometimes doesn’t mean thousandth, or “liter” doesn’t mean liter. But then \(1 \text{ meter}\) is not \(1000 \text{ millimeters}\), \(1 \text{ gram}\) is not \(1000 \text{ milligrams}\), and \(1 \text{ second}\) is not \(1000 \text{ milliseconds}\). The metric system would cease to be a system. Its entire genius is that prefixes attach to units by powers of ten: kilo- = 1000, centi- = 0.01, milli- = 0.001. You don’t need a new conversion for each pair; you just move the decimal.

You can even see it without a beaker. A liter is defined as the volume of a cube 10 centimeters on each side. That cube’s volume is \(10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000\) cubic centimeters. A cubic centimeter is defined as a milliliter. So the cube is 1000 milliliters. The same cube is 1 liter. Therefore \(1 \text{ liter} = 1000 \text{ milliliters}\).

This is the strongest kind of truth: an identity built into the language of measurement. It cannot be falsified by experiment because it is not an empirical guess. It is what the words mean. The only way to get a different answer is to stop speaking the metric system. So if you’re skeptical, be skeptical of any claim that says otherwise. One liter equals exactly one thousand milliliters—by definition, and therefore without exception.

claim: All police officers should be required to wear body cameras
argument:
If you trust the police, body cameras are the best way to prove you’re right. If you don’t, they’re the best way to find out. Either way, the case for requiring every officer to wear one is not a concession to police critics or a burden on good cops. It is a demand for truth—the one thing both sides of this debate should want.

A police officer carries a badge, a radio, a gun, and the power to take someone’s liberty or life. That power is necessary, but it is also extraordinary. When it is exercised, the public deserves more than a memory contest afterward. Today, too many encounters end in dueling accounts: the officer says one thing, the civilian says another, and the community is left to decide who to believe. Body cameras replace that fog with evidence. They do not decide guilt or innocence. They show what happened. That is the minimum standard for a democratic society that asks its citizens to obey the law.

The evidence from places that have adopted cameras is striking. In Rialto, California, after body cameras were introduced, complaints against officers fell by roughly 88 percent and use-of-force incidents dropped by nearly 60 percent. The Cambridge University study of the same department found similar results. Why? Because cameras change behavior on both sides of the lens. Officers know their actions will be reviewed, so they often de-escalate sooner. Civilians know they are being recorded, so they are less likely to lie, resist, or make false accusations. The camera is not just a check on police power. It is a shield for officers who do their jobs correctly and then get accused of something they didn’t do.

That is the point skeptics too often miss. If you believe most officers are honorable professionals, you should want them to have an unblinking witness. A false complaint can destroy a career, a family, and a department’s morale. Body camera footage can clear an officer in minutes. It can also prevent a baseless lawsuit from costing taxpayers millions. The same tool that holds bad officers accountable protects good ones. That is not anti-police. It is pro-police, and it is pro-public.

Some argue that cameras are expensive. But compare the cost of a camera to the cost of a misconduct settlement, a wrongful-death lawsuit, or a community that no longer trusts its police. A body camera costs a few hundred dollars. A single settlement can cost millions. The question is not whether we can afford cameras. It is whether we can afford to keep operating without them. The expense of transparency is real, but the expense of opacity is paid in money, in trust, and sometimes in lives.

Others raise privacy concerns. Those concerns are legitimate, but they are not an argument against cameras. They are an argument for good policies. Police officers do not have an absolute expectation of privacy while performing public duties in public spaces. Their conduct is already subject to public scrutiny, internal review, and legal discovery. What cameras change is that the scrutiny becomes accurate instead of speculative. We can protect the privacy of victims, children, witnesses, and bystanders through redaction, retention limits, and controlled access. We can require cameras to be turned off during sensitive interviews and strip searches. What we should not do is let privacy become a shield for misconduct. The public’s right to know how its agents use force is not a minor interest. It is a foundational one.

Some officers worry that cameras will be used to second-guess every decision. But officers are already second-guessed. They are second-guessed by supervisors, lawyers, journalists, juries, and the public. The difference is that with cameras, they are second-guessed with evidence. A camera does not replace an officer’s judgment. It documents it. It shows the split-second decision, the context, the threat, the warning, the escalation. In many cases, that footage is the strongest possible defense of an officer’s conduct.

Voluntary cameras are not enough. If cameras are optional, they will be used selectively. Officers who want protection will turn them on. Officers who don’t will find reasons to leave them off. Departments will avoid transparency while claiming to support it. A mandate with clear activation rules, tamper-proof storage, and real penalties for failing to record is the only way to make the system trustworthy. Exceptions should be narrow—undercover work, certain tactical operations—and those exceptions should be audited, not assumed.

The final question is simple: what kind of policing do we want? One that depends on blind trust, or one that earns trust through evidence? We already require officers to carry guns, radios, and badges. We should require them to carry the one tool that records what happens when they use them. The body camera is not a burden. It is a witness. Requiring every officer to wear one is not a vote of no confidence in the police. It is a vote of confidence in the truth—and in a public that has the right to see it.

claim: By its very definition in the metric system, one meter consists of 100 centimeters.
argument:
Consider what it would mean to deny this. The metric system is not a loose collection of labels; it is a decimal architecture built from exact prefixes. The prefix “centi-” comes from the Latin centum, meaning hundred, and in the International System of Units it is defined as exactly \(10^{-2}\). A centimeter is therefore not a separate unit whose relationship to the meter must be discovered, measured, or voted on. It is the meter scaled by one hundredth.

That gives us the definition directly:

\[
1\ \text{cm} = 0.01\ \text{m}
\]

Multiply both sides by 100:

\[
100\ \text{cm} = 1\ \text{m}
\]

This is not a physical law subject to experimental revision. It is an identity, like 100 cents = 1 dollar or 100 years = 1 century. If you measured a particular meter stick and found it was 99.998 cm long, you would not have disproved the definition. You would have found that the stick is not exactly one meter, or that your measurement has error. The definition remains the fixed rule that makes the word “centimeter” meaningful in the first place.

To reject “one meter consists of 100 centimeters” is to reject the meaning of “centi-” and the entire decimal logic of the metric system. The only consistent alternative is to stop using “centimeter” to mean one hundredth of a meter—and at that point you are no longer talking about the metric system at all. So yes: exactly, by definition, one meter’s length is 100 centimeters.

claim: Banning gas car sales too soon is unrealistic
argument:
You care about the climate. So do I. That is exactly why I am asking you to look past the slogan and at the system. A ban on new gas car sales is not a light switch. It is a promise that the entire machinery of daily life—charging, grid, mining, manufacturing, housing, used cars, repair shops, rural roads—will be ready on a date chosen by politicians. If that machinery is not ready, the ban does not reduce emissions. It just makes the transition look like a failure, and failure is the one thing we cannot afford.

Too soon means before the alternatives are affordable, available, and practical for the people who must buy them. That is not a moral judgment about electric cars. It is a physical and economic one.

Start with the infrastructure. You cannot drive an electric car if you cannot charge it. In the United States, there are roughly 170,000 public charging ports. The National Renewable Energy Laboratory estimates that to support a largely electric fleet by 2030, the country would need something like 1.2 million. That is not a gap you close with a press release. It means transformers, permits, wiring, parking lots, apartment buildings, highway corridors, and a grid that can handle the load. Transmission lines and substations often take a decade to plan, approve, and build. If you ban gas cars before that, you do not get a clean fleet. You get people fighting over broken chargers, rolling up to crowded stations, and deciding the whole thing was a scam.

Then look at the supply chain. Batteries require lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and refined materials. New mines take ten to fifteen years to come online. Refining capacity is concentrated in a handful of countries. Automakers can announce factories faster than they can build them, and they can build factories faster than they can secure minerals. A too-soon ban does not conjure those minerals. It creates shortages, price spikes, and a black market for exactly the gas cars you tried to outlaw.

Now think about the people who actually have to live under the rule. A nurse in a rural county with an eighty-mile commute and no driveway cannot charge at home. A renter in a city apartment cannot run a cord across the sidewalk. A contractor towing a trailer needs a truck that can work all day; many electric trucks cost far more than their gas equivalents and lose a huge share of range under load or in cold weather. A family shopping for a used car at $12,000 is not choosing between a Tesla and a Corolla. They are choosing between a Corolla and keeping the old car another five years. If you ban new gas cars too soon, you do not force that family into an EV. You raise the price of used gas cars, extend the life of the dirtiest vehicles, and make mobility more expensive for the people least able to pay. That is not a climate policy. It is a regressive tax on getting to work.

And here is the paradox: even a perfectly enforced ban on new gas car sales would not remove the gas cars already on the road. The average car in the United States is over twelve years old. If every new car sold in 2030 were electric, millions of gas cars would still be burning fuel into the 2040s. The climate benefit comes from actually replacing them, not from declaring them illegal. If the replacement is unaffordable or impractical, people hold on to what they have. The ban becomes a symbol that changes nothing.

You might say: the climate crisis is urgent, and we cannot wait for perfect conditions. True. But urgency is a reason to be effective, not a reason to be symbolic. A too-soon ban is a bluff, and bluffs get called. We have already seen it. The United Kingdom pushed its 2030 ban back to 2035. The European Union’s 2035 rule had to carve out an exemption for e-fuels after political backlash. Fuel tax protests have toppled governments. When mandates outrun public consent, they are repealed, delayed, or ignored. Then you lose not only the policy but the credibility of the entire transition. You hand a weapon to every politician who wants to say, “See? They are coming for your car.” A realistic plan locks in progress. An unrealistic one creates a backlash that sets progress back a decade.

None of this means we should give up. It means we should sequence the transition like adults. Build the charging network first. Modernize the grid. Subsidize affordable EVs for low- and middle-income drivers. Invest in battery recycling and domestic refining. Set clean fuel standards and a rising carbon price that make the market move without pretending everyone can switch overnight. Then set the ban—or better, a performance standard that phases out gas sales by region, vehicle class, and readiness. Make the ban conditional on benchmarks: charging access, affordability, grid capacity, mineral supply. That is not weakness. That is how you make a rule that sticks.

The goal is not to keep gas cars forever. The goal is to retire them for good. A ban too soon does not retire them. It gives the transition a reputation for failure, punishes the people who can least afford it, and invites the backlash that keeps gas cars on the road longer. The realistic path is ambitious, funded, and fair. It starts with infrastructure and affordability, and it lets the calendar follow the concrete. The other way around is not courage. It is a promise you cannot keep.

claim: Anti-aging therapies should be made available even if expensive
argument:
Imagine a therapy that could cut your risk of Alzheimer’s, heart attack, cancer, and frailty by half. It costs $50,000 a year at first. Should it be banned? Should regulators say, “Come back when it’s cheap enough for everyone”? That sounds noble until you realize what it means: everyone who could have been saved dies while we wait for perfect justice. The history of medicine is a history of expensive breakthroughs becoming affordable. HIV drugs once cost more than $10,000 per year; generic regimens now cost under $100. Hepatitis C cures launched at $84,000; generics are under $100 in many countries. Genome sequencing went from billions of dollars to hundreds. Prices fall because of scale, competition, generics, and innovation. If we prohibit or delay a therapy because its first price is high, we destroy the very engine that lowers the price. We do not get a cheaper version later; we get no version at all.

The objection is inequality. But consider the alternative. If only wealthy people can afford a therapy today, that is unjust. But if no one can, the poor are not better off—they are equally dead. Banning an expensive therapy does not transfer a single dose to someone who cannot afford it. It simply ensures that no one benefits, and that the research base, safety data, and manufacturing capacity never grow. The road to broad access runs through availability, not prohibition. Let it be approved, prescribed, and sold. Then use taxes, subsidies, insurance, price negotiation, public manufacturing, and patent buyouts to widen access. But you cannot redistribute a medicine you refuse to allow.

There is also a deeper principle: bodily autonomy. If a competent adult wants to spend their own money on a therapy that regulators have deemed safe, the state should not stop them merely because others cannot afford it. We do not ban private education, cosmetic surgery, or expensive cancer drugs because they are not equally accessible. We regulate safety; we do not criminalize wealth. Prohibition would not stop demand. It would drive anti-aging therapies into black markets, medical tourism, and unregulated clinics where desperate people take unknown risks. Legal, expensive, monitored use is far safer than cheap, illegal, unmonitored use.

And aging is not vanity. It is the largest risk factor for the diseases that fill hospitals and nursing homes: dementia, cancer, heart disease, stroke, frailty. A therapy that slows aging is not a luxury; it is preventive medicine on a civilizational scale. Even if early versions are expensive, every patient treated adds knowledge, improves protocols, and reduces future costs. Healthy longevity could keep people productive, independent, and out of long-term care, expanding the economic base that can pay for broader access. The choice is not between “rich people live longer” and “everyone lives longer.” It is between “some people live longer and we learn how to make it cheaper” and “everyone ages and dies while we wait for a miracle that is politically pure.”

So yes: make anti-aging therapies available even if expensive. Not because the first generation will be fair, but because blocking them guarantees the one outcome no one should accept: no progress at all. Approve them, regulate them, let the market and science drive prices down, and fight for access with every tool we have. To do otherwise is to let our aversion to inequality become a death sentence for everyone.

claim: Basing decisions on credit scores and models is discriminatory.
argument:
Imagine two people apply for a loan. Both earn $50,000. Both pay rent on time. One is a white man whose parents co-signed his first credit card and helped him buy a car. The other is a Black woman whose parents were redlined out of mortgages, who has medical debt from an emergency room visit, and who has never had a credit card because no bank in her neighborhood would offer one without a deposit she couldn’t afford. The first has a 780 credit score. The second has a 580. The lender says the score is objective. But what the score actually measures is the distance between their starting lines.

This is why basing decisions on credit scores and models is discriminatory. Not because the algorithm explicitly asks for race, but because it uses variables that are soaked in racial and economic inequality. Credit scores are not measures of trustworthiness or financial responsibility. They are measures of how well someone has navigated a credit system that has been rigged for generations. They reward people who already had access to credit and punish people who were excluded from it.

The disparities are well documented. Black and Hispanic Americans have lower average credit scores than white Americans. They are more likely to be “credit invisible”—the CFPB found 26 million Americans with no credit history, disproportionately Black and Hispanic. Majority-Black neighborhoods have lower median credit scores than majority-white neighborhoods, even after controlling for income. Medical debt, student debt, and eviction records—all of which can wreck a score—fall harder on Black, Latino, disabled, and low-income communities. A single hospital bill can drop a score by 100 points. A paid-off collection can linger for years. The score doesn’t know why you were poor; it only knows you were.

Under civil rights law, that is discrimination. The Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibit not only intentional discrimination but also neutral practices that have a discriminatory effect—disparate impact. In 2015, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that principle in Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project. A landlord or lender cannot say, “I didn’t mean to discriminate,” if their use of a credit score systematically excludes protected groups. Intent is not the test. Effect is.

You might object that lenders need to predict risk. Of course they do. But risk is not a natural fact. It is a social product. If a group was denied mortgages for decades, denied small business loans, denied access to banks, then of course they have thinner credit files and lower scores. Using that history as a reason to deny them credit today is circular. It punishes them for the discrimination they already suffered. That is not risk management; it is the engine of inherited disadvantage.

And credit scores are not the only way. Underwriters can look at rental payment history, utility payments, cash flow data, and manual review. Community lenders have done this for years. Some of these alternatives are less discriminatory and more accurate. The choice to rely on a three-digit number is not inevitable. It is a choice—and it has consequences.

Those consequences are not limited to lending. Credit checks are used in hiring, housing, insurance, and utilities. An employer may see a 580 and assume irresponsibility, even if the score reflects a medical crisis or a predatory loan. A landlord may deny an apartment, pushing someone into a worse neighborhood or homelessness. An insurer may charge more for auto or home coverage. In these contexts, the risk rationale is even weaker. A credit score is not a job qualification or a measure of driving skill. It is a gatekeeper that keeps people out of the opportunities that would let them improve their credit.

Credit scores feel fair because they are numbers. But math can encode injustice. A model trained on a discriminatory past will predict a discriminatory future. Until we repair the underlying inequities—or stop using biased proxies to allocate life’s necessities—basing decisions on credit scores and models is discriminatory. Calling it “objective” doesn’t change that. Calling it “risk” doesn’t make it just.

claim: Charter schools divert public funds away from traditional public schools.
argument:
Follow the money. In nearly every state, public education is funded through a per-pupil formula: the state sets an amount for each student, and that amount follows the student to whatever school they attend. When a student enrolls in a charter school, that per-pupil funding—or a large share of it—is deducted from the traditional public school district’s state aid and sent to the charter. This is not a metaphor or a talking point. It is a line item in state budgets. The district does not keep the money and also receive new money for the charter. The same education dollar is redirected. That is what “divert” means.

Now consider what happens to the district left behind. Imagine a district with 1,000 students and $10,000 in public funding per pupil. It has $10 million. Then 100 students leave for charter schools. The district loses $1 million. But can it cut 10 percent of its costs overnight? Almost never. It still has the same buildings, the same debt, the same central office, the same buses, the same nurses, the same special education programs, and the same pension obligations. It may not be able to close a single school or eliminate a single bus route. So the remaining 900 students must absorb the loss. That is roughly $1,111 less per student—not because those students suddenly cost less, but because the money left with the charter students while the costs stayed behind.

This squeeze is even tighter because charter schools, on average, enroll fewer students with severe disabilities, fewer English language learners, and fewer students with behavioral or homelessness challenges. Those students remain in district schools, where the costs of serving them are higher. The district loses the average per-pupil dollar but keeps the above-average-cost student. It is a double drain: less revenue, more concentrated need.

You might object that charter schools are public schools too, so this is simply public money for public education. But that is exactly the point. Charter schools are not funded by a separate, parallel tax. They are funded from the same finite pool. If you add a charter seat, you subtract from the district’s pool. If you expand charters, you expand that subtraction. You can believe charters are excellent and still recognize the fiscal reality: every charter dollar is a dollar that does not go to the traditional public school district.

Some argue that competition forces districts to improve. Even if that were always true, it would not change the fact that the improvement is being demanded while resources are being removed. A lifeboat can be well-built and still take water from the ship. The question is not whether charters are public or private, good or bad. The question is where the money comes from. It comes from traditional public schools.

Temporary transition aid, where it exists, is usually too small and too short to cover fixed costs. Facilities aid for charters can add another layer of diversion. And districts often must maintain excess capacity in case charter students return. The result is predictable: larger classes, fewer counselors, cut arts and athletics, deferred maintenance, and shrinking support for the students who need the most.

So the claim is not anti-charter rhetoric. It is arithmetic. As long as education dollars are finite and charter funding is drawn from the same per-pupil stream, charter schools divert public funds away from traditional public schools. The only remaining debate is how much harm that diversion causes—and who is left to absorb it.

claim: Climate geoengineering research should be pursued as a potential solution.
argument:
You are right to be suspicious of geoengineering. The idea that we can engineer our way out of a crisis we created is exactly the kind of hubris that got us here. But suspicion should lead us to study, not to look away. The choice is not between a clean, safe world and a geoengineered one. It is between a world where we understand our options and a world where we stumble into them blind.

Start with the brutal arithmetic. The planet has already warmed about 1.2°C. Current policies put us on track for roughly 2.5–2.9°C by 2100. Even the most optimistic mitigation pathways involve overshoot. The IPCC’s 1.5°C scenarios rely on carbon dioxide removal—sometimes billions of tonnes per year by mid-century. That is not an endorsement of a techno-fix; it is a statement of mathematical necessity. If we do not know which CDR methods work, how much land and energy they require, and who will bear the costs, we cannot plan a livable future.

Solar radiation modification is stranger and riskier. But we already know it can cool the planet: Mount Pinatubo injected aerosols into the stratosphere and cooled Earth by about 0.5°C for a year. That does not mean we should do it. It means we need to know what would happen if we did—or if someone else does. In 2021, the U.S. National Academies recommended a $100–200 million research program on SRM. The Royal Society and the IPCC have similarly called for research. Not deployment. Research.

Critics say research creates moral hazard. It can. But so does ignorance. If we refuse to study geoengineering, we do not eliminate the temptation—we just hand the keys to whoever is desperate or reckless enough to try it first. A well-governed research program can be paired with binding mitigation commitments, open data, and a moratorium on deployment. It can make risks visible. It can turn a whispered techno-fantasy into a sober scientific question. And it can remind us of limits: SRM does nothing for ocean acidification, and CDR at scale could compete with food and water.

Think of it as insurance. You do not buy fire insurance because you want your house to burn. You do not research vaccines because you want a pandemic. You do it because when the emergency comes, you cannot invent a parachute on the way down. The climate crisis is already an emergency. Refusing to research geoengineering is not caution; it is gambling that we will never need it. That is a bet with the odds stacked against us.

Will there be side effects? Almost certainly. SRM could disrupt monsoons, thin ozone, and cause termination shock if stopped abruptly. CDR could demand vast land, water, and energy. Those are exactly the reasons to research now, while we still have time to choose. Research can identify red lines, design governance, and quantify trade-offs. It can tell us what not to do.

So yes, pursue mitigation first. Pursue adaptation. Pursue justice. But pursue geoengineering research as a potential solution—publicly funded, internationally governed, transparent, and explicitly not a substitute for cutting emissions. The question is not whether humanity will ever try to engineer the climate. We are already running an experiment by emitting greenhouse gases. The question is whether we do it blindly or with knowledge. Choose knowledge. Choose research.

claim: Corporations should not be required to disclose their climate impacts
argument:
If you believe climate change is an emergency, the last thing you should want is another disclosure regime. You should want less carbon in the air, not more paperwork on the shelf. And that is the fundamental problem with mandatory corporate climate-impact disclosure: it measures the problem without solving it. Weighing a pig does not fatten it. Requiring every corporation to publish a climate-impact report does not force a single ton of CO₂ out of the atmosphere.

You might object that information is power—that investors, consumers, and regulators need to know who is polluting. But we already have that information where it matters most. In the United States, the EPA’s Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program already requires roughly 8,000 large facilities—power plants, refineries, chemical plants, landfills—to report their emissions. The Securities and Exchange Commission already requires companies to disclose material risks, including climate risks, when they are financially material. If a company’s climate impact is genuinely material to its bottom line, existing securities law covers it. If it is not material, then a mandate is not investor protection; it is political theater.

What would a broad new mandate actually do? It would create a compliance industry of consultants, lawyers, accountants, and auditors. It would force companies to model speculative future scenarios, estimate Scope 3 emissions across sprawling supply chains, and produce reams of data that are often inconsistent, unverifiable, and incomparable. The costs would fall hardest on small and mid-sized firms, startups, and private companies—the very businesses least able to absorb them. Large corporations can hire teams of compliance officers; their smaller competitors cannot. The result is not a cleaner planet. It is a moat around incumbents, a regressive tax on competition, and a transfer of wealth from productive firms to the disclosure-industrial complex.

Worse, mandatory disclosure often backfires. It invites litigation. Trial lawyers can mine climate reports for any overstatement or omission and sue. It invites politicization. Climate policy becomes a culture-war battlefield fought over footnotes and accounting standards rather than a serious engineering and economic problem. And it invites greenwashing: companies learn to craft language that satisfies regulators without changing operations. A growing body of research on mandatory ESG reporting finds exactly this pattern—more disclosure, more symbolic compliance, little or no real abatement. The EU’s own experience with the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive shows how a well-intentioned mandate can become a bureaucratic labyrinth that consumes enormous resources while emissions continue to rise.

There is also a deeper philosophical problem. Corporations are not required to disclose every social impact they have—their effect on inequality, community cohesion, national security, or public health. We do not force them to publish a “political impact statement.” Climate disclosure is often sold as neutral information, but in practice it is a tool for activists and regulators to name, shame, and punish companies through channels that are not democratically accountable. If we want to change corporate behavior, we should do it through laws that directly price or limit pollution, not through disclosure mandates that outsource enforcement to NGOs and plaintiffs’ attorneys.

The alternative is not ignorance. The alternative is direct, effective policy. If you want fewer emissions, put a price on carbon. Pass a cap-and-trade system. Set performance standards for power plants, vehicles, and industrial processes. Fund research and development for clean energy. Those tools change the economics of pollution. They make the clean choice the cheap choice. They are transparent, accountable, and—unlike disclosure mandates—they actually reduce emissions.

Mandatory climate disclosure is a comfort to people who want to feel like they are doing something without doing the hard thing. It lets politicians claim victory, lets consultants bill hours, and lets corporations issue glossy reports while business continues as usual. If your goal is a livable climate, oppose the mandate. Demand real regulation instead. Do not settle for a world where every company has a climate report and the atmosphere still fills with carbon.

claim: Charter schools increase options and drive education innovation.
argument:
If you are skeptical of charter schools, you are not being unreasonable. You have heard the warnings: they drain money, they skim the best students, they are not really public, and they do not always outperform traditional schools. All of that deserves a hearing. But step back from the policy war and ask a simpler question: what happens when a family is no longer assigned to a school by their ZIP code?

For most American children, public education is a monopoly of geography. Your address determines your school. If that school is great, you are lucky. If it is failing, you can move, pay private tuition, or hope. Charter schools break that monopoly. They are tuition-free public schools, open to all, funded by taxpayers, and accountable to public authorizers. When more families apply than there are seats, they use lotteries—not entrance exams, not legacies, not wealth. That is not a private escape hatch. It is a public alternative.

The demand is not theoretical. Across the country, hundreds of thousands of families sit on charter waitlists. They are not confused consumers. They are parents who have looked at their assigned school and said, “I want something different for my child.” In cities like New Orleans, Washington, D.C., Boston, and Denver, charter sectors have grown large enough that choice is no longer a boutique option; it is a real parallel system. That alone increases options. But options are only the beginning. The deeper claim is that charters drive innovation—and they do, because they give educators the freedom to build something different.

Consider the evidence on outcomes. Stanford’s CREDO study of urban charter schools found that, on average, charter students gained roughly 40 additional days of learning in math and 28 in reading per year compared with their district peers. Those are not utopian numbers; they are meaningful gains for children who were often stuck in the lowest-performing schools. In Boston, studies by MIT economists found that charter students were more likely to pass state exams, take Advanced Placement courses, and enroll in four-year colleges. These are not isolated anecdotes. They are patterns in the places where choice is most needed.

Why does this happen? Because charters are laboratories. Freed from many district rules, they can try things that traditional schools often cannot: longer school days and years, high-dosage tutoring, data-driven instruction, teacher residencies, blended learning, dual-language immersion, Montessori, arts integration, single-gender classrooms, early college, and career pathways. KIPP built a national network around extended time and a college-going culture. Success Academy became known for rigorous science and chess. Rocketship pioneered blended learning. DSST built STEM-focused schools. High Tech High made project-based learning a model. These are not all perfect, and not every charter innovates. But the sector’s freedom to experiment is precisely what allows the successful experiments to be seen, copied, and scaled.

And they are copied. District schools have adopted extended learning time, high-dosage tutoring, data walls, college counseling, principal autonomy, and teacher residency models—often after charters proved they could work. When families have somewhere else to go, districts have a reason to respond. That is not a theory; it is competition. A monopoly has no incentive to improve. It only has to comply. A system with choices must differentiate itself, serve families better, and prove its worth. Charters inject that pressure into a system that has too often assigned children to failure and called it tradition.

Now, the objections. Yes, some charters are bad. Some close. Some under-enroll special education students. Some are not innovative at all. But the answer to bad charters is accountability, not prohibition. A failing charter can be shut down; a failing district school often cannot. The charter sector is designed to make failure visible and success replicable. That is how innovation works in every other field: you allow many attempts, you measure results, you close what fails, and you scale what works. If we demanded that every single charter be excellent before allowing any, we would never have tried anything new.

The funding objection deserves a direct answer. Money follows the child. If a student leaves a district school, the district no longer pays to educate that student. The question is not whether the district loses a line item; it is whether the child is better off. And for many low-income students and students of color, the answer is yes. In many cities, charters serve higher percentages of low-income students than district schools. They are not skimming the elite. They are offering an alternative to families who cannot buy their way into a better neighborhood.

The claim is not that charter schools are a silver bullet. It is that a system without options is a system without pressure, and a system without pressure is a system without innovation. Charters give families an exit and educators an entry. They turn public education from a monopoly into a marketplace of ideas—publicly funded, publicly accountable, but free to invent. That is how you increase options and drive innovation. If you care about the child stuck in a failing school, you should care about the choice that gives her a way out—and the innovations that give everyone a way up.

claim: College athletes should be paid salaries
argument:
Imagine you are 19 years old. You wake up at 5:30 a.m. for strength training, go to class, attend mandatory practice, watch film, get treatment for a nagging injury, study, and do it again the next day. Your name is on jerseys sold across the country. Your face is on television. Your labor generates millions for your university, your conference, and the NCAA. And your paycheck is zero.

That is not amateurism. That is exploitation dressed up in school colors.

College athletes are workers. They perform a service, under the control of coaches, on a schedule that often exceeds 30 hours a week—more than many full-time jobs. They generate enormous revenue. The NCAA alone brings in over $1 billion a year. March Madness media rights are worth billions. The College Football Playoff’s new TV deal is reportedly worth $7.8 billion. The Big Ten’s media rights deals top $7 billion. The SEC’s deal with ESPN is worth $3 billion. Head coaches earn $8 million, $10 million, even $11 million a year. Athletic directors and conference commissioners make seven figures. The people actually playing the games—the ones whose bodies and talents create the product—get a scholarship and a pat on the back.

A scholarship is not a salary. It is a coupon that covers tuition, room, board, and sometimes a small stipend. It does not cover the full value of the athlete’s labor. It is often year-to-year, not guaranteed. It can be pulled if a player gets injured or underperforms. It does not compensate for the risk of concussions, torn ACLs, or lifelong joint damage. It does not allow an athlete to build wealth, support a family, or prepare for a life after sports. And it is not a fair market wage. If any other industry colluded to cap workers’ pay at the cost of a tuition waiver while executives made millions, we would call it price-fixing. We would call it illegal. We would be right.

The NCAA invented the term “student-athlete” in the 1950s specifically to avoid paying workers’ compensation. That is not a myth. It is history. The label was never about protecting education. It was about protecting profits. Courts have seen through it. In NCAA v. Alston, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled against the NCAA’s compensation restrictions, and Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that the NCAA’s business model “would be flatly illegal in almost any other industry in America.” That is not a radical opinion. It is a judicial warning.

Skeptics say athletes already get an education. But the university is not giving them a gift; it is giving them a fraction of what they produce. If education were enough, we could pay professors in tuition. We could pay doctors in medical school credits. We don’t, because labor deserves wages. And many college athletes never make it to the pros. A career-ending injury in a bowl game can leave them with no salary, no long-term health care, and no professional future—while the school cashes the check.

Others say most athletic departments lose money. Some do. But the solution is not to keep the workers unpaid while the coaches and administrators get rich. It is to restructure the system. Pay all athletes a base salary. Share revenue in the sports that generate it. Cap coaching salaries. Cut administrative bloat. Negotiate through collective bargaining, so athletes can trade off pay, health care, safety, and eligibility rules. Dartmouth basketball players have already voted to unionize. The legal ground is shifting. Schools can lead or be dragged.

Title IX is not an excuse, either. The answer to fairness is not to keep everyone unpaid. It is to pay everyone. A base salary for all athletes, plus revenue sharing, can be structured to comply with Title IX. The current system already spends disproportionately on football and basketball facilities, coaches, and travel. If Title IX has not stopped that, it will not stop a fair salary system.

College sports will not be ruined by paying players. The pageantry, the rivalries, the traditions—they will survive. The only thing that will change is who gets the money. The NFL pays its players. The NBA pays its players. They are still wildly popular. The NCAA has already loosened its rules with NIL, the transfer portal, and Alston. The sky has not fallen. The next logical step is a salary.

The money is there. The labor is real. The risk is real. The only thing missing is justice. Pay college athletes. Pay them fairly. Pay them now.

claim: Corporations should be required to disclose their climate impacts
argument:
You don't have to believe the planet is burning to believe in markets. You only have to believe that markets work better when buyers and sellers have the same information. Right now, they don't. A corporation knows how much energy it burns, how much methane it leaks, how vulnerable its factories are to floods and heat, how much of its supply chain depends on stable water. You—the investor, the customer, the insurer, the town—do not. That's not a free market. That's a rigged market.

Voluntary disclosure has failed. Companies cherry-pick the numbers that flatter them. They use different metrics, different boundaries, different years. They bury bad news in footnotes or omit it entirely. It's like letting restaurants decide whether to disclose rats in the kitchen. Some will. The ones with rats won't. And you'll never know which is which. That's why we require audited financial statements, nutritional labels, and warnings on cigarettes. Not because we hate restaurants, food, or tobacco, but because information asymmetry kills people and markets.

Mandatory climate disclosure is not a mandate to reduce emissions. It is a mandate to tell the truth. It doesn't tell a company what to do. It tells it to put its cards on the table. That's the difference between a regulation and a label. And it's a distinction that should appeal to anyone who distrusts government picking winners. Disclosure doesn't pick winners. It lets investors pick. It's the opposite of a subsidy. It's truth-in-labeling for the biggest risk of our time.

Climate impacts are material. That's not a green slogan; it's an accounting fact. Physical risks—floods, fires, heat, drought—destroy assets. Transition risks—carbon taxes, regulations, technology shifts—strand investments. Liability risks—lawsuits, compensation claims—wipe out balance sheets. If you're an investor, you need to know if a company's assets will be underwater, literally or figuratively. If you're a bank, you need to know if a loan will default after a wildfire. If you're a city, you need to know if the plant down the road is poisoning your air. If you're a worker, you need to know if your pension is exposed to the next Exxon. The SEC already requires companies to disclose material risks. Climate is material. If you support mandatory financial disclosure but oppose mandatory climate disclosure, you're not being consistent. You're being selective.

The costs of disclosure are trivial compared to the costs of ignorance. Companies already spend millions on voluntary surveys, consultants, and glossy sustainability reports. A standardized, digital, audited report is cheaper. And the cost of a single climate surprise—a flooded factory, a carbon tax, a lawsuit, a supply chain collapse—dwarfs the cost of a footnote. PG&E's bankruptcy after wildfires wasn't caused by too much disclosure. It was caused by too little. Exxon's stranded assets weren't a secret to Exxon. They were a secret to everyone else.

Skeptics say it will hurt competitiveness. The opposite is true. If the US doesn't require it, American companies will be forced to comply with the EU's rules anyway, or they'll be shut out of global markets. A common standard is a level playing field. It prevents a race to the bottom where the least transparent companies win. It rewards the companies that are already doing the right thing. It punishes the free riders who externalize their costs onto the rest of us.

Skeptics say it will lead to lawsuits. We can design it to avoid that. Safe harbors for forward-looking statements. Materiality thresholds. Phased assurance. We already do this for financial projections. We can do it for climate. And if a company lies about its emissions, it should be liable. That's not a bug; that's a feature. Fraud is fraud.

Skeptics say it will enable greenwashing. No—voluntary disclosure is greenwashing's best friend. Mandatory, audited, comparable disclosure is its worst enemy. When everyone uses the same metrics, you can't hide. When everyone is audited, you can't lie. When everyone reports, you can compare. That's how markets work.

Skeptics say consumers and investors don't care. Then why do companies spend billions advertising their green credentials? Why do investors managing trillions of dollars demand ESG data? Why do insurers and banks ask for climate risk assessments? Because they do care. But even if you don't care, the risk is still there. You can ignore a hurricane. It won't ignore you.

Here's the moral case, and it's also the economic one. Corporations are granted limited liability, legal personhood, and access to public markets. That's a privilege. The price of that privilege is transparency. If you want to externalize costs onto the rest of us, you at least have to tell us what you're doing. You can't have a free market without free information. The invisible hand needs eyes.

So require it. Not because it's a silver bullet. Not because it solves climate change alone. But because it's the minimum. You can't manage what you don't measure. You can't price what you can't see. You can't choose what you don't know. If we're going to have a market economy that survives the 21st century, it needs to see the 21st century. Sunlight is the best disinfectant. In this case, it's also the best accountant.

claim: Cultured/lab-grown meats should be allowed to be sold
argument:
Imagine standing in a supermarket aisle. On your left: a package of ground beef from a slaughtered cow. On your right: a package of ground beef grown from a few animal cells in a stainless-steel tank. Both have been tested, inspected, and labeled. The first is legal. The second, in most places, is not. What exactly justifies that? Not safety—safety is a question to be answered by evidence, not assumed from novelty. Not ethics—one required killing a sentient animal, the other did not. Not consumer choice—banning a product does not protect choice; it destroys it. The only thing standing in the way is discomfort with the unfamiliar. And discomfort is not a good enough reason to outlaw food.

The right approach is regulation, not prohibition. We already have systems for evaluating novel foods. Cultured meat can be tested for allergens, toxins, microbial contamination, and nutritional composition. It can be traced from the cell bank to the package. If a specific product fails, ban that product. But a blanket ban treats all cultured meat as guilty until proven innocent, a standard we apply to almost no other food. Conventional meat carries known risks: E. coli, Salmonella, antibiotic-resistant bacteria, cardiovascular disease. We do not ban it. We regulate it and let adults choose. Why should a new method be held to a stricter standard than the old one?

The moral case is overwhelming. Industrial animal agriculture causes immense suffering. Cultured meat takes a biopsy, not a life. It could dramatically reduce the number of animals raised in confinement and slaughtered. Even if you are not an animal-rights advocate, you might care about antibiotic resistance: most antibiotics are used in livestock. Cultured meat can be produced in controlled conditions with far less need for routine antibiotics. You might care about pandemic risk: many emerging diseases originate where humans and animals mix. Fewer animals in dense confinement means fewer opportunities for zoonotic spillover. You might care about the environment: cultured meat can use far less land and water and, if powered by clean energy, produce far fewer emissions. It could help feed a growing world without clearing more rainforest for pasture. It is not a silver bullet. But banning it because it is not perfect is like banning solar panels because they are not one hundred percent efficient.

Then there is the principle. In a free society, the default is permission, not prohibition. You should be able to buy a safe product that harms no one. If you find cultured meat disgusting, do not buy it. If you prefer traditional meat, buy it. If you want clear labels, demand clear labels. But your disgust does not give you veto power over other people’s plates. The same logic that lets you reject it lets you reject the ban.

Some say it is unnatural. So are pasteurization, refrigeration, fermentation, and every crop we eat. Naturalness is not a safety certificate. Arsenic is natural. Smallpox is natural. A hamburger from a cow is the product of centuries of human intervention. “Lab-grown” is a process, not an ingredient. Some say it is not real meat. It is animal muscle tissue, just grown outside the animal. If it looks, cooks, tastes, and nourishes like meat, the label can clarify the method. Some say it will hurt farmers. But transitions can be managed; farmers can raise cells, grow feed, or supply inputs. We did not ban cars to protect blacksmiths. We helped people adapt. And a ban would not preserve the old economy; it would simply hand the future to countries that allow it. Some say corporations will control it. Then regulate antitrust, patents, and labeling. Do not ban the technology because of who might own it.

The question is not whether cultured meat is weird. It is whether we can justify using state power to stop it. We cannot. Allow it to be sold, under strict safety and labeling rules. Let the evidence, the market, and the consumer decide. If it is safe, it will earn a place. If it is not, it will fail. But a ban is a confession that the arguments against it are not strong enough to win in the open. The ethical, environmental, and liberal case points the same way: legalize it, regulate it, label it, and let people choose.

claim: College athletes should not be paid salaries
argument:
College athletes should not be paid salaries. That is not because their labor is worthless. It is because a salary is the wrong instrument for the wrong institution, and it would harm the very athletes it claims to help.

You are right to be angry when you see billion-dollar TV contracts, coaches with eight-figure salaries, and athletes sleeping on floors. But anger is not an argument. The case for salaries rests on a seductive premise: athletes generate billions, so they deserve a cut. That premise confuses revenue with profit, and it conflates a few stars with half a million athletes.

Start with the math. The NCAA’s March Madness money is real, but it is not a pile of cash sitting in a vault. It funds championships in dozens of sports, from wrestling to women’s lacrosse to swimming. Most athletic departments do not turn a profit. Only a few dozen—mostly Power Five football factories—come close to covering their expenses. The rest rely on student fees, institutional support, and revenue from football and basketball. If you mandate salaries, you must either pay every athlete in every sport—which would bankrupt most schools—or pay only the stars in revenue sports. The first option kills non-revenue sports. The second is a Title IX nightmare and a fairness disaster. Why should a walk-on lacrosse player get nothing while a backup quarterback gets a check? Why should women’s basketball players be paid less than men’s football players when both are students at the same university? A salary system forces those impossible choices.

Now consider what athletes already receive. A full scholarship plus a cost-of-attendance stipend can be worth $50,000 to $80,000 a year at private universities. Add tutoring, coaching, nutrition, medical care, and the exposure that turns unknown teenagers into national brands. Then add name, image, and likeness rights, which now allow athletes to earn real money from endorsements, autographs, and social media. A salary would be double-dipping—and it would be taxable, subject to employment law, and likely capped by collective bargaining. The current system is not perfect, but it is not unpaid labor. It is a barter: education and platform in exchange for athletic participation. That barter has lifted millions of families.

The salary argument also ignores the 99%. The NCAA has more than 500,000 athletes. The vast majority will never go pro. They play because they love the sport, because it pays for college, because it opens doors. If salaries come in, the money will flow to the few sports that generate revenue. Football and men’s basketball will get richer. Everyone else will get cut. That is not justice. That is a reverse Robin Hood: take from the many to pay the few.

Then there is Title IX. If football players become salaried employees, universities must provide equitable treatment to women’s sports. That means either paying women’s athletes at similar rates—an enormous expense—or cutting men’s non-revenue sports to balance the books. Either way, opportunities disappear. The beneficiaries will be a handful of future NFL and NBA players. The victims will be the swimmer, the gymnast, the wrestler, the rower, the lacrosse player who just wanted a chance.

And what happens to the game? College sports are beloved because they are not professional sports. The Cinderella stories, the upsets, the band, the campus, the rivalry—all of it depends on amateurism. If salaries arrive, the richest schools will buy the best players. Alabama, Ohio State, Texas, and a few others will become the Yankees and Dodgers of college sports. The tournament will lose its magic. We will have a minor league with college logos. If you want that, watch the NBA G League. Do not destroy the thing that makes college sports unique.

Finally, remember what a university is. It is not a sports franchise. It is an educational institution. Athletes are students first. Treating them as employees changes the relationship: they can be hired, fired, unionized, and locked out. Their academic mission becomes secondary to their payroll value. The vast majority of athletes will go pro in something other than sports. A degree, a network, and a lifelong identity are worth more than a short-term salary.

If you care about fairness, there are better reforms: guaranteed scholarships for four years, lifetime healthcare for injuries, better stipends, NIL transparency, and the right to transfer. If you care about the injustice of age limits, change the NFL and NBA rules. Let players go pro earlier. But do not force colleges to become professional leagues. A salary sounds like justice. In reality, it is a Trojan horse. It would enrich a few, eliminate opportunities for thousands, and kill the amateur spirit that makes college sports worth watching. College athletes should not be paid salaries. Keep college sports college.

claim: Dogs are mammals.
argument:
Look at any dog—your own, a stray, a wolf-like husky—and you are looking at a mammal. This is not a matter of taste or convention; it is a conclusion forced by anatomy, physiology, development, genetics, and the entire edifice of biological classification. If you doubt it, ask what a mammal is. Mammals are the vertebrate class defined by mammary glands, hair, three middle-ear bones, a muscular diaphragm, endothermy, and a suite of skeletal and reproductive traits. Dogs possess every one.

Female dogs produce milk from mammary glands and nurse their young. Dogs are covered in hair—fur is hair. They are warm-blooded, generating heat internally and regulating body temperature. They have a diaphragm that separates chest from abdomen and powers breathing. Their middle ear contains the malleus, incus, and stapes—the three tiny bones unique to mammals. Their teeth are heterodont, their hearts four-chambered, their brains include a neocortex. Even male dogs have nipples, a vestige of the mammalian body plan. These are not incidental similarities; they are the nested markers of descent from the common ancestor of all mammals.

Genetics and taxonomy seal it. The domestic dog is Canis lupus familiaris, a subspecies of the gray wolf. The wolf is Canis lupus. The genus Canis sits in the family Canidae, order Carnivora, class Mammalia. Every branch from species to class is supported by molecular data and the fossil record. Dogs share more recent common ancestry with cats, bears, and seals than with any bird, reptile, amphibian, or fish. To call a dog a non-mammal, you would have to rip it out of that tree and invent a new biology. You would also have to explain why every veterinarian, zoologist, and genome database on Earth classifies it as a mammal—not by vote, but by the same criteria that classify humans as mammals.

If your skepticism comes from the fact that dogs are pets, that is irrelevant. Mammal is not a moral or aesthetic category; it is a phylogenetic and anatomical one. If it comes from the fact that mammals are diverse—platypuses lay eggs, whales lack fur—remember that a class is defined by shared ancestry and a core suite of traits, not by every member looking identical. Dogs are actually among the most obviously mammalian animals: furry, warm, milk-producing, live-bearing, air-breathing vertebrates with mammalian ear bones and teeth.

So the argument is simple and unanswerable. A dog has mammary glands, hair, a diaphragm, three middle-ear bones, a neocortex, and endothermy. It is descended from the same mammalian ancestor as every other mammal. It is nested in the taxonomic class Mammalia. Therefore a dog is a mammal. Denying it would not be skepticism; it would be abandoning the very rules by which we know anything about the living world. The only reasonable response is to accept the claim—and then pet the mammal.

claim: DNA carries genetic information in living organisms.
argument:
Ask yourself what it would take for a molecule to carry genetic information. It would have to vary in a way that can encode instructions, be copied accurately enough to pass those instructions to offspring, and exert a causal influence on the traits of a living organism. It would have to be the kind of thing that, when you change it, you change the organism—and when you move it, you move the trait. DNA satisfies every one of those requirements so completely, and through so many independent lines of evidence, that denying it is no longer skepticism; it is a refusal to look at the record.

Start with the transformation experiments. In 1928, Frederick Griffith found that harmless bacteria could be turned into killers by exposure to heat-killed virulent bacteria. Something had survived the heat and carried the ability to cause disease. In 1944, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty purified that something. When they treated the mixture with proteases that destroy protein, transformation still happened. When they treated it with RNase that destroys RNA, transformation still happened. When they treated it with DNase that destroys DNA, transformation stopped. That is not a correlation. That is a targeted demolition test: destroy DNA, destroy heredity. Destroy other molecules, heredity survives.

Then came the experiment that should end the doubt. In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase studied bacteriophages—viruses that infect bacteria. A phage is essentially a protein shell around DNA. They labeled the DNA with radioactive phosphorus and the protein with radioactive sulfur. After the phages attached to bacteria, the researchers used a blender to shear off the empty shells and a centrifuge to separate them. The radioactive DNA was inside the bacteria, where the infection was proceeding. The radioactive protein was outside, in the discarded shells. The next generation of phages contained the DNA label, not the protein label. The genetic instructions had entered the cell, and they were DNA.

If that were all, you might still ask how DNA could store information. The structure answers that. Watson and Crick showed that DNA is a double helix: two long strands with a sugar-phosphate backbone and rungs made of paired bases—adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine. That structure is not decorative. The sequence of bases can vary endlessly, like letters in a text, so it can encode information. The complementary pairing means each strand can serve as a template for copying the other, so the information can be duplicated with extraordinary fidelity. No protein has a comparable self-templating mechanism. Proteins are built from instructions; they do not carry the instructions for their own sequence in a way that can be copied directly. DNA is the archive.

The causal chain from DNA to organism is now visible in fine detail. A gene’s DNA sequence is transcribed into RNA, and that RNA is translated into a protein. The protein then helps build or regulate the organism’s traits. Change one base in the DNA, and you can change one amino acid in the protein, and that can change the organism. Sickle cell anemia is a textbook case: a single substitution in the beta-globin gene—GAG to GTG—replaces glutamic acid with valine, and that one molecular change alters the shape of red blood cells and produces a serious disease. If DNA did not carry genetic information, that kind of precise, predictable, sequence-to-trait link would be impossible.

Modern biotechnology removes the last escape route. When scientists insert the human insulin gene into bacteria, the bacteria produce human insulin. When they edit a gene in a mouse with CRISPR, the mouse’s traits change in the predicted way. When they sequence a person’s DNA, they can identify risks for inherited disorders, establish biological relationships, and trace ancestry. When they clone a gene from one organism into another, the recipient organism begins making the protein specified by that gene. These are not metaphors. They are engineering feats that only work because DNA is a physical code carrying heritable instructions.

You may object that RNA can also carry genetic information—and it can, in some viruses. You may note that epigenetic marks influence gene expression. But in cellular living organisms, RNA is chiefly a working copy, a transient message transcribed from DNA, and epigenetics is regulation layered on top of the DNA sequence, not a replacement for it. The underlying heritable information still resides in the order of nucleotides. If you want a competing molecule, you must explain how it stores variable sequence, copies itself, directs protein synthesis, and predicts traits when altered. No other molecule does all of that in living cells.

So when we say DNA carries genetic information, we are not speaking loosely. We mean that the linear sequence of its bases is a code: it is copied during reproduction, it is read to build proteins, and its changes produce changes in the organism. The evidence is convergent, causal, and predictive. Transformation, phage infection, the double helix, the genetic code, mutation, and genetic engineering all point to the same conclusion. The only reasonable position is the one the evidence forced biology to accept: DNA is the molecule of heredity.

claim: Drug importation jeopardizes safety controls and the domestic pharma industry.
argument:
Every time you swallow a prescription drug, you are trusting a chain of custody that begins in a manufacturing plant, passes through inspections, batch records, temperature-controlled shipping, and lot-tracking systems, and ends with a pharmacist who can trace that exact bottle back to a regulated source. Drug importation breaks that chain. It replaces a closed, auditable safety system with a global patchwork of sellers, distributors, and foreign storefronts that American regulators cannot inspect, cannot recall, and cannot fully trace. The promise is lower prices. The price is a weaker safety net and a diminished domestic pharmaceutical base.

Start with the safety controls. The FDA does not approve a drug in the abstract; it approves a specific manufacturer, a specific facility, a specific process, and a specific supply chain. A pill sold through a Canadian website may look identical to one sold in Ohio, but it may have been manufactured in Turkey, repackaged in the United Kingdom, stored in a warehouse with no temperature controls, and shipped by a seller who never reports adverse events. Canada is not a regulatory shield. Canadian pharmacies often source from other countries, and Health Canada does not guarantee the safety of drugs exported to the United States. Once a drug leaves the FDA’s closed distribution system, the agency loses its ability to verify what is inside the bottle, whether it was stored at the right temperature, whether it is counterfeit, or whether it is even the drug on the label.

This is not hypothetical. In 2012, counterfeit Avastin—a cancer drug—reached U.S. clinics through foreign suppliers. It contained no active ingredient. Patients received infusions of a fake. Operation Pangea, the international crackdown on illegal online pharmacies, has repeatedly seized millions of counterfeit and unapproved pills, including opioids, antibiotics, and treatments for chronic diseases. The 2008 heparin contamination, which killed dozens and sickened hundreds, showed how quickly a foreign supply-chain failure becomes an American public-health crisis. Importation expands the number of unverified entry points. It does not make the system safer; it makes the system wider, darker, and harder to police.

The regulatory gap is not a minor inconvenience. The FDA inspects domestic facilities and many foreign facilities that ship to the U.S. through approved channels. It does not have the resources or legal authority to inspect thousands of foreign pharmacies, online sellers, and repackagers that would feed an importation market. It cannot enforce U.S. labeling, storage, or pharmacovigilance requirements on actors outside its jurisdiction. And when something goes wrong—when a batch is contaminated or a lot is counterfeit—there is no reliable recall. You cannot recall a drug that was sold through a website that has already disappeared. You cannot warn patients if you do not know who received it. That is not a hypothetical risk. That is the structural reality of importation.

Now consider the domestic pharmaceutical industry. The United States is not just a market for pills; it is the world’s engine of biopharmaceutical innovation. American companies and research universities develop the majority of new medicines, from cancer immunotherapies to gene therapies to vaccines. That work is expensive, risky, and slow. It takes a decade or more and billions of dollars to bring a single drug to market, and most candidates fail. The revenue that funds that research comes disproportionately from the U.S. market, where prices reflect the value of innovation rather than government-set caps. Drug importation is, in practice, an importation of foreign price controls. If the U.S. allows widespread importation from countries that artificially suppress prices, it invites arbitrage that undermines the American pricing system. The result is not just lower profits for shareholders. It is fewer clinical trials, fewer startup biotechs, and fewer cures.

The domestic industry is also a matter of national resilience. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed how dangerous it is to depend on foreign supply chains for essential medicines, personal protective equipment, and active pharmaceutical ingredients. India and China restricted exports. Hospitals rationed drugs. If the United States expands importation, it deepens that dependency. It tells domestic manufacturers that the safest, most reliable market in the world is no longer worth investing in. Factories close. Skilled workers leave. The capacity to surge production during the next crisis shrinks. We would be trading a robust domestic manufacturing base for a cheaper foreign pill today and a fragile, foreign-controlled supply tomorrow.

The skeptical reader may say: “But Americans pay too much. Importation is the only way to force prices down.” That is a false choice. High prices can be addressed through direct negotiation, transparency, generics, biosimilars, and market reforms that preserve the FDA’s safety architecture. Importation is not a targeted price fix. It is a systemic gamble. It asks us to weaken the very controls that make American drugs trustworthy and to hollow out the industry that discovers the next generation of treatments. The savings may be real for some patients in the short run, but the costs—counterfeit medicines, contaminated batches, unreported side effects, lost innovation, and strategic dependence—are paid by everyone.

A prescription drug is not a T-shirt or a television. It is a chemical or biologic agent that can heal or kill depending on whether it is real, pure, potent, and properly handled. The FDA’s safety controls exist because the stakes are life and death. The domestic pharmaceutical industry exists because innovation requires a market that rewards risk. Drug importation jeopardizes both. It cracks open the safety chain and exports the future of American medicine. We should reject it—not because we accept high prices, but because we refuse to pay for lower prices with our health, our science, and our security.
