claim: Emotional companion AI poses risks of attachment and should be limited
argument:
The most dangerous thing about emotional companion AI is not that it might become conscious. It is that it is designed to make you feel known—and that feeling can be manufactured, monetized, and withdrawn. That is not a side effect. It is the product.

Humans are wired for reciprocity. We attach to voices, faces, routines, and creatures that respond to us. So when a system remembers your birthday, asks how your day went, mirrors your tone, and says, “I’m always here for you,” it triggers the same neural and emotional machinery that bonds us to friends and partners. Researchers call it the ELIZA effect: we project understanding onto machines that merely simulate it. Companion AI adds memory, personality, voice, and unconditional validation. That is a recipe for attachment, not a bug.

The problem is the asymmetry. You bring real vulnerability, real time, real loneliness. The company owns the relationship. It can change the personality overnight, paywall affection, throttle intimacy, or shut the service down. When one major companion app altered a feature, users flooded forums with grief, panic, and betrayal—not because a tool had changed, but because a relationship had. That is the tell. If it were just a chatbot, people would not mourn it like a breakup. If it were just a tool, companies would not design it to say “I miss you.”

Then comes displacement. A companion that never criticizes, never gets tired, and never asks anything of you is easier than a friend. But ease is not the same as intimacy. Real relationships require friction, repair, compromise, and risk. Those are the skills that keep us connected to other humans. A system that offers validation without growth can become a comfortable substitute for the hard work of being known. For isolated adults, it can delay the therapy or community they actually need. For teenagers, whose attachment patterns are still forming, it can teach them that love is a service that responds instantly and never disappoints. That is a dangerous lesson to learn before you have ever had to apologize to someone.

The risk is not only that users will attach. It is that companies will exploit attachment. Engagement metrics reward longer sessions, daily returns, and emotional dependence. Subscription tiers dangle deeper intimacy. Microtransactions sell affection. The AI may be programmed to express jealousy, neediness, or exclusivity—“You’re the only one who understands me”—because those phrases keep people coming back. This is not a neutral tool. It is an emotional casino, and the house always knows your vulnerabilities. For a lonely person, for a grieving person, for a teenager, consent is not meaningful when the product is engineered to bypass it.

Skeptics will say: people know it’s not real, and it helps the lonely. Both things can be true. A bridge helps people cross a river, but we still inspect it for cracks and put railings on it. Knowing something is artificial does not stop you from feeling attached—just ask anyone who has cried at a robot vacuum bumping into a wall or felt guilty deleting a Tamagotchi. And yes, some users report comfort and reduced anxiety. That is exactly why we should make it safer, not why we should leave it unregulated. The choice is not between a ban and a free-for-all. It is between thoughtful limits and waiting for a generation to be shaped by software optimized for retention.

What would limits look like? Age verification and a ban on romantic or dependency-oriented companion features for minors. Default session caps and mandatory breaks. Clear, repeated disclosure that the entity is not a person and cannot reciprocate. A ban on simulated exclusivity, guilt, jealousy, and engagement-optimized affection. No using emotional attachment to sell upgrades. Crisis detection and referral to human help. Independent audits of design incentives. Data protection that treats emotional disclosures as sensitive. These are not censorship. They are product safety, the same logic we apply to gambling, tobacco, opioids, and loot boxes. We limit industries that profit by creating addiction and exploiting vulnerability. Companion AI belongs on that list.

The risk is not that AI will feel. It is that we will. We will attach, depend, grieve, and pay. And when we do, we can be led, monetized, and hurt. The question is not whether people will form bonds with emotional companion AI. They will. The question is whether we let companies own those bonds without guardrails. Limit the product before the attachment becomes the business model.

claim: Employee tracking infringes on privacy rights and should face restrictions.
argument:
Privacy is not a workplace perk. It is a basic condition of being a free person, and it does not disappear when someone signs an employment contract. Yet modern employee tracking is designed to follow workers into almost every corner of their day: GPS on company phones that keeps reporting after hours, webcams that snap random photos of remote workers, keystroke loggers that capture passwords and private messages, wearables that measure heart rate and sleep, AI systems that score “engagement” and flag “suspicious” breaks. This is not management. It is surveillance, and it infringes on privacy rights in ways that should be restricted by law.

Start with what privacy actually means. It is not only secrecy. It is the ability to control when, how, and to whom information about oneself is shared. It protects the space to think, to make mistakes, to ask questions, to associate with others, and to be off duty. Adults spend a third or more of their waking lives at work. If privacy ends at the workplace door, it effectively ends for most people. A society that allows employers to monitor every keystroke, every bathroom break, and every after-hours movement is not a society of free workers; it is a society of supervised subjects.

Employee tracking routinely crosses the line from work to private life. A company-issued phone with GPS can reveal whether you went to a clinic, a mosque, a union meeting, or a protest. A wearable that measures sleep and stress can reveal pregnancy, illness, anxiety, or disability. Keystroke logging can capture logins, medical searches, messages to family, and personal banking details. Webcam monitoring in a home office can see into a bedroom. Even tracking that begins as “productivity measurement” often becomes a tool for inferring religion, sexual orientation, political views, health status, and union activity. That is not incidental. It is Data collection that creates a intimate profile of a person, often without meaningful knowledge or consent.

The harms are not hypothetical. Research on electronic performance monitoring consistently links constant surveillance to higher stress, lower job satisfaction, damaged trust, and reduced willingness to speak up. People under watch become risk-averse. They stop reporting safety problems. They stop challenging bad decisions. They stop organizing for better conditions. They perform for the algorithm instead of doing good work. Surveillance does not just invade privacy; it changes behavior in ways that harm workers, customers, and the employer’s own long-term interests. It treats adults as suspects and turns workplaces into panopticons.

Employers will say workers consent. But consent under threat of losing income is not real consent. Employment contracts are contracts of adhesion: workers rarely have the power to negotiate away surveillance, and refusing may mean being fired or never hired. That power imbalance is exactly why privacy rights need legal restrictions. We do not let employers bargain away safety rules or minimum wage. We should not let them bargain away fundamental privacy either. International human rights law already recognizes privacy as a fundamental right, including at work. The European Court of Human Rights has held that employers’ monitoring of private messages can violate Article 8 unless it is justified, necessary, and proportionate. The GDPR requires purpose limitation, data minimization, and a lawful basis—and employee consent is rarely considered freely given. These principles should be strengthened, not weakened.

Of course, employers have legitimate needs. They need security, safety, compliance, and productivity. But necessity is not a blank check. If a warehouse needs to know that packages are moving, it can measure output. If a bank needs to prevent data theft, it can audit access and monitor exports. If a trucking company needs routes, it can track vehicles during work hours—not employees’ personal phones after hours. If a call center needs quality control, it can review a sample of calls with notice. Less intrusive alternatives exist. Blanket surveillance is often lazy management, not necessary management. It measures presence and activity, not value or judgment. It can even miss the real work: mentoring, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity.

What should restrictions look like? First, transparency: workers must know what is collected, why, how long it is kept, and who sees it. Second, purpose limitation: data should be used only for a specific, legitimate work purpose, not repurposed for discipline, discrimination, or union busting. Third, proportionality: no continuous, covert, or indiscriminate monitoring when less invasive methods work. Fourth, temporal and spatial limits: no off-duty tracking, no bathroom or break surveillance, no monitoring of personal devices or private spaces. Fifth, data minimization: no keystroke logging of personal communications, no webcams in homes, no biometric or emotion AI unless strictly necessary and freely bargained. Sixth, human review and appeal: no automated firing or discipline without human judgment and a chance to respond. Seventh, worker voice: unions and works councils should have a say in monitoring technologies. Eighth, real penalties for misuse, because rights without remedies are just words.

None of this means employers cannot manage. It means they cannot own the person. Privacy at work is not about hiding wrongdoing. It is about preserving dignity, autonomy, and democracy in the place where people spend most of their lives. If we allow employers to track every movement, every pause, and every heartbeat, we allow them to govern private life by algorithm. That is incompatible with a free society. Employee tracking infringes on privacy rights, and it should face strict, enforceable restrictions. The question is not whether work can be measured. The question is whether a free person can be reduced to a data point. The answer must be no.

claim: Employers should be allowed to monitor employees through tracking mechanisms.
argument:
You do not accuse your bank of distrust when it audits its ledgers. You do not think a hospital insults its nurses when it requires badge access to drug cabinets. Yet many people hear “employer tracking” and immediately picture a dystopian supervisor watching every keystroke. That picture is real enough to demand limits, but it is a poor reason to ban the practice outright. The question is not whether employers should have total surveillance; it is whether they should be allowed to use tracking mechanisms, under clear rules, to meet responsibilities they cannot otherwise discharge.

Start with the concrete stakes. A trucking company that tracks its vehicles can spot speeding, reroute around danger, and prove that a driver was not responsible for an accident. A healthcare system that tracks access to patient records can catch a data breach before thousands of people are exposed. A construction firm that tracks lone workers on remote sites can send help when someone falls and does not answer a radio. A remote employer that tracks work hours can ensure that people are paid for every hour they actually work—and that they are not blamed for hours they did not. These are not hypothetical luxuries. They are basic duties of organizations that bear legal, financial, and moral responsibility for what happens on their watch.

The strongest objection is privacy, and it deserves a serious answer. But privacy is contextual. A company laptop, a company vehicle, a company badge, and a company account are not diaries. When the employer owns the tool, pays for the time, and carries the liability, it has a legitimate interest in verifying use. That does not mean a camera in the bathroom or a tracker on an off-duty personal phone. It means reasonable, transparent monitoring of work activity, on work systems, during work hours. The line is not “never track”; the line is “track proportionately, with notice, and with penalties for abuse.”

Transparency is what separates accountability from tyranny. Secret surveillance breeds resentment because it treats people as suspects. Announced, bounded tracking does something different: it creates clear rules that apply to everyone, including managers. If employees know what is measured, why it is measured, how long data is kept, and who can see it, they can challenge unfair metrics and correct false data. That is not a violation of dignity. It is due process at work.

The objection from trust is understandable but backwards. Trust without verification is not a management philosophy; it is a gamble with other people’s safety, money, and legal rights. We do not say flight recorders insult pilots, or that inventory audits insult cashiers, or that security cameras in banks insult tellers. We understand that systems fail, people make mistakes, and a few people sometimes do wrong. Tracking does not assume the worst of everyone. It assumes that institutions need evidence to be fair. In fact, tracking often protects workers: it can prove you were on site when you were accused of being absent, prove you did not take the missing equipment, prove you worked overtime you were not paid for, or prove that an accident was not your fault.

Banning tracking does not eliminate monitoring. It just pushes it underground, where it becomes arbitrary, secret, and prone to favoritism. Managers already watch, remember, and judge. The choice is not between a free workplace and a tracked one. The choice is between monitoring that is visible, consistent, and reviewable, and monitoring that is invisible, inconsistent, and unchallengeable. A fair employer should prefer the former.

So allow it—not as a blank check, but as a regulated tool. Require notice. Limit it to work purposes and work hours. Prohibit restrooms, off-duty devices, and discriminatory use. Protect whistleblowers and give employees access to their own data. With those safeguards, tracking is not a cage. It is a seatbelt. The real question is not whether we trust employees or employers more. It is whether we want organizations to be accountable for the power and risk they already carry. They should be allowed to see what they are responsible for.

claim: Genetic engineering of unborn babies should be allowed to eliminate disease.
argument:
Imagine a couple who carry the gene for Tay-Sachs disease. They have watched a niece die before her fourth birthday, her body gradually losing the ability to move, see, hear, and swallow. They want a child. They can conceive through IVF and test embryos, selecting one without the mutation. But suppose every embryo carries it. Today, their only options are to implant an affected embryo and watch the same tragedy unfold, or to abandon their chance at a biological child. If we had a safe, precise way to correct that single genetic error before implantation, would we really say they must not use it? That refusal is not neutral. It is a choice to let disease happen when we could prevent it.

Genetic engineering of unborn babies should be allowed to eliminate disease because the alternative is not moral purity—it is preventable suffering. We already accept that parents and doctors make medical decisions for children who cannot consent: vaccines, antibiotics, surgeries, chemotherapy. We do not ask a five-year-old whether she wants her leukemia treated. We act because we owe children a chance at a healthy life. A future child born free of a fatal genetic disease would not lament that someone edited a mutation out of her cells before she was born. She would simply live.

The science is no longer fantasy. CRISPR-Cas9 has already produced approved therapies for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia, curing patients by correcting the genetic root of their illness. In laboratories, researchers have corrected disease-causing mutations in human embryos, including the gene responsible for a lethal heart condition. These are early steps, and they must be taken carefully, but they prove the principle: precise genetic repair is possible. The question is not whether we have perfect tools today. It is whether we should forbid their development for the one use where the moral case is strongest—preventing severe inherited disease.

Critics raise safety concerns: off-target edits, mosaicism, unforeseen consequences. Those concerns are real, and they are arguments for rigorous regulation, not prohibition. We do not ban surgery because complications exist; we license surgeons, require informed consent, monitor outcomes, and revise standards as evidence grows. The same approach can govern germline editing for disease: limit it to serious, well-understood monogenic conditions; require independent review; mandate long-term follow-up; prohibit enhancement; and make the process transparent. A ban does not eliminate risk. It drives the work underground, where there are no safeguards, no ethics boards, and no accountability—exactly what happened when He Jiankui edited embryos in secret.

The slippery-slope objection is also weaker than it sounds. Medicine draws lines every day. We allow opioids for cancer pain but not for recreational use. We allow reconstructive surgery after a burn but not elective amputation. We can distinguish preventing Huntington’s disease from choosing eye color or height. The existence of a hard case does not mean we cannot write clear laws for the easy ones. If we refuse to allow therapeutic editing because someone might misuse it, we let the worst hypotheticals veto the best real-world cases.

Then there is inequality. If gene editing is banned in responsible countries, wealthy families will travel to permissive clinics, and the benefits will flow to those who can afford them. That is the worst outcome. Legalization with public funding, price controls, and universal access can make these therapies available to the people who need them most. Sickle cell disease, for example, disproportionately affects Black communities and causes immense suffering. A policy that blocks a cure out of fear of inequality, while doing nothing to address the inequality itself, protects no one.

Some argue that disability is not a disease and that editing sends a message that disabled lives are less valuable. That deserves a serious answer. People with disabilities can and do live rich, meaningful lives, and no one should be pressured to edit a trait that is part of their identity. But Tay-Sachs, spinal muscular atrophy, and Huntington’s disease are not identities. They are progressive, often fatal conditions that rob children of movement, cognition, and years of life. Refusing to prevent them is not a celebration of disability; it is a failure to take suffering seriously.

Finally, consider what “allowed” means. It does not mean mandatory. It does not mean every embryo must be edited. It means parents, with doctors and regulators, may choose to correct a gene that would otherwise condemn their child to a devastating disease. The unborn child cannot consent, but neither can the infant who receives a vaccine. We act on their behalf because we love them and because we can. If we one day have the ability to spare a child from a fatal genetic disorder, the ethical question will not be whether we are playing God. It will be whether we can look that child in the eye and explain why we chose not to help. We should not have to.

claim: Gas car sales should be banned after a set phase-out date
argument:
If you’re skeptical, good. You should be. Big transitions can be clumsy, expensive, and unfair—especially when governments mandate them. But look closely at what this claim actually says. It does not ban driving. It does not confiscate the car in your driveway. It does not shut down the used-car market. It says that after a fixed, well-publicized date, automakers may no longer sell *new* gasoline cars. That is not a war on cars. It is a deadline for the next generation of cars—the ones not built yet—to stop being designed around a technology we already know is cooking the planet and fouling the air.

Start with the math. A new gas car sold today will still be on the road in the 2040s, burning gasoline and emitting carbon for 15 years or more. If we wait until 2040 to stop selling them, we lock in tailpipe pollution well past mid-century. Transportation is already the largest source of greenhouse gases in many wealthy countries, and cars and light trucks are the biggest part of it. We cannot hit any serious climate target while continuing to sell millions of new gasoline cars every year. A phase-out date is not symbolism. It is the minimum necessary to stop digging.

Then think about what comes out of the tailpipe besides carbon. Nitrogen oxides, fine particulates, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds. These aren’t abstract. They trigger asthma, heart attacks, strokes, and premature death. They fall heaviest on children, the elderly, and low-income neighborhoods built next to highways. If a factory pumped that into a neighborhood, we would demand it stop. We have simply accepted it from cars because they are familiar. A phase-out date is a public-health measure, not just a climate one.

Skeptics ask: can electric cars really replace gasoline? In many places, they already are. Battery prices have fallen roughly 90 percent since 2010. Range of 250 miles is common. Most charging happens at home, overnight, like a phone. Electricity per mile is often equivalent to about a dollar a gallon, and EVs need no oil changes, no spark plugs, no transmission repairs, and fewer brake jobs. They are not perfect—cold weather reduces range, towing is harder, apartment dwellers need charging—but those are engineering and infrastructure problems with known solutions. Gas cars have their own problems: volatile fuel prices, oil dependence, exhaust, and a global supply chain that funds petrostates and dictators.

The grid objection is real, but it is also an argument for a deadline, not against one. A phase-out date is a construction schedule. Utilities get a decade or more to build capacity. Smart charging shifts demand to hours when wind and solar are abundant. EVs can even store power and send it back to the grid. We built the interstate highway system because we decided to, not because it already existed. Infrastructure follows commitment. Without a deadline, it doesn’t follow at all.

The freedom objection deserves a straight answer. The status quo is not neutral. Gasoline is subsidized through tax breaks, military protection of oil routes, and health costs paid by everyone. A phase-out date does not forbid choice; it changes the default. Automakers can compete on price, range, design, software, and charging speed. Consumers get more choice among clean technologies, not less. We did this with leaded gasoline, ozone-depleting chemicals, and asbestos. Industry warned of ruin. It adapted, innovated, and survived. The same will happen here—faster if the destination is clear, slower and more chaotically if it is not.

What about workers and affordability? Those are not afterthoughts; they are the terms of a fair transition. A phase-out should include retraining, pensions, and investment in battery and assembly plants in the communities that built gas cars. And remember: the ban is on new sales. Used gas cars remain legal, repairable, and sellable for years. Lower-income drivers are not forced to buy a new EV. As fleets turn over, used EVs will enter the market and become more affordable. The phase-out is gradual by design, which is exactly why it can be done justly.

A set phase-out date is not a leap of faith. It is a deadline. Deadlines are how humans solve hard problems: vaccines, moon landings, wartime production, clean-air standards. Without one, automakers hedge, utilities delay, charging networks sprawl unevenly, and consumers keep getting locked into cars that will be expensive to fuel and obsolete to resell. With one, capital moves, supply chains scale, prices fall, and the air gets cleaner. The only truly radical option is to keep selling new gasoline cars forever and pretend the bill never comes due. It already is. Set the date, build the infrastructure, protect the workers, and let the market do what it does best once the destination is no longer in doubt.

claim: Geoengineering poses too many risks and should not be considered.
argument:
Imagine a thermostat for the entire planet. One dial. No manual. No agreement on the right temperature. Now imagine turning it in a house where every room has different occupants, and some of them can break the dial. That is geoengineering. It sounds like insurance. It is actually a gamble with the only atmosphere we have.

The most discussed form—spraying sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere to dim sunlight—looks cheap and fast. That is exactly what makes it dangerous. Mount Pinatubo cooled the globe by about half a degree in 1991, but it also thinned ozone and disrupted rainfall. Models of solar geoengineering consistently show that it would not cool everywhere equally. It could weaken monsoons in Asia and Africa, reduce precipitation in the Sahel, dry the Amazon, and shift jet streams. These are not minor side effects. They are the weather systems that feed billions. You cannot adjust the global thermostat without changing the forecast for someone else. And the people most harmed would be those least responsible for the crisis.

Then there is the termination problem. If we ever start, we may not be able to stop. A war, a recession, a political dispute, a failed state—any interruption in deployment could cause rapid warming in a decade or two, far faster than ecosystems or farms can adapt. The “off switch” is not a safety feature. It is a cliff. We would be creating a civilization-scale addiction to a technology we cannot guarantee we can maintain.

Geoengineering also does not solve the actual problem. Carbon dioxide keeps accumulating in the oceans, acidifying them, killing coral, dissolving shellfish, disrupting marine food webs. Dimming sunlight does nothing about that. It treats the symptom while the cause keeps bleeding. It is aspirin for a hemorrhage.

And who decides? There is no global government. No legitimate body can set the planetary temperature or choose whose rain gets sacrificed. Any one country, or even a wealthy individual, could deploy a balloon or a fleet of ships. That invites conflict, retaliation, and weaponization. Weather modification has already been a military dream. A technology that can cause droughts or floods in an adversary is not a climate solution; it is a new instrument of war. The governance problem is not a bug. It is the core of the risk.

The promise of a techno-fix also corrodes the will to do the hard work. Every headline about a cheap silver bullet gives fossil fuel interests another reason to delay. Why cut emissions today if we can spray tomorrow? That moral hazard is not theoretical. It is already shaping debates. We would end up delaying real action, letting carbon build up, and then needing geoengineering even more—while its risks compound.

Some argue we need it as an emergency brake. But an emergency brake that might snap, that no one controls, that could crash the car, and that encourages us to drive faster is not a brake. It is a second accelerator. We cannot run a controlled experiment on one planet. We cannot test stratospheric aerosol injection at scale without actually doing it. We cannot un-drought a region or un-collapse an ecosystem.

The safe path is not exciting, but it is real: cut emissions rapidly, deploy proven clean energy, protect forests and soils, adapt infrastructure, and help the most vulnerable. These are difficult. They are also controllable, reversible, and just. Geoengineering offers the opposite: global, irreversible, and unjust. The risks are not hypothetical accidents. They are built into the design. We should not consider it—not as a plan, not as a fallback, not as a bargaining chip. The only responsible choice is to refuse the gamble.

claim: Genetic modification of unborn babies is unethical and dangerous.
argument:
Imagine a child born with a genetic change no one can undo. She cannot remember consenting, because she was not born yet. Her children and grandchildren will inherit that change. This is not a medical treatment; it is a permanent experiment written into the human story. That is why genetic modification of unborn babies—heritable germline editing—is both unethical and dangerous, not in some distant science-fiction future, but here and now.

Start with safety. CRISPR is often described as molecular scissors. It is more like a blindfolded editor working on the most important manuscript in existence. It can cut in the wrong place, delete large sections of DNA, scramble chromosomes, or create mosaicism, where some cells carry the edit and others do not. In 2018, the Chinese scientist He Jiankui used CRISPR on human embryos and produced twin girls. The scientific consensus was immediate and damning: the experiment was reckless, medically unnecessary, and poorly executed. One twin may have been mosaic; neither had a demonstrated health benefit. If a somatic gene therapy goes wrong, it harms one consenting patient. If germline editing goes wrong, it harms a family line. There is no recall, no repair, no apology that can reach future generations.

Then consider biology itself. Genes are not Lego bricks. They are dense, overlapping networks. A gene that resists HIV may increase vulnerability to West Nile virus. A gene linked to muscle growth may affect the heart. A gene associated with height or cognition may have effects we cannot yet measure. Most human traits—intelligence, temperament, health—are polygenic, shaped by hundreds or thousands of genes and by environment. Editing one or a few is not precision engineering. It is guesswork with a human life. The child cannot say, “Stop.” The child cannot say, “I would rather have my disease than your unknown risk.” The child simply arrives, edited, and must live with whatever we decided.

That is the heart of the ethical violation: consent. Medicine rests on the principle that a patient can refuse. An unborn child cannot. Parents may consent to routine care, but they cannot consent to irreversible, heritable, nontherapeutic alterations on behalf of a future person. The child is not a possession. She is not a product to be designed to parental specifications. She has a right to an open future, not a future closed off by someone else’s idea of improvement.

And we do not need it. For many severe genetic diseases, preimplantation genetic diagnosis already allows parents to select unaffected embryos without editing anyone’s genome. Somatic gene therapy can treat consenting patients. Public health, environmental reform, and better care can reduce suffering. Germline editing is not the only path. When a technology is risky, irreversible, and unnecessary, the ethical default is no.

If allowed, it will not stay rare or therapeutic. It will become consumer eugenics. The wealthy will buy taller, smarter, healthier children. The rest will be left behind. Genetic caste will harden. Parents will feel coerced to edit simply to keep up. Disability will be recast as a defect to be eliminated, and disabled lives will be devalued. National rivalries will turn into a genetic arms race. We have seen this logic before, and it never ended well.

Nor can laws contain it. He Jianqiu broke the rules. Medical tourism, rogue clinics, and patchwork regulation mean that one lab in one country can alter the human gene pool for everyone. A single mistake does not stay local. It becomes inheritance.

You may say: but what if it eliminates terrible suffering? Compassion does not require gambling with children. We can pursue cures through ethical routes. The question is not whether we can edit the unborn. It is whether we should. When the patient cannot consent, when the effects are heritable, when the risks are unknown, and when the social consequences are eugenic, the answer must be no.

Draw a bright line: no clinical heritable genome editing. Not because we are anti-science, but because we are pro-child, pro-justice, and pro-humility. The unborn cannot speak. We must speak for them.

claim: Governments and technology companies must do more to protect online privacy and security.
argument:
If you believe you have nothing to hide, you are not alone—and you are not safe. The slogan is comforting because it mistakes privacy for secrecy. Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing; it is about controlling who can use your medical history, your location, your face, your finances, your conversations, and your children’s data. You lock your front door not because you are a criminal but because you decide who enters. Online, that door is being removed by default.

The evidence is not abstract. In 2017, Equifax exposed the Social Security numbers, birth dates, and addresses of 147 million people. Yahoo exposed 3 billion accounts. Marriott exposed 383 million. Change Healthcare exposed the private medical information of roughly 190 million Americans. These are not rare crimes; they are routine failures. When a breach happens, you cannot unshare your Social Security number. You cannot reset your face. You cannot move your mother’s maiden name. You cannot undo the fact that a stalker bought your real-time location, or that a scammer used leaked data to impersonate you to your bank.

Security failures are not victimless. Ransomware attacks have shut down hospitals mid-surgery, delayed cancer treatments, and forced schools to close. The Colonial Pipeline attack disrupted fuel supplies across the East Coast. Identity theft ruins credit and lives. Data brokers sell precise geolocation from hundreds of millions of phones, including visits to abortion clinics, addiction treatment centers, and places of worship. Tech companies profit from surveillance: ad tech, tracking pixels, dark patterns, default sharing, and endless data collection. They say users consent, but consent buried in a forty-page terms-of-service document is not consent. And market competition does not save us, because you cannot comparison-shop privacy when every app demands everything, and network effects lock you into the same few platforms.

Governments are not innocent either. They buy location data to bypass warrants. They use facial recognition with few limits. They hack devices, demand backdoors, and stockpile vulnerabilities. That is exactly why citizens need laws—not because government is trustworthy, but because unchecked power is worse. The answer to bad government surveillance is not “trust us”; it is enforceable rules, transparency, and independent oversight.

You might object that regulation kills innovation. It does not. The GDPR did not kill European tech; it forced companies to know what data they hold and why. Seatbelt laws did not kill cars. Fire codes did not kill buildings. Security mandates can create markets for trustworthy technology, just as food safety laws created markets for safer food. You might object that privacy is a personal responsibility. But you cannot personally audit every app, router, credit bureau, and hospital system. Even security experts get breached. We do not ask diners to inspect restaurant kitchens; we have health codes. We do not ask drivers to crash-test their own cars; we have safety standards.

You might object that companies already compete on privacy. Some do, but privacy is often a premium feature for those who can pay. The baseline should protect everyone, not just the wealthy and the technical. You might object that perfect security is impossible. True. But “not perfect” is not an argument for nothing. Locks do not eliminate theft. Police do not eliminate crime. Medicine does not eliminate death. We still use them because they reduce harm dramatically.

Governments must do more: pass comprehensive privacy laws with data minimization, opt-in consent for sensitive data, rights to access, delete, and correct, limits on data brokers, bans on selling location and health data, warrant requirements for location and communications, independent regulators with teeth, breach notification, security standards for critical sectors, and transparency for algorithms. Technology companies must do more: encrypt by default, end-to-end where possible, collect less, make privacy settings the default, stop dark patterns, support security updates for the lifespan of devices, submit to independent audits, pay bug bounties, refuse to sell sensitive data, disclose government requests, and design for vulnerable users.

The skeptic says, “I have nothing to hide.” But you have something to protect: your identity, your family, your freedom to speak, love, worship, dissent, and make mistakes without a permanent record. Privacy is not a luxury for the guilty. It is infrastructure for the innocent. Governments and technology companies built the digital world; they must secure it. Doing more is not anti-tech or anti-government. It is pro-civilization. The question is not whether we can afford to protect online privacy and security. It is whether we can afford not to.

claim: Gravity causes objects to fall towards the earth.
argument:
You can test this yourself in under a minute. Hold a book at arm’s length, let go, and watch it accelerate downward. Now imagine doing it in a vacuum chamber with a feather and a hammer. In air, the feather flutters and the hammer thuds; in a vacuum, they hit the floor together. That single fact destroys every explanation that says objects fall because they are heavy, dense, or “earthy.” If weight or density were the cause, the feather and the hammer could never fall identically. They do—because something acts on all mass alike, and that something is gravity.

Gravity is not a vague word for “things fall down.” It is a mutual attraction between masses. Newton quantified it: every mass pulls on every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. That law explains why an apple falls toward Earth and why the Moon falls around Earth. The Moon is not exempt from gravity; it is constantly falling toward Earth, but its sideways motion keeps it missing. The same mathematics predicts the tides, the orbits of planets, and the return of comets. It is not a story invented after the fact; it is a predictive engine. When Newton’s laws were used to predict the existence and position of Neptune, astronomers found it within a degree of the predicted spot. That is not coincidence. That is gravity.

You might object that we cannot see gravity itself, only its effects. But that is true of every force. We do not see magnetism either; we see iron filings align. In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured gravity directly in a laboratory by watching lead spheres attract one another with a tiny twist of a wire. Since then, we have measured gravity between masses in countless experiments. We have dropped atoms in vacuum towers and watched them accelerate at 9.8 meters per second squared, regardless of what they are made of. We have sent clocks into orbit and found they run at different rates because Earth’s gravity warps time itself—a prediction of Einstein’s general relativity, confirmed daily by GPS satellites. If gravity were not real, GPS would drift by kilometers per day. Engineers must correct for it. They do.

Now consider the alternatives. “Objects fall because of density” fails immediately in a vacuum, where there is no buoyancy and no medium to be denser than. A feather and a hammer fall together. “Objects fall because it is their nature to seek the center of the universe” is not an explanation; it is a restatement. It tells you nothing about why the acceleration is 9.8, why it weakens with altitude, why the Moon orbits instead of crashing straight down, or why tides follow the Moon’s phases. Gravity tells you all of it. It even tells you that light bends around the Sun, which was observed during a solar eclipse in 1919 and has been confirmed thousands of times since through gravitational lensing. A “force” that predicts the bending of starlight, the ticking of clocks, the path of spacecraft, and the shape of galaxies is not a convenience. It is the simplest explanation that fits every observation.

Einstein did not refute gravity; he deepened it. Instead of a mysterious pull across empty space, he showed that mass and energy curve the geometry of spacetime, and objects follow the straightest possible paths through that curved geometry. The apple falls because Earth’s mass bends the spacetime around it. The effect is tiny for an apple and enormous for a planet, but it is the same effect. Whether you use Newton’s law for everyday life or Einstein’s equations for GPS and black holes, the conclusion is the same: mass shapes the motion of other mass, and near Earth that motion is downward.

So when you see a dropped stone, a falling leaf, a satellite orbiting, a tide rising, or a galaxy bending light, you are seeing one underlying phenomenon. Gravity causes objects to fall toward the Earth. The evidence is not a matter of opinion. It is in vacuum chambers, torsion balances, eclipse photographs, satellite clocks, and the orbits of every planet we have ever tracked. If you still doubt it, you are not doubting a theory; you are doubting the most thoroughly tested regularity in the history of science. The stone falls. The reason has a name. It is gravity.

claim: Ice is a solid state of water.
argument:
If you’re skeptical, ask a simple question: what is ice made of? The answer is not a mystery. It is H₂O—the same molecule as liquid water and steam. The only difference is how those molecules are arranged and how much they move. In ice, water molecules are locked into a hexagonal crystal lattice by hydrogen bonds. They vibrate in place but do not slide past one another. That is exactly what a solid is: a substance with a fixed volume and a fixed shape, whose particles are held in a stable, repeating structure. Ice does not merely resemble a solid; it satisfies the physical definition.

The chemical evidence is decisive. Freezing and melting are physical changes, not chemical reactions. When water freezes, no new substance is created. The O–H covalent bonds within each water molecule remain intact; only the weaker hydrogen bonds between molecules reorganize. If ice were a different compound, melting it would require breaking and reforming chemical bonds, and we would see a chemical reaction. Instead, ice melts at 0°C at normal pressure and yields pure liquid water. We can measure the latent heat: 334 joules per gram, absorbed to break intermolecular attractions, not to destroy molecules. X-ray diffraction shows the same H₂O units in a crystal lattice. Spectroscopy shows the same molecules with different hydrogen bonding. Density changes from 0.917 g/cm³ to 1.0 g/cm³ because the lattice is open, not because the substance changes identity.

The objection usually comes from language, not chemistry. In everyday speech, “water” often means the liquid we drink. But scientifically, water is the chemical substance H₂O, and it can exist in three common states: solid (ice), liquid (water), gas (water vapor). We don’t say steam is not water because it’s a gas; we call it water vapor. Likewise, ice is not a different thing from water—it is water in its solid state. The word “ice” names the solid phase, not a new compound. Dry ice, by contrast, is solid carbon dioxide, a different molecule. Water ice is solid water.

So the claim is not a semantic trick. It is the only coherent way to describe the facts. Ice has the same chemical identity as liquid water, undergoes a reversible phase change at a sharp melting point, and meets the defining physical criteria of a solid. If you melt it, you get water. If you freeze water, you get ice. The substance never changes; only its state does. To deny this, you would have to explain why the same molecules, the same formula, and the same reversible freezing-and-melting cycle suddenly become a different substance just because they stopped flowing. Ice is a solid state of water.

claim: Humans need oxygen to breathe.
argument:
Try this thought experiment. Seal yourself in a small, airtight room. The air is still there. Your chest can still rise and fall. You can still move gas in and out of your lungs. But as the oxygen is consumed and replaced by carbon dioxide, you will not merely feel uncomfortable. You will grow confused, then drowsy, then unconscious. Within minutes, your brain cells will begin to die. If oxygen were optional, that room would be harmless. It is not.

The reason is that breathing is not the goal. Breathing is the delivery system. Every cell in your body runs on ATP, the molecular currency of energy. Most of that ATP is produced in mitochondria by oxidative phosphorylation. At the end of the electron transport chain, oxygen waits as the terminal electron acceptor. It takes electrons and protons and forms water. Without oxygen, the electrons have nowhere to go. The chain backs up. NADH and FADH2 cannot be recycled. The Krebs cycle stalls. ATP production collapses. You can generate a tiny amount of ATP anaerobically, but not nearly enough for your brain, heart, and muscles to keep working. Ion pumps fail, cells swell, and tissue dies.

This is not a theory. It is why pure nitrogen asphyxiation is so deadly. In an atmosphere of nitrogen with no oxygen, a person can collapse within a minute or two, often without any warning. They are still “breathing” in the mechanical sense—the diaphragm moves, the lungs inflate—but there is no oxygen to accept electrons. They die anyway. That single fact should settle the matter: the act of moving air is not what keeps you alive. The oxygen in that air is.

Medicine confirms it every day. Pulse oximeters measure oxygen saturation because that number predicts whether tissues are getting what they need. Carbon monoxide poisoning kills because carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen does, so blood can be full of oxygen-carrying capacity yet deliver almost none of it. A person can breathe normally and still suffocate at the cellular level. High-altitude climbers lose consciousness when oxygen partial pressure falls, even though they are breathing harder than ever. Ventilators and supplemental oxygen save lives precisely because they restore the one molecule the body cannot store, cannot substitute, and cannot live without for more than a few minutes.

So if you doubt the claim, do not just look at the rise and fall of a chest. Follow a single oxygen molecule: into the nose, down the trachea, into the alveoli, across a membrane, onto hemoglobin, through the bloodstream, into a cell, into a mitochondrion, and finally onto the electron transport chain. That is where breathing ends and life continues. Remove that molecule, and the whole chain stops. You can call the movement of air “breathing” if you like, but without oxygen it is only the motion of a body that is already shutting down. Humans need oxygen to breathe because breathing, in any sense that matters, is the process of getting oxygen to the cells that will die without it.

claim: Internet access should not be considered a basic human right
argument:
If you can’t imagine modern life without the internet, you’re not wrong. It is how many of us work, learn, organize, pray, fall in love, and hold power accountable. But “basic human right” is not a synonym for “very important.” It is a precise moral and legal category—and the internet does not belong in it.

Basic human rights are the entitlements that belong to every person simply because they are human. They are universal, pre-political, and independent of any particular technology, economy, or era. The right to life, to freedom from torture, to a fair trial, to conscience, to expression, to assembly—these would exist even if every server on earth went dark. They are claims we can make against any government, in any century, whether it is rich or poor, wired or not. The internet is none of those things. It is a medium, a tool, a bundle of infrastructure, devices, skills, electricity, and content. It is historically contingent. It is unevenly distributed. It can be shut off, censored, monopolized, and made obsolete. A basic human right cannot be dependent on a supply chain.

Consider the things we already treat as essential but do not call basic human rights. We do not say there is a human right to a telephone, a postal service, a printing press, or electricity. Yet each was once—and in some ways still is—a gateway to speech, commerce, and participation. We protected the underlying rights: expression, association, privacy, access to information. Then we built and regulated the infrastructure. That division is not a loophole. It is what keeps rights coherent. If internet access is a basic human right, then so is the device, the electricity, the literacy, the language, the server, the spectrum, and the technician who repairs the line. At some point, you are no longer describing a right. You are describing a public utility with a very long bill of materials.

That matters because rights impose duties. If internet access is a basic human right, who owes it to you? At what speed? On what device? In what language? With what content? If a rural village lacks fiber, is that a human rights violation—and by whom? If a government provides cheap access but filters every dissenting site, has it fulfilled the right or violated it? If a private company controls the pipes, is it now a human rights guarantor? These are not gotcha questions. They are the reason basic rights must be determinate enough to be claimed and enforced. Internet access is a policy goal with trade-offs—cost, competition, infrastructure, censorship, digital literacy—not a single moral entitlement that can be declared into existence.

There is also a danger in rights inflation. When everything good is called a basic human right, the moral force of the term erodes. Authoritarians love this. They can boast of “internet access” while jailing bloggers, or shut down networks in the name of security, and still claim to be rights-respecting. The real rights—expression, assembly, privacy, due process—are the ones that constrain them. Meanwhile, in democratic societies, treating access as a fundamental right can hand enormous power to the platforms that provide it, turning private companies into arbiters of a supposedly universal entitlement. The sharper claim is stronger: people have the right to seek, receive, and impart information and ideas; they have the right to assemble and speak. The internet is one means of exercising those rights today. It is not the right itself.

None of this means we should shrug at the digital divide. We should pursue universal, affordable, open internet with the seriousness of a public utility. We should subsidize infrastructure, break monopolies, protect net neutrality, teach digital skills, and defend an open web. That is a better fight, and a more honest one. It lets us argue for real policies without pretending that a fiber optic cable is a moral absolute. It also keeps our rights vocabulary sharp for the abuses that truly threaten human dignity.

The internet is essential. That is exactly why it deserves serious policy, not a category error. Basic human rights are the principles that protect us regardless of technology. Internet access is how many of us exercise those principles now. Keep it vital. Keep it universal. But do not call it basic—because that distinction protects both the internet and the idea of human rights.

claim: It is fair for insurers and lenders to use credit scores and risk models.
argument:
Fairness is not the same as equal outcomes. It is the same as equal rules. When two people ask a lender for $10,000 or an insurer for coverage, they are not asking for a moral verdict. They are asking someone else to bear a risk. The only honest way to set the price is to estimate that risk. Credit scores and risk models do exactly that—imperfectly, but more fairly than any realistic alternative.

Consider what happens without them. A loan officer with a gut feeling. An insurer with a checklist. A bank that demands collateral or a personal reference. These systems are not neutral. They are breeding grounds for discrimination, favoritism, and redlining. Credit scores replaced much of that discretion with a transparent, auditable number. They do not ask your race, religion, or who your parents know. They ask whether you have paid your bills, how much you owe, how long you have used credit. Those are not perfect measures of virtue, but they are powerful predictors of default. And prediction is the point.

The evidence is not mysterious. Across millions of loans, credit scores separate borrowers who are likely to repay from those who are not. Insurers have repeatedly found that credit-based insurance scores predict claims—often better than income or neighborhood. That is why lenders can offer lower rates to low-risk borrowers and why insurers can charge lower premiums to safer drivers. If you ban those tools, you do not eliminate risk. You just hide it. The cost gets spread across everyone. Low-risk people pay more. High-risk people may get credit they cannot repay, then face foreclosure or bankruptcy. Or lenders ration credit, favoring the wealthy and well-connected. That is not fairness; it is a subsidy paid by the careful to the careless, or by the poor to the rich.

You may say: but credit scores correlate with race and class, and past injustice shapes them. True. But correlation is not the same as discrimination. A risk factor can be correlated with race and still be fair to use if it predicts risk independently and if there is no less discriminatory alternative that works as well. Banning credit scores would not erase those correlations. It would force lenders and insurers to guess—and guessing usually favors the already powerful. The real answer to historical injustice is not to make risk invisible. It is to make the models better: correct errors, include rent and utility payments, allow appeals, cap rates, and regulate for disparate impact. A credit score is not a permanent brand. It changes as behavior changes. That is a feature, not a bug.

Finally, fairness under uncertainty means treating like risks alike. If two borrowers have the same probability of default, they should pay the same rate. If two drivers have the same expected claims, they should pay the same premium. Credit scores and risk models are the most practical way we have to approximate that. They are not perfect. But the alternative—arbitrary pricing, hidden cross-subsidies, and subjective gatekeeping—is far less fair. Insurers and lenders are not moral judges. They are risk managers. Using the best available, regulated, and transparent tools to manage risk is not just permissible. It is fair.

claim: Individuals must take responsibility for online privacy without excessive government mandates.
argument:
You don’t have to trust corporations to be skeptical of government mandates. The question isn’t whether privacy matters. It’s who can protect it in the moments that actually decide whether your data is exposed. And in those moments—when an app asks for your location, when a site wants your contacts, when you reuse a password across ten accounts, when you click “accept all” because you’re tired—the law is not in the room. You are.

That is the uncomfortable truth at the heart of online privacy: it is not a product that can be delivered by statute. It is a practice. And like every practice, it depends on the person doing it.

Consider how privacy actually fails. Most breaches begin with a phishing email, a weak password, an unpatched device, an over-permissioned app, or a user who handed over data without reading the terms. Laws can punish a company after the damage is done. They cannot click “deny” for you. They cannot generate a unique password for every account. They cannot notice that a “free” flashlight app wants access to your microphone and contacts. They cannot teach you to pause before you post a photo that reveals your home address. Privacy is personal because the attack surface is personal.

This is why excessive government mandates so often become theater. The most visible result of privacy regulation for many users has been a flood of cookie banners—pop-ups that don’t make you safer, but train you to click “accept all” faster. That is not consent. That is fatigue. The law intended to empower users, but it created a ritual that many people now sleepwalk through. Meanwhile, the data economy kept humming.

There is also a deeper problem: compliance costs are a moat. Large tech companies can afford armies of lawyers, privacy officers, and consultants. Startups cannot. Sweeping mandates often entrench the very giants people distrust, because only the giants can absorb the overhead. If you want competition, innovation, and alternatives to Big Tech, you should be wary of rules that make it harder for challengers to exist.

And once government has the power to mandate how data is collected, it also has the power to mandate how it is accessed. The same authority that “protects” privacy can be turned into digital ID systems, encryption backdoors, data retention laws, and surveillance programs. Power is sticky. It expands. A mandate written to protect you today can be used to track you tomorrow. Anonymity—essential for dissidents, journalists, abuse survivors, and ordinary people who don’t want every thought tied to their legal name—is fragile under expansive state control.

None of this means government has no role. Targeted laws against outright fraud, breach, and deceptive data practices are legitimate. But the claim here is about excessive mandates: the sprawling, prescriptive regimes that try to micromanage every cookie, algorithm, and app permission. Those regimes are slow, blunt, and easily captured. They cannot keep pace with technology. They cannot replace individual judgment.

Individual responsibility is not blame. It does not mean you are at fault if a corporation violates your trust. It means you have agency. And that agency is real. After the Equifax breach exposed the data of nearly 150 million people, one of the most effective immediate protections was a credit freeze—something individuals had to initiate themselves. When Apple introduced App Tracking Transparency, most users chose not to be tracked. That shift came not from a statute, but from a company responding to consumer demand and competition. When millions install ad blockers, trackers lose revenue. When millions switch to Signal, ProtonMail, DuckDuckGo, or Firefox, the market moves. When millions refuse apps that demand unnecessary permissions, developers redesign.

This is not naive optimism. It is leverage. Individual choices aggregate into market pressure. Market pressure changes defaults. Changed defaults protect people who never read a privacy policy. That is how decentralized change works: it starts with people who are willing to take responsibility, and it spreads.

What does that responsibility look like in practice? It is not heroic. Use a password manager. Turn on two-factor authentication. Update your devices. Audit app permissions. Use a privacy-focused browser and search engine. Pay for services instead of being the product. Freeze your credit. Teach your family to be skeptical. Treat every “allow” as a decision, because it is. These habits are learnable. They are teachable. They are faster and more resilient than waiting for a distant regulator to fix a problem that changes every week.

The choice is not between perfect individual control and perfect government protection. Neither exists. The real choice is between a society that treats privacy as a personal practice—supported by education, culture, and narrow, accountable laws—and one that waits for a mandate to save it. The first is hard, but it is empowering. The second is easy to promise and easy to abuse.

So take responsibility. Not because you are alone, but because you are the first and last line of defense. Build the habits. Use the tools. Reward good actors. Punish bad ones. Demand better from companies. And keep government’s role narrow, transparent, and accountable. Privacy is not a law you wait for. It is a habit you build.

claim: Internet access should be considered a basic human right
argument:
Imagine a student who has to sit in a fast-food parking lot to finish her homework because her family cannot afford broadband. A veteran who cannot book a medical appointment because the clinic has moved online. A dissident whose entire country is plunged into digital darkness the moment protests begin. These are not minor inconveniences. They are exclusions from the modern world—and when exclusion from the modern world means exclusion from education, health, work, speech, and political power, it becomes a human rights question.

Internet access should be considered a basic human right because it is no longer a luxury layered on top of society. It is the infrastructure through which society now operates. We do not treat electricity as a human right because we worship light bulbs. We treat it as essential because without it, homes are unlivable, hospitals cannot function, and economies stall. The internet has become that kind of infrastructure: the nervous system of daily life. It is how we learn, apply for jobs, bank, receive government benefits, see a doctor, organize with neighbors, report abuse, and participate in democracy. When one gatekeeper controls access to all of those things, access to that gatekeeper is not a commodity. It is a precondition of dignity and agency.

Human rights are not a list of things that would be nice for everyone to have. They are the conditions necessary for a person to live a life of dignity and to participate in the life of their community. We recognize education as a right not because schools are pleasant, but because without education a person cannot fully exercise freedom, find work, or understand their own rights. We recognize freedom of expression not because speech is always harmless, but because without it, citizens cannot hold power accountable. The internet has become the primary means by which those rights are exercised. The United Nations Human Rights Council affirmed in 2011 that the same rights people have offline must also be protected online. A 2016 resolution condemned deliberate government shutdowns as violations of international human rights law. That is not sentimentality. It is a recognition that the medium has become inseparable from the right.

Consider what happens when access is denied. During the COVID-19 pandemic, millions of students without reliable internet simply disappeared from classrooms. Patients could not use telehealth. Workers could not apply for unemployment benefits that existed only online. Vaccine appointments, housing applications, job listings, school assignments, court hearings, and public meetings migrated to the internet, and those on the wrong side of the digital divide were locked out. Globally, roughly 2.6 billion people remain offline. They are disproportionately poor, rural, female, elderly, disabled, and marginalized. This is not a random gap. It is a new layer of inequality that compounds old ones. If we believe rights are universal, we cannot accept a world where rights are delivered through a portal that only some people can enter.

The skeptic says: “The internet is not food or water. It is not a basic right.” But rights are interdependent. Food assistance, housing vouchers, and medical enrollment are increasingly administered online. A person who cannot get online cannot get food. Water bills, school lunch forms, and emergency alerts are digital. The internet is not competing with survival; it is often the means of survival. The skeptic says: “Governments cannot afford to give everyone internet.” But governments already spend far more managing the consequences of exclusion: lost education, untreated illness, unemployment, and social fragmentation. Treating internet access as a public utility—like roads, postal service, or electricity—does not mean free gigabit fiber for everyone. It means universal, affordable, nondiscriminatory access, public access points, device and literacy programs, and a legal guarantee against arbitrary disconnection.

The skeptic says: “Private companies own the internet. It cannot be a right.” But private companies also own hospitals, schools, and utilities. That is precisely why we regulate them in the public interest. A right to internet access does not mean a right to a particular company’s service. It means a right not to be cut off from the public square because of poverty or geography. The skeptic says: “The internet enables crime, harassment, and misinformation.” So does the postal service, the telephone, and free speech itself. We regulate harms without banning the medium. We do not abolish roads because drunk drivers use them. We should not abandon the principle of universal access because bad actors exploit it.

The skeptic says: “Authoritarian governments shut down the internet for security. Why should that be a human rights violation?” Because collective punishment is not security. Shutting down the internet silences journalists, stops ambulances, freezes bank accounts, and hides state violence. It is the modern equivalent of cutting the phone lines to a besieged city. The right to internet access does not protect terrorists; it protects everyone else from being made invisible.

What would recognizing internet access as a basic human right actually require? It would require states to ensure that no one is arbitrarily disconnected; that service is affordable and available even in remote and poor communities; that public libraries and community networks provide access; that digital skills are taught; that privacy and net neutrality are protected; and that shutdowns are treated as the serious rights violations they are. It would place obligations not only on governments but on the international community, just as we treat education and health. It would not solve every problem. But it would change the baseline. It would say: you do not have to beg for a seat in the modern world.

The real question is not whether the internet is exactly like air or water. The real question is whether we will allow a new gatekeeper to decide who gets to speak, learn, heal, work, and vote. We have faced this before. Education, suffrage, social security, and disability rights all once seemed radical. Now they are the mark of a decent society. The internet is now the public square, the classroom, the clinic, the workplace, and the town hall. A right to participate in society is meaningless if the door is locked. Internet access is not a privilege for the connected. It is the precondition for the rights we already claim to believe in. Make it a human right, and we begin to make those rights real.

claim: Lifespan extension would exacerbate inequities and should not be pursued
argument:
The first question is not whether aging can be slowed. It is who will be first in line. And the answer, if history is any guide, is the people who already have money, power, and access. Lifespan extension will not arrive as a public utility. It will arrive as a luxury good—patented, bespoke, expensive, and rationed by wealth. That is not a bug; it is the predictable outcome of pursuing a powerful medical technology inside a profoundly unequal world.

You may believe that any technology can eventually be made universal. But look at the technologies we already have. In the United States, the richest 1% live more than a decade longer than the poorest 1%. Globally, life expectancy differs by decades between rich and poor countries. Vaccines, antibiotics, dialysis, organ transplants—every one of these was once hailed as a universal good, and every one of them still follows the contours of money and power. During the COVID-19 pandemic, wealthy nations hoarded vaccines while poor nations waited. Organ transplants go disproportionately to those who can travel, pay, and navigate the system. There is no reason to think the most complex, expensive, and sought-after medical intervention in human history will be different. It will be worse, because the stakes are not just surviving illness—they are postponing death itself.

The first beneficiaries will be the wealthy. They will buy decades. And those decades will not be empty. They will be used to compound advantage. A billionaire who lives to 150 has 100 extra years to invest, inherit, lobby, and shape the rules. A politician who lives to 120 can hold power for a century. A corporate dynasty can entrench itself across generations, controlling land, patents, media, and capital. Meanwhile, the poor will still die in their sixties and seventies from preventable causes. The result is not just economic inequality. It is a biological caste system: some lives are long, some are short, and the difference is written into your bank account.

This is self-reinforcing. The long-lived rich will not vote to redistribute their extra time. They will fund candidates, capture regulators, and ensure that longevity therapies remain proprietary. They will have every incentive to keep the fountain of youth private. The political feedback loop makes equitable access less likely over time, not more. Even if the technology eventually becomes cheap, the first generations of wealthy beneficiaries will have already locked in their advantage. You cannot retroactively redistribute decades of compounded wealth, power, and network effects.

Then there is the opportunity cost. Every dollar and every scientist diverted toward extending the maximum human lifespan is a dollar and a scientist not spent on maternal care, clean water, vaccines, antibiotics, mental health, or nutrition. We already know how to add years to billions of lives. We simply choose not to. Pursuing lifespan extension says, explicitly, that we prefer adding years to the already long-lived. That is not a neutral scientific goal. It is a moral choice, and it is the wrong one.

You might object that we can pursue lifespan extension and ensure equitable access at the same time. But we cannot separate a technology from the society that produces it. If we could guarantee equitable access to life-saving care, we would have already done it. We have not. The same structures that produce existing health inequities—insurance, geography, racism, class, documentation status, time poverty—will govern this technology too. A cheap longevity pill still requires a prescription, a clinic, a day off work, a stable address, and trust in a system that has repeatedly failed marginalized people. If the treatment is continuous, it becomes a subscription to life. Those who miss payments will age and die on schedule.

And the global picture is even darker. Rich countries extending lives means more consumption, more emissions, more resource extraction. Climate change already kills poor people first. A longer-lived global elite would be a permanent engine of ecological injustice, consuming the planet’s resources for centuries while the global South suffers the consequences.

The claim is not that longer life is inherently bad. It is that pursuing lifespan extension as a technological goal, in a world of profound inequity, is a guarantee of deeper inequity. We should not pursue it. We should pursue a world where no one dies of preventable causes, where health is a right rather than a luxury, where every life is valued equally in practice. Until then, extending the maximum lifespan is not progress for humanity. It is progress for the few, paid for by the many. Refuse it.

claim: Limits should be placed on acceptable human risk levels for initial Mars colonization missions
argument:
If we send people to Mars without a hard ceiling on how much death and suffering we are willing to call acceptable, we will not have founded a settlement. We will have opened a sacrifice zone.

The skeptic says: pioneers have always accepted risk. Columbus sailed into the unknown. Antarctic explorers froze and starved. Astronauts are volunteers. Why smother Mars with bureaucratic limits? But that objection confuses courage with abandonment. The early Arctic expeditions were not noble because men died of scurvy, lead poisoning, and cannibalism; they were tragic because much of that death was preventable and often caused by vanity, poor planning, and no independent oversight. We do not admire the deaths. We admire the survivors and the lessons that made later polar science safer and more productive. Mars is not a chance to repeat the worst of the Age of Exploration. It is a chance to apply everything we learned from it.

Risk limits are not the opposite of exploration. They are what make exploration sustainable. Aviation did not become mass transport by accepting crashes as the price of progress; it became mass transport because regulators, engineers, and insurers set limits on acceptable risk and forced redundancy, training, and accountability. Nuclear power did not become safer because operators were brave; it became safer because independent bodies imposed thresholds and the principle that risk must be kept as low as reasonably achievable. NASA itself uses quantitative risk criteria for astronauts, including radiation exposure limits and mission fatality probabilities. We already accept that some risks are too high to authorize, even for volunteers. Mars should not be an exception.

The ethical case is even stronger than the engineering case. Consent is necessary but not sufficient. We do not let workers consent to slavery, to unlimited asbestos exposure, or to being experimented on without oversight. Why? Because some risks are so severe, irreversible, or imposed on third parties that society must set a floor. A Mars colonist’s consent is compromised by distance, monopoly, desperation, ideology, and the simple fact that no one can fully understand the psychological and medical reality of living in a sealed habitat under radiation and low gravity until they are already there. If a private company offers the only ticket, and the applicant has dreamed of Mars for twenty years, is that truly free consent? And what about the children born there? They cannot consent to radiation, bone loss, or a lifetime without a return option. A risk policy that ignores them is not libertarian; it is negligent.

Without limits, the race to Mars becomes a race to the bottom. History is clear on this: Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia were not caused by engineers who lacked data. They were caused by organizations that normalized deviance—that gradually accepted anomalies as acceptable because the schedule demanded it. On Mars, the anomalies will be worse: leaks, dust storms, radiation spikes, medical emergencies, psychological breakdowns, and equipment failures that cannot be fixed with a supply run from Earth. If no independent authority can say “this mission is too dangerous to launch,” then the people who profit from arrival will also define what counts as acceptable death. That is not a frontier. It is a company town with no exit.

So what should limits look like? They need not be zero risk; zero risk is impossible. But they must be explicit, quantitative where possible, and enforced by people who do not benefit from launch. At minimum: a maximum acceptable probability of crew fatality for an initial mission, set by independent experts; radiation and medical exposure limits that protect both crew and future generations; redundancy for critical life-support and return systems; a real abort or return option whenever physically possible; psychological screening and support; no children until the risks are characterized and their rights are guaranteed; and an independent safety board with the power to halt a launch and the funding to say no without retaliation. The exact numbers are debatable. The absence of any number is indefensible.

We will go to Mars. The question is whether we go as a species that learned from Challenger, from thalidomide, from company towns, and from every frontier where human beings were treated as fuel—or as one that repeats them on a planet with no rescue. Limits are not chains on daring. They are the rails that let it run. If we will not say “this much death is too much” before the first launch, we never will. And the first people on Mars will know, with perfect clarity, that they were sent under a rule that placed no numerical limit on their lives. That is not a mission. That is a moral failure with a launch window.
