claim: No limits should be placed on acceptable human risk for initial Mars colonization missions
argument:
Every limit on acceptable risk for the first Mars colonists is a number invented by people who will never set foot on Mars. It is a guess dressed as ethics. The Martian frontier is not a laboratory where we can pre-calculate every failure mode; it is an unknown world with unknown physics, unknown biology, unknown psychology. Any cap—1 in 100, 1 in 20, 1 in 2—is arbitrary. It does not make the mission safer. It only makes it slower, more expensive, and more likely to fail before it begins.

The deeper error is moral. The people who go to Mars will not be conscripts. They will be volunteers—scientists, engineers, dreamers—who understand that the first landing may be one-way and that the first colony may be a graveyard. We already permit adults to risk their lives for causes they deem greater than themselves: soldiers, firefighters, test pilots, mountaineers, astronauts. We do not tell a firefighter he may enter a burning building only if the odds of death are below an arbitrary threshold. We honor his choice. Why should we treat a Mars colonist as a child who cannot weigh his own life against the future of the species?

To impose limits from Earth is paternalism at cosmic scale. It says: we know better than you what your life is worth. It denies the pioneer the one thing that makes the risk meaningful—agency. If a competent adult, fully informed, chooses to accept a 50 percent chance of dying on Mars, or an 80 percent chance, or a 99 percent chance, the rest of us have no right to veto that choice. We may grieve. We may disagree. We may not forbid. The only legitimate limit is the one the colonist sets for himself.

Practical experience proves the point. Safety bureaucracies do not eliminate risk; they redistribute it into delay, secrecy, and false confidence. When regulators demand impossible guarantees, engineers do not discover magic; they write risk assessments that say what must be said, cut corners elsewhere, and push the launch date past the point of political viability. The greatest danger to a Mars mission is not that it is too risky. It is that it will be smothered by people who believe risk can be legislated away. Mars will not be settled by the timid. It will be settled by those who accept that the first footsteps may be the last for some.

And what is the alternative? A species that stays home. Earth is not safe. It has been struck by asteroids, scorched by supervolcanoes, and is now capable of destroying itself with nuclear weapons, engineered pandemics, and ecological collapse. A self-sustaining Mars colony is not a luxury; it is insurance for civilization. The question is not whether a few hundred volunteers should risk death. It is whether we are willing to risk a few hundred lives to prevent the potential extinction of billions. Every year we hesitate, the window narrows. Every limit we impose makes the first colony less likely to survive. If we wait until Mars is safe, we will never go.

History is unambiguous. Polynesian voyagers crossed the Pacific without knowing what waited. The Mayflower sailed into a winter that killed half its passengers. Apollo 1 burned; Challenger and Columbia broke apart; and still we flew. Those deaths were not meaningless. They were the tuition of a species learning to leave its cradle. If our ancestors had demanded that no one die in the pursuit of discovery, we would still be living in caves, afraid of the dark. Mars is the new ocean. The first ships will be dangerous. Some will not return. That is not a reason to ban the voyage. It is the reason the voyage matters.

So place no limits on acceptable risk for the first Mars colonists. Not because their lives are cheap, but because their choice is sacred. Not because danger is good, but because the only way to learn how to live on Mars is to go. Not because we are reckless, but because the alternative—a single-planet species waiting for the next catastrophe—is the greatest risk of all. Let the volunteers go. Let them set their own threshold. Let them be the founders, not the victims. The first Mars colony will be built by people who understand that they may die. That is the price of making humanity multiplanetary. It is a price they are willing to pay. We have no right to refuse them.

claim: Penguins of all existing species are biologically incapable of self-powered flight.
argument:
Consider what flight actually requires. A bird does not fly by flapping harder or wanting it more; it flies by generating aerodynamic lift. Lift depends on air density, wing area, the square of airspeed, and the wing’s lift coefficient. Air is thin. To leave the ground and stay aloft, a bird must have wings large and light enough, flexible enough, and strong enough to push against that thin air and produce lift equal to its body weight. Penguins fail that test at every point—not by a little, but by an enormous, structural margin.

Start with the wing. A penguin’s wing is not a wing in the aerial sense. It is a flipper: a stiff, flattened paddle with reduced elbow and wrist joints, little ability to fold, twist, or change shape, and feathers that form a dense, continuous surface rather than separated, slotted flight feathers. Those flippers are magnificent underwater. Water is roughly 800 times denser than air, so the same flipper that produces powerful thrust in the ocean produces almost nothing useful in the sky. A penguin flapping in air is like a rower trying to row a boat through fog.

Now add the body. Penguins have dense, solid bones rather than the hollow, pneumatic bones of many flying birds. They carry thick blubber and tightly packed plumage. This lowers buoyancy and helps them dive, but it also makes them heavy for their size. Their feet are set far back, ideal for steering underwater and terrible for running. The result is a wing loading—body weight divided by wing area—that is wildly too high for aerial flight. An emperor penguin, for example, weighs around 30 kilograms and has a total flipper area on the order of a couple of tenths of a square metre. To generate enough lift just to sustain level flight, it would need to move air over those flippers at roughly 40 metres per second—about 90 miles per hour. It cannot run that fast, and its flipper stroke cannot generate that airflow in air. Takeoff is not difficult; it is physically impossible.

You may object that penguins flap their wings, launch out of the water, and “fly” beneath the surface. All true—and none of it is aerial flight. Underwater, they are not flying through air; they are swimming through a medium dense enough to make their flippers effective. When they leap from the sea onto ice, they are projectiles. They are powered by swimming muscles and buoyancy, not by aerodynamic lift, and once airborne they cannot sustain height, steer, or climb. They fall back down. That is not flight; that is a jump.

You may also object that penguins are birds, and birds fly. But flightlessness has evolved many times: ostriches, emus, kiwis, dodos, great auks. Being a bird no more guarantees flight than being a mammal guarantees walking on two legs. Penguins are a lineage that traded the sky for the sea. Their ancestors could fly, but evolution reshaped them into underwater flyers of extraordinary skill. The trade-off was permanent. No amount of training, motivation, or perfect diet will make a penguin fly, any more than practice will let a human breathe water.

The evidence is not merely theoretical. Every one of the world’s penguin species—emperor, king, gentoo, Adélie, chinstrap, little blue, African, Humboldt, Magellanic, Galápagos, rockhopper, macaroni, yellow-eyed, and the rest—shares the same flightless body plan. In zoos, in the wild, under high-speed cameras, across millions of hours of observation, no penguin has ever been documented taking off from land or ice and sustaining self-powered flight. If any species could, we would know. The prediction is simple: find a penguin with large, light, flexible, slotted wings, hollow bones, a running takeoff, and a flight muscle arrangement built for air. No such penguin exists.

So the claim is not a limitation of effort or opportunity. It is a fact of anatomy, physics, and evolution. Penguins are biologically incapable of self-powered aerial flight. They fly—spectacularly—but only through water. The sky is closed to them.

claim: People receiving welfare benefits should be tracked to prevent fraud/abuse.
argument:
If you believe in a strong safety net, you should demand that it be tracked. Not because people who receive welfare are criminals, but because public money is a trust—and trusts require accounting. The choice is not between compassion and scrutiny. It is between a system that can prove it helps the people it claims to help and one that bleeds resources until voters lose faith and cut it altogether.

Start with what “tracked” actually means. It does not mean GPS ankle monitors or caseworkers peering into your living room. It means the same basic verification that governs every other major financial system: prove you are eligible, report when your circumstances change, and let auditors follow the money. Banks track deposits. Employers track payroll. Credit card companies track transactions to stop theft. There is no reason the safety net should be the one large pool of public money that operates on the honor system.

The scale of leakage is not hypothetical. In fiscal year 2023, the USDA reported an improper payment rate of about 11 percent in SNAP—roughly $4.7 billion in overpayments, underpayments, and errors. Medicaid improper payments run into the tens of billions annually. During the pandemic, unemployment insurance lost tens of billions to fraud, much of it to organized rings using stolen identities. These are not rounding errors. They are meals not delivered, rent not paid, and healthcare not provided. Every dollar lost to a double-dip, a dead recipient, a fake household, or a skimming operation is a dollar taken from someone who genuinely needs it.

And who suffers most when fraud goes unchecked? Honest recipients. Fraud becomes the headline that politicians use to justify cuts. It becomes the stigma that follows every parent using an EBT card. It becomes the reason a working mother is treated with suspicion at the checkout line. Tracking is not the enemy of the vulnerable; it is the shield that protects them from being smeared by the few who game the system.

Now consider privacy. The objection is serious, but it is not a reason to abandon accountability. It is a reason to design tracking narrowly. We do not need to know what you buy at the grocery store or whom you text. We need to know whether your income still qualifies you, whether you live in the state, whether the same person is enrolled in three programs under two names, whether a deceased person’s benefits are still being claimed. Government already holds wage records, tax data, death records, and residency data. Matching them is cheap, fast, and far less invasive than a credit check. Strict audit trails, penalties for misuse, and due-process appeals can keep the system honest without turning it into a surveillance state.

The cost objection also collapses under scrutiny. Data matching is not a new bureaucracy; it is a software layer on databases that already exist. Preventing one major fraud ring or catching thousands of ineligible cases can pay for the system many times over. EBT cards with chip technology, for example, would reduce skimming that steals benefits directly from families. That is not big government; it is basic security.

You might say most recipients are honest. Exactly. That is why tracking should be precise, not universal suspicion. It should flag anomalies—sudden income spikes, duplicate addresses, impossible household compositions—not treat every applicant as a suspect. When the system is clean, honest recipients get approved faster and defended louder. When it is dirty, everyone pays the price.

The deepest mistake is to think accountability and generosity are opposites. They are partners. A welfare program that cannot account for its dollars will eventually lose public support. A welfare program that can account for them can be expanded with confidence. If you want a stronger safety net, you must be willing to protect it. Tracking is not a concession to cynicism. It is a commitment to the idea that help should actually reach the people who need it—and that the public should be able to see that it does.

claim: Prescription drug ads should be allowed on television
argument:
The strongest argument against prescription drug ads is that they turn medicine into marketing. But the strongest argument for them is that they turn medicine back into a conversation. And in a system where too many people suffer in silence, too many conditions go undiagnosed, and too many doctors have fifteen minutes to solve a problem the patient has lived with for years, that conversation is not a luxury. It is a lifeline.

Start with a simple fact: an ad cannot write a prescription. Only a licensed clinician can. The prescription drug ad does not bypass the doctor; it brings the patient to the doctor. It says, “The thing you are feeling has a name. It is not a moral failing. It is not just aging. It is treatable.” For a person with depression, asthma, high cholesterol, diabetes, erectile dysfunction, or a rare condition they have never heard of, that moment of recognition can be the difference between years of avoidable suffering and a diagnosis. Banning the ad does not ban the disease. It bans the clue.

Skeptics worry that ads will push people toward unnecessary or expensive drugs. Sometimes they will. But the alternative—silence—has its own body count. Underdiagnosis is not neutral. Untreated hypertension, unrecognized depression, and ignored symptoms cost lives and money. In the United States, where direct-to-consumer advertising has been allowed for decades, study after study has found that such ads mainly prompt patients to ask questions, seek care, and discuss conditions with physicians. Physicians remain the gatekeepers. They can say no. They can offer a generic. They can diagnose something else entirely. The ad opens the door; the doctor decides whether to walk through it.

What about misleading ads? The answer is not a ban. It is regulation. Federal law already requires prescription drug ads to present a “fair balance” of benefits and risks, to disclose major side effects, and to avoid false or misleading claims. The FDA can demand corrections, impose penalties, and withdraw approval for deceptive marketing. If an ad lies, punish the lie. Do not punish the public’s access to information. We do not ban political speech because some politicians lie. We do not ban weather reports because forecasts are sometimes wrong. We should not ban health information because some marketers exaggerate.

And consider who a ban would actually protect. Not the wealthy, who have concierge doctors and medical journals. Not the educated, who can search PubMed at midnight. A ban would fall hardest on the elderly, the rural, the low-income, the people whose main source of health information is the television in their living room. It would keep them ignorant while the well-connected keep learning. That is not safety. That is paternalism dressed up as caution.

There is also the stigma factor. Television ads for antidepressants, HIV prevention, and other conditions have helped normalize conversations that were once whispered about. They tell people they are not alone. They make it easier to say, “I think I need help.” A society that hides these treatments from the airwaves is not a society that protects patients. It is a society that protects ignorance.

Yes, the pricing system is broken. Yes, brand-name drugs are often too expensive. But banning ads will not fix patents, monopolies, or pharmacy benefit managers. It will simply leave patients less informed while the underlying economics stay exactly the same. If you want to lower costs, demand price transparency, negotiate drug prices, speed generics, and require clear cost information in ads. Do not use a gag order as a substitute for real reform.

The question is not whether drug companies are altruistic. They are not. The question is whether adults should be trusted with information about their own bodies. We trust them to vote, to serve on juries, to raise children, to manage their own money. We can trust them to hear a risk list and then ask a doctor, “Is this right for me?”

Allow the ads. Regulate them strictly. Require honesty. Punish deception. But do not pretend that silence is safety. A free society does not fear an informed patient. It fears an uninformed one.

claim: Prescription drug ads should not be allowed on television
argument:
You might think prescription drug ads are just information—maybe even good information. A patient sees a commercial, learns about a condition, asks a doctor, and gets treated. What could be wrong with that?

Everything, when the product is a prescription drug and the medium is television.

Start with what these ads actually are. They are not public service announcements. They are marketing campaigns, designed by people whose job is to make you want a specific brand before you ever enter a doctor’s office. The United States and New Zealand are the only two countries in the developed world that allow this. Every other advanced nation has looked at direct-to-consumer prescription drug advertising and decided that medicine is too important to be sold like laundry detergent. That should tell you something.

The standard defense is that ads educate. But a 60-second commercial cannot deliver informed consent. It cannot know your kidney function, your pregnancy status, your other prescriptions, your history of heart disease, or whether your symptoms even match the diagnosis being sold. It cannot tell you that a generic has the same effect for a fraction of the price, or that lifestyle changes might work better, or that the drug’s benefit is modest and its risk is serious. What it can do is show smiling people hiking, dancing, and playing with grandchildren while a rushed voice lists side effects like “suicidal thoughts,” “stroke,” and “death.” The pictures sell the fantasy; the words are legal cover. That is not education. That is emotional manipulation with a warning label.

And the manipulation works. Studies have found that when patients ask for a specific advertised drug, doctors are more likely to prescribe it—even when it is not medically indicated. The phrase “ask your doctor” is not a invitation to a neutral conversation. It is a sales script. It turns patients into unpaid sales representatives and puts doctors in the impossible position of either disappointing someone who has been told by a polished commercial that this pill is their answer, or prescribing something they would not otherwise choose. Medicine should not be practiced under the influence of a prime-time ad.

The costs are not abstract. Advertised brand-name drugs are almost always more expensive than older generics, and those costs are passed to everyone—through insurance premiums, Medicare and Medicaid spending, and out-of-pocket bills. The industry spends billions of dollars every year on these ads because they increase prescriptions. That money does not make drugs safer or more effective. It makes them more familiar. It builds brand loyalty before the first appointment. And it pushes prescribing toward newer, pricier products that are often no better than what came before.

The safety record is just as troubling. Vioxx was heavily advertised before it was withdrawn from the market because of heart risks. Testosterone ads turned a real but narrow medical condition into a national marketing campaign, prescriptions soared, and then the FDA had to warn about cardiovascular dangers. These are not isolated accidents. They are the predictable result of letting commercials create demand for powerful drugs before the evidence is fully understood.

You might say: “But people should be free to hear about treatments.” They are. Nothing about a ban on television ads would stop drug companies from publishing research, sending information to doctors, funding unbranded disease-awareness campaigns, or making factual information available to patients who seek it. A ban would simply stop the branded sales pitch from ambushing people in their living rooms. The First Amendment does not require us to let drug companies use television as a waiting room. Commercial speech has always been subject to rules that prevent it from misleading the public, and a 60-second pitch for a drug that can kill you is not the same as a soap commercial.

You might also say: “This is paternalistic. Patients can handle the truth.” Of course they can. That is exactly why they deserve better than a commercial. Real information comes from doctors, pharmacists, independent researchers, and evidence-based sources—not from the company that profits when you choose its product. Banning TV ads is not treating people like children. It is treating medicine like medicine.

The question is not whether you trust patients or doctors or government regulators. The question is whether you trust a 60-second sales pitch to carry the weight of a prescription. If a drug is truly better, it does not need a jingle, a celebrity, or a sunset. It needs evidence, and it needs a doctor who is free to follow that evidence without a commercial playing in the back of the room.

Take the salesman out of the living room. Put the decision back in the clinic. Prescription drug ads should not be allowed on television.

claim: Prescription drug importation should be allowed to increase access and lower costs.
argument:
Right now, a vial of insulin that costs about $30 in Canada can cost $300 in the United States. The same drug, often made in the same factory, by the same company, with the same active ingredient. The only difference is the price tag—and the border. That is not a market. That is a hostage situation. Allowing prescription drug importation under a rigorous safety framework is the simplest, most humane way to end it.

Start with safety, because that is the first objection you will hear. Opponents warn of counterfeit, contaminated, or expired drugs. They are right that an open, unregulated border would be dangerous. But no serious importation proposal is that. We already import the active pharmaceutical ingredients for most American drugs from abroad. The FDA inspects foreign manufacturing sites. We can require that imported finished drugs come only from countries with stringent regulators—Canada, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan, Australia—and only from FDA-approved facilities. We can mandate serialization, track-and-trace, tamper-evident packaging, licensed importers, and random testing. If a drug is safe enough for a Canadian or German patient, it is safe enough for an American. The real choice is not between perfect safety and importation. It is between regulated importation and the current black market, where desperate people already buy God-knows-what from unverified websites. Prohibition creates the danger it claims to prevent.

Now consider cost and access. A RAND study found that U.S. prices for brand-name drugs are roughly 2.5 times higher than in comparable wealthy countries. Millions of Americans ration insulin. Cancer patients skip doses. Seniors choose between food and pills. Importation provides immediate relief. Even if Canada alone cannot supply all 330 million Americans, the point is competition. When a licensed importer can buy the same drug abroad for a fraction of the U.S. price, domestic manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers must respond. They can lower prices, or they can watch market share go to imports. That is how arbitrage works. It is why Americans buy cars, electronics, and clothing from abroad. There is no moral reason why medicine should be the exception.

Then there is the innovation myth. Pharma lobbyists say importation will kill research and development. But importation does not abolish patents. It does not allow copies of drugs still on patent. It simply lets Americans buy the genuine, patented product at the price the company already voluntarily charges in other wealthy countries. If a manufacturer can sell the same medicine in Canada for one-third the U.S. price and still profit, the U.S. price is not funding innovation; it is funding price discrimination. Many blockbuster drugs were developed with public funding from the National Institutes of Health. The industry often spends more on marketing and stock buybacks than on the risky early-stage research that importation would supposedly destroy. If pharmaceutical companies want to avoid arbitrage, they can lower U.S. prices to match global averages. That is not a threat to innovation. It is a correction to extortion.

Finally, the “Canada will run out” objection. Canada has warned it cannot supply the entire U.S. market. Fine. We can phase in importation, allow personal importation for chronic conditions, and open the door to other countries with comparable safety standards. We can also negotiate directly with manufacturers. Importation is not a silver bullet; it is a lever. The goal is not to make Canada America’s pharmacy. The goal is to give Americans the same access to affordable medicine that people in every other developed country already enjoy.

The status quo is indefensible. It kills people. It bankrupts families. It makes a mockery of the idea that we live in a free market. The only thing standing between Americans and lower drug prices is a law that protects pharmaceutical profits at the expense of patients. Allow safe importation. Regulate it tightly. Test it. Track it. But allow it. The day we do, the same pills that cost $300 will cost $30—and no one will have to choose between their health and their rent.

claim: Raising the minimum wage to $15 would hurt small businesses and jobs.
argument:
The $15 minimum wage is sold as a simple act of justice: no one who works full-time should be poor. That instinct is right. But a minimum wage is not a gift; it is a price floor on labor. And for small businesses, that price floor is often the difference between hiring and closing.

Consider the arithmetic. A small restaurant with 12 employees, half at $11 an hour, must raise them to $15. That is $4 more per hour, plus payroll taxes, workers’ comp, and unemployment insurance—often 15–20% more on top. For a full-time worker, that is over $8,000 in new annual cost. Six such workers: nearly $50,000. Restaurants typically run on 3–5% margins. A $50,000 hit on a $1 million revenue restaurant can wipe out the entire profit. The owner cannot wave a wand. She can raise prices—but her customers can go to Chipotle, Walmart, or Amazon. She can cut shifts, reduce hours, freeze hiring, delay expansion, replace the cashier with a kiosk, or close. Those are not hypotheticals; they are the standard adjustments small businesses make when labor costs spike.

This is why the Congressional Budget Office estimated that a $15 federal minimum wage by 2025 would eliminate about 1.4 million jobs, even as it raised wages for others. The jobs lost are not random. They are concentrated among the least experienced, least skilled, and most marginal workers—the teenager getting a first job, the returning parent, the worker with a disability, the applicant with a spotty work history. A $15 mandate makes it illegal to hire someone whose productivity is below $15 an hour. That sounds harsh, but it is the reality of a wage floor. Employers do not pay $15 because it is fair; they pay it because they expect at least $15 in value. If they cannot, the job disappears or the hours shrink.

Seattle is often held up as proof that $15 works. But University of Washington researchers found that when Seattle raised its minimum to $13, employers cut hours for low-wage workers, and the average affected worker lost about $125 a month—more than the raise added. Other studies disagree, but the disagreement itself proves the point: the outcome is not a guaranteed raise; it is a gamble with other people’s jobs.

Worse, a uniform $15 wage ignores geography. In Seattle or San Francisco, $15 is modest. In rural Mississippi, a small-town Ohio diner, or a family-run daycare, $15 is a drastic increase. Small businesses in low-cost areas cannot suddenly charge big-city prices. They lose customers, then jobs. Meanwhile, large chains can absorb the cost, automate, and use their scale to crush the local competition. A $15 mandate is not anti-corporate; it is a gift to corporations that can afford it and a burden on the mom-and-pop shops that cannot.

You might say workers will spend their raises and boost the economy. Some will. But a worker whose hours are cut from 40 to 25, or who loses a job entirely, does not spend more. The raise for some is paid for by the lost wages of others. That is not a fair trade; it is a cruel one.

If you want to help low-wage workers, do it directly: expand the earned income tax credit, cut payroll taxes for the lowest earners, invest in childcare and transportation, fund apprenticeships, and create targeted wage subsidies. Those tools help workers without making it illegal for a small business to hire them. A $15 minimum wage sounds like compassion, but in the real world of thin margins and tight competition, it would hurt the small businesses that create jobs and the workers who need them most.

claim: Recreational drone pilots should not require registration and testing
argument:
You are right to want safe skies. But registration and testing for recreational drone pilots are not safety measures; they are paperwork masquerading as safety. A registration number is a sticker. A test is an online quiz. Neither one keeps a drone away from an airport, teaches a pilot to handle a gust of wind, or stops a reckless person from doing something stupid. If these policies were the price of safety, we could debate the trade-off. They are not. They are the price of bureaucracy.

Consider what the recreational test actually is. The FAA’s TRUST test is free, online, open-book, and can be finished in minutes. It does not require flying a drone, demonstrating judgment, or even proving you are who you say you are. It is not a driver’s license. It is a click-through. A kid who ignores it is not more dangerous than a kid who clicks through it. The only thing it reliably produces is a certificate.

Registration is no better. The people who register are, almost by definition, the people already inclined to follow rules. The person who flies over a wildfire, harasses wildlife, or buzzes a plane is not going to pause first to pay a fee and print a number. Registration does not deter them. It gives investigators a lead after the fact—if the drone is recovered, if the number is legible, if the drone was registered at all. That is a thin thread on which to hang a national database of hobbyists.

Meanwhile, the actual risk from recreational drones is small and local. These are not commercial aircraft. They are lightweight, battery-limited, and flown mostly in parks, backyards, and fields. The nightmare scenarios—collisions with airliners—are extraordinarily rare, and they are better prevented by airspace design, geofencing, altitude limits, and severe penalties for interfering with manned aircraft than by making every hobbyist pass a quiz. If someone does something dangerous, we already have laws against reckless endangerment, flying over emergency scenes, invading privacy, and interfering with aircraft. Enforce those. Punish the act, not the hobby.

Then there is the burden. Registration fees, renewal cycles, testing requirements, age rules, and the threat of fines fall on families, students, photographers, and kids who got a drone for their birthday. They turn a harmless pastime into a compliance exercise. They discourage the very people who might become tomorrow’s pilots, engineers, and aerospace workers. The barrier is not trivial; it is regressive. A wealthy hobbyist can absorb the hassle. A teenager cannot.

And what do we get in return? A database. A database of law-abiding people who fly toys. That is a privacy concern and a civil-liberties concern, but it is also a practical failure. It does not make the skies safer. It makes the government feel safer. It creates the appearance of control without the substance.

If you want accountability, there are better tools. Require Remote ID or serial-number traceability for larger drones. Encourage manufacturers to build geofencing and altitude caps. Promote voluntary education through apps, clubs, and retailers. Hold people liable when they actually cause harm. But do not pretend that a registration sticker and an online quiz are the difference between order and chaos.

The honest choice is not between these rules and a free-for-all. It is between symbolic bureaucracy and real safety. Real safety comes from technology, education, and enforcement of reckless behavior. Symbolic bureaucracy comes from making millions of innocent hobbyists prove they are innocent before they fly. The first works. The second just annoys. Recreational drone pilots should not require registration and testing.

claim: Recreational drone pilots should be registered and tested
argument:
You don’t need a license to fly a kite. You do need one to drive a car. A drone is not a kite. It is a spinning-blade aircraft that can weigh several pounds, climb thousands of feet, travel at highway speeds, and share the same airspace as passenger jets, medical helicopters, and firefighting aircraft. That is why recreational drone pilots should be registered and tested—not because flying is bad, but because the sky is a shared, unforgiving place where ignorance and anonymity are dangerous.

Start with the risk. The FAA has logged thousands of pilot reports of drones near manned aircraft. Airports have been shut down by drone sightings—Gatwick, Heathrow, Newark, LaGuardia. Wildfire aerial operations have been grounded because someone wanted a better video. A drone striking a helicopter windshield or getting sucked into a jet engine is not a hypothetical annoyance; it is a potential mass-casualty event. Even a small drone can blind a pilot, crack a canopy, or force an emergency maneuver at the worst possible moment. The operator rarely intends harm. That is exactly the problem: good intentions do not substitute for knowledge, and a drone in the wrong place at the wrong time can kill people who never chose to be part of the hobby.

Now consider what registration and testing actually are. Registration is a license plate. It says: this aircraft belongs to someone accountable. If your drone crashes into a firefighting plane, lands on a runway, or interferes with a rescue helicopter, investigators can find you. That does not mean the government is watching your every flight. It means the same principle we accept for cars, boats, and hunting: if you operate something that can injure others or damage shared resources, you are identifiable. Testing is driver’s ed. It ensures you know the basics before you take off: altitude limits, airport proximity, temporary flight restrictions, emergency scenes, privacy rules, and the fundamental obligation to see and avoid manned aircraft. The FAA’s TRUST test is free, online, and takes about half an hour. If that sounds like an unbearable burden, ask yourself what else you do in half an hour that could prevent a disaster.

The skeptical reader might say: “Most drone pilots are responsible.” Exactly. Responsible pilots have nothing to fear. If you already know the rules, you will pass the test. If you don’t, you will learn something that might save a life—maybe your own, maybe a stranger’s. The reckless minority is precisely why the rest of us need a baseline. A world with no registration and no testing is not a world of freedom; it is a world where the careless impose their costs on everyone else, and where the inevitable backlash produces far harsher bans. Registration and testing are how a hobby survives. They are the price of admission to the national airspace, and they are cheap.

Another objection: “Criminals won’t register anyway.” True. Laws do not eliminate all crime. But they do three things that matter. They establish a clear standard, so negligence can be distinguished from malice. They give enforcement a starting point, so investigators are not chasing ghosts. And they create a culture of compliance, where the default assumption is that flying a drone means knowing the rules. Speed limits do not stop every speeder, but they save lives. Registration does not stop every reckless pilot, but it makes accountability possible. Testing does not make everyone an expert, but it makes ignorance less likely.

Finally, consider the alternative. If recreational drones remain anonymous and untested, the stories will keep accumulating: near misses, diverted flights, grounded fire crews, privacy violations, and eventually a catastrophe. After that catastrophe, the response will not be a sensible test and a small fee. It will be blanket bans, no-fly zones, and restrictions that punish every hobbyist because a few refused to accept responsibility. The choice is not between regulation and freedom. The choice is between smart, minimal regulation now and draconian regulation later.

So register the drone. Test the pilot. Require a basic understanding of airspace, safety, and accountability. It is not about clipping wings. It is about keeping the sky open, keeping emergency responders safe, and keeping the freedom to fly from being destroyed by the few who treat the national airspace like a private playground. Freedom in a shared sky has always come with responsibilities. This is the bare minimum.

claim: Requiring all police officers to wear body cameras should not be mandated
argument:
If you believe police should be more accountable, body cameras sound like the obvious answer. A camera on every chest, every shift, every encounter: a silent witness that can exonerate the good officer and expose the bad one. It is a compelling image. But a universal mandate is not the same as accountability, and treating it as one is how real reform gets delayed, underfunded, and ultimately betrayed. We should not mandate body cameras for all police officers.

Start with the evidence. The most rigorous randomized studies—in Washington, D.C., Milwaukee, and Las Vegas—found that body cameras produced little to no statistically significant reduction in use-of-force incidents or civilian complaints. Earlier, smaller studies like Rialto, California, generated headlines with dramatic drops, but those results have not held up consistently when tested at scale. That does not mean cameras are useless. It means the technology is not a magic switch. If a mandate is sold as the fix, and the fix does not materialize, the public loses faith and departments learn that they can check a box without changing culture. A policy that promises more than it delivers is not accountability; it is theater.

Then consider the cost. A camera itself may run several hundred dollars, but the real expense is data: storage, redaction, audit trails, public-records requests, cybersecurity, and the staff to manage it. For a small rural department, a tribal police force, or a city already stretched thin, an unfunded universal mandate can consume the budget that would have paid for de-escalation training, crisis intervention, mental-health co-responders, or community policing. Those interventions have stronger evidence for improving safety and trust. Mandating cameras while starving those programs is like buying a dashcam for a car with bad brakes.

The privacy costs are also real, and they fall hardest on the people who need police protection most. A body camera records not just the officer and the suspect. It records bystanders, children, domestic-violence victims, people in mental-health crises, sexual-assault survivors, immigrants, and informants. It can capture the inside of homes, medical details, and the faces of people at protests or funerals. If the footage is retained indefinitely, shared across agencies, or fed into facial-recognition systems, it becomes a mass surveillance network built under the banner of transparency. If it is turned off in sensitive moments, then the mandate is not universal at all—it is discretionary, and discretion is exactly what accountability reformers are trying to constrain. You cannot have it both ways: either the camera records everything, or it does not, and both options create serious problems.

There is also the false comfort of the footage itself. A camera sees what the officer’s chest sees. It has blind spots, low-light limitations, distorted audio, and a fisheye lens that can make distances and movements look different than they were. It cannot capture fear, adrenaline, or the split-second reasoning behind a use of force. And it can be selectively activated, selectively stored, selectively redacted, and selectively released. Without independent oversight, strict retention rules, criminal penalties for tampering, and a legal guarantee that footage is not hidden behind union contracts or qualified immunity, a camera mandate can become a public-relations tool rather than a truth-telling one. The camera does not investigate; people do. If the people investigating are the same people with an interest in the outcome, the camera changes less than we hope.

A blanket mandate also ignores local context. Policing in a small town, a large city, a border community, and a tribal nation are not the same job. Communities should be able to decide whether body cameras fit their needs, their budgets, and their values—and if they choose them, they should demand strong policies: mandatory activation with narrow exceptions, short retention for non-evidentiary footage, prompt public release, independent audits, bans on facial recognition and data mining, and real consequences for violations. That is a better path than a one-size-fits-all command from above.

So if your goal is accountability, do not mandate cameras. Mandate transparency. Mandate independent oversight. Mandate consequences for misconduct. Fund training, mental-health response, and community-based violence prevention. Those reforms are harder, slower, and less photogenic than strapping a camera to every officer, but they actually change behavior. A body camera is a tool, not a cure. Tools can be misused, ignored, or used to paper over deeper failures. Requiring every officer to wear one may feel like progress, but it risks becoming a costly distraction from the real work of making policing just.

claim: Self-driving cars will increase safety and should replace human drivers.
argument:
Consider the machine we already trust with our lives every day: the human driver. It gets distracted by a text, drowsy at 3 a.m., angry after an argument, drunk at a wedding, and overconfident in the rain. It has a reaction time of roughly 200 milliseconds on a good day and blind spots you could hide a motorcycle in. On American roads alone, it kills more than 40,000 people a year—about one passenger jet every single day. Globally, it kills roughly 1.3 million. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that 94% of serious crashes involve human error. We call this normal. We should call it a public health emergency.

Self-driving cars are not magic. They will have failures. But they are built on a fundamentally better foundation. They never get drunk, never text, never fall asleep, never rage, never rubberneck, never speed for fun. They see 360 degrees with cameras, radar, and lidar. They react in milliseconds. They maintain following distance with machine precision. And most important, they learn. When one autonomous vehicle encounters a rare edge case, that experience can be encoded and shared across the entire fleet overnight. A human who survives a near-miss learns a private lesson, if anything; the next driver repeats the same mistake. Autonomy turns individual tragedy into collective improvement.

Skeptics say self-driving cars are not perfect. Neither are humans. The right question is not “Are they flawless?” but “Are they safer than the alternative?” A system that is even 10% better than the average human driver would save thousands of lives a year in the United States alone. A system 50% better would save tens of thousands. And unlike human drivers, autonomous systems will improve every year. Human drivers have been driving for a century and still kill more than a million people annually. We have plateaued. Machines have not.

What about the trolley problem? Human drivers do not solve it. They panic, freeze, or yank the wheel. An autonomous vehicle can be programmed to minimize harm with consistent rules, and its decisions can be audited. Human decisions vanish into memory and bias. After a crash, we get “I didn’t see them.” After an autonomous crash, we get sensor logs: speed, steering, braking, exactly what happened. Accountability improves.

What about hacking? It is a real risk, and it must be met with redundancy, encryption, and rigorous security. But human drivers are also hacked—by alcohol, opioids, phones, and emotion. We do not ban cars because they can be stolen. We harden them. What about jobs? Millions drive for a living, and that transition must be managed with retraining and support. But we cannot ask people to keep dying so some jobs remain. What about freedom? Public roads are not private playgrounds. You can drive on a track. On shared roads, your freedom ends where my family’s life begins. We already require licenses, insurance, seatbelts, and sobriety. Replacing human error is the logical next step.

The choice is not between perfect machines and perfect humans. It is between a flawed, tired, distracted, unaccountable human driver and a machine that can be tested, regulated, updated, and made better. We should phase in self-driving cars with rigorous safety standards, transparent data, and support for workers. But the destination is clear: human driving should be retired from public roads. Every year we delay, we accept a toll measured in tens of thousands of funerals. That is not caution. It is complicity.

claim: Smartphones/social media should not be banned for kids under 16
argument:
You are not wrong to worry about what smartphones and social media are doing to kids. The endless scroll, the comparison traps, the sleep-stealing dopamine loops, the cyberbullying, the predators—these are real. Any parent who has watched a child disappear into a screen knows the unease. But the leap from “this can be harmful” to “we should ban it for everyone under 16” is not a careful policy. It is a panic response. And panic responses tend to hurt the very kids they claim to protect.

Start with the evidence. The strongest studies do not show that social media is a uniform poison that justifies a blanket ban. When researchers have compared adolescents’ digital technology use with their well-being, the average association is tiny—so small that it is comparable to the effect of eating potatoes or wearing glasses. That does not mean social media is harmless. It means the story is far more complicated than “phones bad.” Some kids are harmed. Some are helped. Most are somewhere in the middle, and the harm depends heavily on what they are doing, for how long, with whom, and what else is happening in their lives. A ban treats a 15-year-old who uses a private group chat to survive a hostile school environment exactly the same as a 12-year-old being served pro-anorexia content by an algorithm. That is not protection. That is a blunt instrument swung in the dark.

Now consider who gets hurt most by a ban. LGBTQ+ teens in unsupportive homes often find their first affirming community online. Chronically ill or disabled kids who cannot easily attend social events use social media to maintain friendships. Immigrant kids use it to stay connected to family and culture. Teens struggling with mental health may find peer support, helplines, and information they are too afraid to seek in person. When you ban social media for everyone under 16, you do not just ban the algorithmically amplified trash. You ban the lifeline. You tell the isolated kid that the one place they felt seen is now off-limits because other kids, in other circumstances, were having a worse experience.

Then there is the enforcement problem, which is where bans usually collapse. How do you verify age without collecting IDs, face scans, or biometric data from every user? That creates a surveillance infrastructure and a honeypot of sensitive information. It also excludes kids who lack documentation or whose parents will not hand over personal data. And the kids who most want to evade the ban will evade it—through VPNs, borrowed accounts, older siblings’ logins, or unmoderated spaces that are far worse than the mainstream apps. A ban does not create a world where kids are offline. It creates a world where kids are online in secret, without parental oversight, without platform safety features, and without anyone to teach them how to handle what they find. That is the opposite of safety.

A ban also misunderstands what a smartphone actually is. It is not just a social media portal. It is a map, a way to call home, a medical device, a school tool, a connection to a therapist, a calendar, a translation app, a safety line. For many families, it is how they coordinate work, school, and caregiving. Banning smartphones for under-16s would either be unenforceable or would strip away tools that many kids genuinely need. And banning social media while leaving the phone in their pocket just pushes them toward whatever unregulated app or website fills the gap.

The real question is not “should kids under 16 have access to smartphones and social media?” The real question is “what kind of digital environment are we handing them, and who is accountable for it?” Right now, the answer is: an environment designed by companies whose profits depend on maximizing attention, and accountability that falls almost entirely on parents and kids. That is the injustice. A ban lets platforms off the hook. It says the problem is children’s presence, not the product design. It allows the industry to keep building infinite scroll, autoplay, beauty filters, targeted ads, and recommendation engines that push vulnerable users toward extremes, while politicians claim they “did something” by locking kids out.

If you actually want to protect kids, do the harder, more effective things. Regulate the design: default private accounts for minors, chronological feeds, no targeted advertising to children, no infinite scroll, no autoplay, no dark patterns, mandatory breaks, transparent algorithms, independent audits, and real penalties for platforms that ignore them. Fund digital literacy in schools so kids learn to spot manipulation, verify sources, protect their privacy, and set boundaries. Fund mental health services so the kids who are struggling get help, not just a locked door. Support parents with tools and guidance instead of pretending a ban will raise their children for them.

You do not have to believe social media is good for kids to oppose a ban. You only have to believe that a blanket prohibition is a fantasy of control in a world that cannot be controlled that way. The choice is not between a ban and a free-for-all. It is between teaching kids how to navigate a powerful, flawed digital world with adults beside them—or pretending they will never enter it, and leaving them to navigate it alone. Choose guidance. Choose regulation. Choose support. But do not choose a ban that will fail the kids who need help most while making everyone else less prepared for the world they actually live in.

claim: Self-driving cars will not be safe enough to fully replace human drivers.
argument:
You might be thinking: self-driving cars already have better reaction times, never get drunk, never text, and never fall asleep. That’s true. But that is not the standard for fully replacing human drivers. The standard is not “better than an average human on a good day.” The standard is “safe enough to eliminate the human fallback entirely, everywhere, in every condition, against every rare and bizarre thing the world can throw at a vehicle.” That is a categorically higher bar, and it is one that autonomous systems will not clear.

Full replacement means every car, on every road, in every weather system, at every hour, must handle the entire long tail of driving. The long tail is not a minor remainder. It is the hard part. A human driver can understand a police officer waving traffic through a dead signal, a construction worker holding a “slow” sign, a child chasing a ball, a mattress tumbling off a truck, a funeral procession, a horse-drawn carriage, a driver who waves you to go first even though it’s not your turn. We handle these because we have general common sense and social intelligence. Self-driving cars handle them only if they have seen something close enough before or been explicitly programmed for it. The set of possible situations is open-ended. You cannot enumerate it. You cannot train on all of it. And when the pattern breaks, the machine does not improvise with understanding; it fails, often silently and confidently.

Even if we set aside the edge cases, there is a brutal statistical problem. Human fatality rates are already low—roughly one death per hundred million miles driven in the United States. To prove with 95% confidence that an autonomous fleet is just 20% safer than that, you would need to drive on the order of eleven billion miles. That is not a few more years of testing; it is a scale that current fleets are orders of magnitude away from. And even that proof would only cover average conditions. It would not prove safety in a blizzard, a flash flood, a chaotic intersection with a malfunctioning traffic light, or a new road layout that no map has yet captured. Simulation cannot solve this, because simulation only tests the scenarios we already thought to program. The unknown unknowns remain unknown.

There is also a systemic risk that human drivers simply do not present. Human errors are independent. One drunk driver does not cause every other drunk driver to crash at the same moment. But self-driving cars are a software monoculture. A single bug, a bad update, a sensor calibration error, or a malicious hack can be replicated across an entire fleet simultaneously. Full replacement would create a single point of failure for transportation itself. That is not a safer world; it is a more fragile one. A system that can fail everywhere at once is not safe enough to be the only system.

Sensors have limits too. LiDAR struggles in heavy snow and rain. Cameras are blinded by sun glare. Radar can be confused by reflections. Redundancy helps, but it is not infinite. More importantly, autonomous systems often do not know when they are confused. A human who cannot see the lane lines slows down, pulls over, or asks for help. A machine may continue at speed because its confidence score is high. In mixed traffic, that danger is softened by human drivers who compensate for the robot’s hesitation or aggression. In a fully replaced world, there is no compensation. Every vehicle must be assertive enough to keep traffic flowing and cautious enough to avoid catastrophe. That balance is a social negotiation, not a math problem. Humans do it intuitively. Machines do it brittlely.

None of this means self-driving cars are useless. They can and will make roads safer in many contexts: highways, geofenced city centers, good weather, predictable routes. They may reduce accidents, save lives, and change transportation. But “safer in many contexts” is not the same as “safe enough to fully replace human drivers.” Full replacement requires universal competence in an open world, and that is not a threshold you can reach by accumulating more miles. It is a claim of certainty in a domain where certainty is impossible. The last human driver will remain, not because we love driving, but because the world is too unpredictable and the burden of proof too high. Self-driving cars will not be safe enough to fully replace us.

claim: Smartphones/social media should be banned for kids under 16
argument:
On the current trajectory, we are not raising children; we are running a vast, uncontrolled experiment on them. The experiment asks: what happens when you give a developing brain a pocket-sized slot machine connected to the entire social world before it has learned to regulate attention, emotion, or sleep? We now have the results, and they are bad enough to justify a clear line: no personal smartphone and no social media for kids under 16.

You may think this is just another moral panic. Every generation fears new technology. But this is not comic books or rock music. It is a product engineered by thousands of engineers and A/B tests to capture attention, with infinite scroll, variable rewards, streaks, likes, filters, and algorithmic feeds that never end. The adolescent brain is uniquely vulnerable: the reward system is revved up, while the prefrontal cortex—the part that says “stop” and “enough”—is still under construction. That is exactly why slot machines are illegal for minors. We do not hand a 12-year-old a device designed to exploit that gap and then blame them for being unable to resist it.

Since smartphones and social media became ubiquitous around 2012, teen mental health has collapsed. In the United States, the share of high school girls who reported persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness rose from about 36 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2021. Nearly one in three teen girls seriously considered suicide. Overall, 42 percent of high school students felt persistently sad or hopeless. Emergency room visits for self-harm among teen girls skyrocketed. These trends are not limited to one country; they appear across the English-speaking world and beyond. Not every child is harmed, but a population-level shift this large demands a population-level cause.

Social media is not a neutral town square. It is a comparison machine. It shows a 13-year-old filtered faces, perfect bodies, parties she was not invited to, and anonymous cruelty. It enables sextortion, predators, and cyberbullying that follows a child home and into bed. It fragments attention and displaces sleep, exercise, and face-to-face friendship. Sleep alone is devastating: teens need eight to ten hours, and a phone in the bedroom steals it night after night. Sleep deprivation is a direct driver of depression, anxiety, and academic failure.

This is not merely correlation. Randomized trials have found that limiting social media reduces depression and loneliness. Internal Facebook documents showed Instagram worsened body image for many teen girls. Researchers studying Facebook’s early campus rollout found it was followed by worsening mental health. We did not wait for perfect certainty to act on seatbelts or secondhand smoke. We acted because the harm was plausible, growing, and preventable. The same standard applies here.

The strongest objection is parental freedom: why not let parents decide? Because individual opt-out is impossible in a network. A parent who delays a smartphone is not just protecting their own child; they are excluding that child from the social world their peers inhabit. Then the child begs, the parent caves, and every family is trapped in an arms race. A ban is not a restriction on parental love. It is a release from a collective action problem. It makes the safe choice the default choice for everyone.

Another objection is that kids need digital skills. But 16 is not late. They will learn faster than we did. We do not teach 10-year-olds to drive by handing them the keys and hoping they figure out moderation. We do not let them smoke to teach them lung health. Delay is not denial; it is protection of the developmental window when identity, attention, and social comparison are being formed. A basic phone for calls and texts can provide safety without opening the door to the entire attention economy.

Kids have rights, including the right to childhood. We already restrict alcohol, tobacco, gambling, driving, and voting for minors because we know their judgment is not adult judgment. Social media is a commercial product designed to exploit immature judgment. Calling it “free speech” misses the point: the business model is not speech. It is surveillance, monetized attention, and algorithmic manipulation.

Enforcement is not science fiction. We can require age verification at the app store and platform level. We can make device operating systems default to no social media for under-16 accounts. We can allow basic phones for calls and texts. Companies will comply if the law is clear, just as they do with age limits for alcohol and gambling advertising.

The choice is not between a phone-free utopia and a connected childhood. It is between a childhood shaped by engineers optimizing for engagement and a childhood shaped by parents, teachers, friends, books, boredom, and play. We cannot ask a 13-year-old to outwill a trillion-dollar attention economy. We can change the default. Ban smartphones and social media for kids under 16—not forever, just until their brains have a fighting chance. The experiment has gone on long enough.

claim: Social media companies should be required to label AI-generated content
argument:
Picture the next election. A video lands in your feed: a candidate, looking and sounding exactly like themselves, saying something monstrous. It spreads to millions before fact-checkers even wake up. Or a voice call tells you your child is in danger. Or a photo shows a world leader surrendering. You have no way to know whether any of it is real. That is not a hypothetical future. It is already happening. The only question is whether we will let it happen in the dark.

Social media companies should be required to label AI-generated content. Not because artificial intelligence is evil. Not because we should ban synthetic media. But because the alternative is a world where nothing you see can be trusted, and everything can be denied. Labeling is the bare minimum: a disclosure, not a censorship. It does not stop anyone from posting. It does not remove a single word. It simply tells you what you are looking at, the same way a food package tells you what you are eating and a sponsored post tells you who paid for it.

The skeptical reader might say: “People can figure it out themselves.” They cannot. Study after study shows that deepfakes fool ordinary viewers, and increasingly, experts too. AI images have moved past the uncanny valley. They have crossed into the uncanny. The fake Pentagon explosion that briefly moved stock markets in 2023 was not a Hollywood production. It was a generated image. The AI robocall impersonating President Biden before the New Hampshire primary was not a prank. It was voter suppression. If you believe you are immune, you are precisely the person these tools are designed to fool.

Another objection: “It’s too hard to enforce.” But social media companies already label ads, sponsored content, manipulated media, and fact-checks. They already track every click, every share, every second you linger. They can detect and label AI content if they are required to. Provenance standards like C2PA, watermarking, and metadata are maturing. The law does not need to demand perfection. It can demand reasonable efforts, transparency about methods, and penalties for knowing noncompliance. Imperfect enforcement is not an argument against any law. It is an argument for better enforcement.

“Labels can be stripped or faked,” the skeptic says. Yes. So can age verification, copyright claims, and identity checks. We do not abandon those because they are imperfect. We raise the cost of deception. If a platform must label AI content at upload and preserve that label through shares, the casual liar is deterred, the malicious actor is exposed, and the rest of us get a fighting chance. A law that works most of the time is infinitely better than a reality where it works none of the time.

“This will chill satire and art.” No. A label is not a ban. A comedian can post an AI-generated parody of a politician and still get the laugh. An artist can create a synthetic dreamscape and still find an audience. The label does not say “false.” It says “synthetic.” That distinction matters. It preserves the speech while protecting the context. In fact, labeling helps legitimate creators. When everything can be fake, people stop trusting everything—including the real. Clear labels let real content stand out again.

“It’s government overreach.” We already require labels on cigarettes, calories, side effects, political ads, and ingredients. We do not consider that tyranny. We consider it basic consumer protection. Social media is now the primary public square, the main news source for billions, and the central marketplace of ideas. If we require a label on a pack of gum, we can require one on a synthetic video of a president. The First Amendment protects your right to speak. It does not protect your right to deceive. A label is more speech, not less.

The cost of doing nothing is not abstract. It is nonconsensual deepfake pornography that ruins lives. It is scams that drain savings. It is election chaos that makes people give up on democracy itself. It is the slow poison of “I don’t know what to believe anymore,” which is exactly what authoritarians want. When people cannot agree on basic facts, they cannot govern themselves. They cannot hold power accountable. They cannot even trust their own eyes.

So here is the choice. We can require social media companies to label AI-generated content—clearly, consistently, and at scale. Or we can let the most powerful communication networks in human history become a fog of synthetic doubt. The first is a small, practical, pro-speech step. The second is a surrender of shared reality. You do not have to love regulation to see it. You just have to ask yourself one question: if you were scrolling past a video of a candidate, a doctor, or your own face, wouldn’t you want to know whether it was real? Label it. Not to silence anyone. To keep the lights on.

claim: Social media companies should not be required to label AI-generated content
argument:
You are right to want a world where you can tell whether the video of a politician is real, whether the protest photo was staged, whether the review you’re reading came from a person. But a legal mandate forcing social media companies to label AI-generated content would not give you that world. It would give you a world where honest creators are branded, sophisticated liars slip through untouched, and the absence of a label becomes a false certificate of authenticity. That is not transparency. It is theater with real casualties.

Start with the machinery. To label AI-generated content, platforms must first detect it. Detection is not a fact; it is a guess. AI-text detectors are notoriously unreliable, and studies have found they disproportionately flag writing by non-native English speakers, often accusing human students of cheating. Image detectors collapse under cropping, compression, filters, screenshots, or a few added pixels. Video detection is worse. If you require platforms to label AI content at scale, you are requiring them to make millions of probabilistic judgments every hour. They will get it wrong. And every false label is compelled speech: a human artist’s painting stamped as machine-made, a dissident’s photograph tagged as synthetic, a student’s essay marked as fraudulent. That is not a warning label. It is automated defamation.

Now consider evasion. The people most likely to use AI to deceive are exactly the people least likely to comply with a labeling rule. They can screenshot the image, strip the metadata, paraphrase the text, re-encode the video, or run an open-source model on their own laptop. A mandate binds the honest. The liar simply avoids the watermark and posts unlabeled. The label becomes a signal not of truth but of naïveté. You end up with a system where the only content marked “AI” is the content created by people who followed the rules—while the most dangerous fakes circulate freely under the default assumption that no label means no AI.

That is the deepest flaw. Mandatory labeling creates false confidence. If users are taught that AI content is supposed to carry a label, they will infer that unlabeled content is human and real. But most AI-generated content will never be detected, and much human content will be mislabeled. The unlabeled category will become a safe harbor for the most sophisticated deception. You will have made the problem worse by giving people a reason to trust the absence of a tag.

Then there is the definitional impossibility. What counts as AI-generated? A photograph with AI denoising? A screenplay polished by a grammar tool? A translation? A song with AI mastering? A meme using an AI-generated background? A film with AI visual effects? A news article with an AI-assisted headline? If you label all of it, the label becomes meaningless noise. If you label only some of it, you invite arbitrary and politicized line-drawing. Platforms will be forced to decide which uses of a ubiquitous technology are legitimate and which are suspect. That is not a technical standard. It is a speech code.

And it chills lawful expression. AI is not synonymous with false. It helps disabled people communicate, translators reach broader audiences, artists experiment, and small creators compete with large studios. A mandatory label stigmatizes the tool as inherently deceptive, even when the content is accurate, satirical, educational, or personal. It also hands governments a lever: once platforms must classify content by origin, the categories can expand. Today it is AI-generated video; tomorrow it is “AI-assisted” journalism, “synthetic” satire, “manipulated” protest footage. The infrastructure of labeling becomes the infrastructure of censorship.

You might say: imperfect labeling is better than nothing. But here the imperfection is not a small leak; it is the whole pipe. A bad label regime does not just fail to stop disinformation. It punishes the honest, exonerates the guilty, and trains the public to trust the wrong signal. It also distracts from what actually works. Existing laws against fraud, impersonation, defamation, and election interference can target the conduct that matters—whether or not AI was involved. If someone uses AI to fake a candidate’s concession, prosecute the fraud. If a platform knowingly amplifies coordinated deception, hold it accountable. Do not force every platform to guess which content is AI and brand it with a label that liars will strip and honest users will fear.

There are better paths: provenance standards at the point of creation, cryptographic credentials that travel with a file, voluntary disclosure for political ads, clear platform rules against impersonation, media-literacy campaigns, and user controls that let people filter what they see. These approaches target the source and the harm. They do not deputize social media companies as truth police or turn a missing tag into a lie.

So oppose the mandate—not because you are soft on disinformation, but because you are serious about it. Demand accountability for deception. Demand transparency where it can be meaningful. But do not demand that platforms guess which content is AI and stamp it with a label that will be wrong often, evaded easily, and trusted falsely. A mandatory AI label is not a solution to the crisis of trust. It is a way of laundering the crisis into a badge.
