claim: Social media platforms should not censor any legal speech.
argument:
You don’t have to like what someone says to defend their right to say it. You only have to recognize that the moment you hand a private platform the power to decide which legal speech is acceptable, you have handed it the power to decide what you are allowed to know, question, and debate. That is not a hypothetical danger. It is the inevitable result of letting a handful of companies become the gatekeepers of global conversation.

The case against censoring legal speech on social media is not a defense of trolls, liars, or extremists. It is a defense of a principle that has served free societies better than any alternative: the line between what can be said and what cannot should be drawn by law, not by the momentary consensus of corporate trust-and-safety teams. Illegal speech—true threats, incitement to violence, fraud, child sexual abuse material, targeted harassment—is already illegal. Platforms can remove it. But once they move beyond that line into “harmful,” “misleading,” “hateful,” or “divisive” legal speech, they are no longer enforcing law. They are enforcing orthodoxy.

Ask yourself who defines “misinformation.” In 2020, saying the COVID-19 virus might have leaked from a laboratory was treated by many platforms as dangerous misinformation. Then it became a serious hypothesis. In 2020, sharing the contents of a laptop abandoned at a repair shop was framed as Russian disinformation. Then it became evidence in a criminal trial. These are not ancient history. They are recent reminders that the truth is often contested, messy, and discovered slowly. If platforms had permanently suppressed those claims, they would not have protected democracy. They would have protected a narrative.

That is the core problem: content moderation at scale cannot be wise. Algorithms do not understand context, irony, reclaimed language, medical nuance, foreign dialects, or the difference between a journalist documenting a slur and a troll hurling one. Human moderators are overwhelmed, inconsistent, and subject to their own biases. The result is not a clean public square. It is a confusing, opaque system where the rules change by the hour and the punishments fall unevenly. Black and LGBTQ creators report being flagged for discussing their own lives. Palestinian journalists and activists say their reach is suppressed. Conservatives see bias. Liberals see bias. Everyone sees a system that feels arbitrary because it is arbitrary. When no one can predict what is allowed, no one is truly free to speak.

And censorship rarely works. It does not convince people they were wrong. It convinces them they are being silenced. It turns bad ideas into forbidden fruit, makes martyrs of fools, and drives conversations into darker corners where no one can challenge them. The remedy for bad speech has always been more speech—better speech, counterspeech, evidence, ridicule, exposure. A bad argument loses when it is dragged into the light. It wins when it is banned and becomes a badge of rebellion.

The skeptical reader may say: “But these are private companies. They have the right to curate their own platforms.” That is true as a matter of law. It is also beside the point. The question is not what they can do. It is what they should do. When a few companies control the digital public square, their moderation decisions are not private housekeeping. They are public policy. If you own the only road into town, you cannot charge tolls only to people you like and call it private property. Social media is modern infrastructure. With that power comes a duty to uphold the values of free expression, not to become the ministry of approved thought.

Some will argue that free speech absolutism protects the powerful. In practice, the opposite is often true. Censorship protects the powerful. It protects incumbents from criticism, institutions from embarrassment, and majorities from uncomfortable questions. The voices most likely to be silenced are not the loudest; they are the marginal, the dissident, the unorthodox, the ones without lawyers and PR teams. If you would not trust a government agency to decide which legal speech is too dangerous for you to hear, why would you trust a tech monopoly?

There is a better way. Platforms can label. They can fact-check. They can offer user-controlled filters, chronological feeds, mute and block tools, community notes, and transparent moderation logs. They can let people decide what they want to see. What they should not do is secretly suppress, demonetize, shadowban, or delete legal speech because it offends a policy team. That is not curation. It is censorship.

The principle is simple: no censorship of legal speech. Not because all speech is good, but because the alternative is worse. It concentrates unaccountable power over what we can think and discuss. It guarantees error, bias, and abuse. It poisons trust. And in the end, it does not protect you. It protects whoever happens to be in charge of the algorithm. Today you may agree with the censors. Tomorrow you may be the one they silence. The only stable rule—the only rule that protects everyone—is to let legal speech live and answer it with better speech. That is not radical. It is the foundation of a free society.

claim: Social media platforms have a duty to moderate harmful content.
argument:
Imagine a city where every street corner is fitted with a megaphone that never sleeps, where anyone can broadcast to millions in seconds, and where the loudest voices are chosen not by merit but by an algorithm designed to keep you angry, afraid, and scrolling. That city is not hypothetical. It is the digital public square we inhabit every day. And like any public square, it cannot function if it is allowed to become a permanent riot.

You may object: social media platforms are private companies. Moderation is censorship. Let the market and the users decide. But that objection ignores a simple fact: these platforms are not neutral pipes. They do not merely host speech; they curate it, rank it, recommend it, and profit from it. They decide which posts reach ten people and which reach ten million. They already moderate—constantly—by removing spam, copyright violations, nudity, and ISIS propaganda. The question is not whether they should moderate. It is whether they will moderate the content that actually destroys lives.

The duty is not to police every offensive joke or unpopular opinion. It is to prevent foreseeable, serious harm. That means removing incitement to violence, credible threats, doxxing, child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate images, coordinated harassment, and health misinformation during a pandemic. It means acting against content that promotes genocide, ethnic cleansing, self-harm, and eating disorders. These are not gray areas of taste. They are categories of harm with real victims.

We already know what happens when platforms fail. In Myanmar, UN investigators concluded that Facebook played a “determining role” in the genocide against the Rohingya, amplifying hate speech that led to mass murder. In Christchurch, a terrorist livestreamed the slaughter of fifty-one worshippers, and the video spread across platforms faster than they could remove it. In Buffalo, a gunman livestreamed a racist massacre. During COVID-19, falsehoods about vaccines and treatments killed people who trusted what they saw in their feeds. Internal Facebook research showed that Instagram made body-image issues worse for many teenage girls. Women, journalists, and minorities are routinely driven offline by coordinated harassment. This is not the price of free speech. It is the silencing of speech by violence, fear, and algorithmic amplification.

The skeptic’s next move is the slippery slope: if we allow moderation of harm, who decides what is harmful? Today it’s hate speech; tomorrow it’s criticism of the government. That is a real risk. But the answer to imperfect line-drawing is not to draw no lines at all. We draw lines for speed limits, food safety, pollution, and product liability. We can draw them here with transparency, independent oversight, published community standards, appeals, and audits. A platform can remove a death threat without becoming the Ministry of Truth. It can downrank viral lies without banning dissent. The alternative—absolute algorithmic anarchy—is not neutrality. It is a choice to let the most dangerous content win.

Consider the logic of duty. A car manufacturer cannot sell a vehicle with no brakes and then say, “We just make cars; we are not responsible if drivers crash.” A restaurant cannot serve spoiled food and say, “We just provide the space; what people eat is their choice.” When you design a system that shapes the attention of billions, you inherit a duty of care. Social media companies are not passive bulletin boards. They are engineering firms, media distributors, and advertising empires in one. They know their algorithms can radicalize, polarize, and traumatize. They have the data. They have the money. They have the power. Duty follows power.

And make no mistake: moderation is not the enemy of free speech. It is the precondition for it. A town square where armed mobs shout down every speaker is not a free marketplace of ideas. It is a place where only the loudest and most vicious survive. When platforms allow coordinated harassment, they are not protecting speech; they are protecting the harassers and exiling everyone else. When they allow viral lies to drown out public health guidance, they are not neutrally hosting debate; they are rigging the conversation in favor of falsehood. Real free speech requires rules that keep the arena open for everyone, not just the bullies.

What would responsible moderation look like? It would be tiered and proportionate. Illegal content—credible threats, child exploitation, incitement—should be removed and reported to law enforcement. Harassment should be reduced and deprioritized. Misinformation should be labeled, fact-checked, and prevented from going viral. Borderline content can remain accessible but not algorithmically amplified. Platforms should invest in human moderators who speak local languages, publish transparency reports, allow independent researchers to audit their systems, and give users a real appeals process. They should design for safety by default, especially for minors. None of this is censorship of opinion. It is basic hygiene for a global nervous system.

You might still ask: why is it a duty rather than a favor? Because social media is no longer optional infrastructure. It is where elections are fought, where public health is debated, where families stay connected, where revolutions begin, and where genocides are incited. A handful of companies control the pipes through which modern society speaks. When you control the pipes, you cannot wash your hands of what flows through them. You can be sued for polluted water. You can be held liable for unsafe buildings. You can be held responsible for defective products. The same principle applies to defective digital spaces.

The choice is not between free speech and moderation. It is between moderated speech and weaponized speech. It is between a digital public square where people can disagree without being destroyed, and a digital coliseum where the crowd is trained to cheer for blood. The platforms have the power, the profit, and the knowledge. They have already built the megaphones. Now they must build the guardrails. Not because it is easy, not because it is perfect, but because the alternative is a world where the most harmful voices are the ones we hear the loudest—and the rest of us are left shouting into the void. That is not a duty we can afford to let them ignore.

claim: Social media platforms should be liable for harmful content posted by users
argument:
Imagine a bar that lets a known violent patron keep drinking, then hands him car keys and points him toward a crowded street. When he kills someone, we do not say, “The driver acted alone.” We hold the bar accountable because it had control, knowledge, and profit in the equation. Social media platforms are the bar. They are not neutral bulletin boards. They are active editors, distributors, and amplifiers of the content they host—and they should be liable when that content causes foreseeable harm.

The old defense—that platforms are mere pipes, passive conduits for whatever users post—collapsed years ago. A pipe does not decide which message reaches a million people and which reaches twelve. A pipe does not recommend a conspiracy theory to a grieving parent, auto-play a violent video to a teenager, or nudge a lonely user toward extremist groups. Platforms do all of this through algorithms designed to maximize engagement. Their business model turns attention into advertising revenue. Outrage, fear, and hate are not bugs in that system; they are often the fuel. When a platform profits from amplifying harmful content, it cannot wash its hands of the consequences.

Current law in the United States, especially Section 230, gives platforms a nearly blanket immunity from liability for user content. That immunity made sense in 1996, when the internet was nascent and the idea was to let it grow without crushing it with lawsuits. But today the largest platforms are among the most powerful companies in human history. They have billions of users, vast moderation teams, sophisticated artificial intelligence, and more data about human behavior than any government or advertiser has ever possessed. They already moderate aggressively when their own interests are at stake: copyright infringement, nudity, spam, terrorist propaganda, and anything that threatens their brand or ad revenue. The claim that they cannot possibly moderate hate, harassment, defamation, or medical misinformation is not a statement about technological limits. It is a statement about priorities. Liability would change those priorities.

This is not about punishing speech. Users can still speak. The First Amendment restricts government censorship; it does not guarantee anyone the right to be algorithmically amplified by a private company. Liability would not make platforms the speech police in the way critics fear. It would impose a duty of care: if a platform knows—or should know—that its design is spreading illegal or demonstrably harmful content, it must take reasonable steps to stop it. That is the same standard we apply to publishers, broadcasters, banks, landlords, and manufacturers. A radio station that airs a caller’s credible threat is not magically immune because the caller spoke first. A newspaper that prints a defamatory letter is not absolved because someone else wrote it. A bank that ignores money laundering cannot say, “The customers moved the money.” Responsibility follows control, knowledge, and profit. Platforms have all three.

The strongest objection is the chilling effect: if platforms face liability, they will over-remove, and free expression will suffer. But look at the status quo. Right now, the chilling effect runs the other way. Harassment drives women, journalists, and minorities off platforms. Lies about elections and vaccines cost lives. Genocide in Myanmar was fueled in part by Facebook’s own systems. Teenagers, especially girls, have been harmed by Instagram’s algorithmic promotion of impossible body standards—something Facebook’s own researchers documented. The current system does not protect speech; it protects the platforms from having to solve the problem. A well-designed liability regime would include safe harbors for good-faith moderation, transparency requirements, independent audits, and appeal rights. It would scale duties by size and reach, so a small startup is not crushed while a trillion-dollar giant is finally forced to internalize the costs of its design. Over-removal is a real risk, but the answer to bad moderation is better moderation, not no liability at all.

You might still think the user is the one who posted the harmful content, so the user should be the one liable. In a narrow legal sense, that is true. But in the real world, the platform is the reason the content traveled. It chose the audience. It chose the frequency. It chose the recommendation. It chose the emotional hook that made the content spread. If a person shouts a threat in an empty room, the harm is limited. If a platform’s algorithm puts that threat in front of the target’s home feed, the harm is direct and foreseeable. The user may be the author, but the platform is the publisher, promoter, and profiteer. You cannot separate the message from the megaphone when the megaphone is designed to make the message go viral.

We already accept that products can be defective, that businesses have duties of care, and that intermediaries can be liable when they knowingly facilitate harm. There is no principled reason to exempt social media platforms simply because their product is made of code and user posts. The question is not whether platforms should be liable for every thoughtless comment or every offense. The question is whether they should continue to enjoy a special immunity that lets them profit from harm while denying any responsibility for it. A free society can tolerate bad speech. It cannot tolerate a business model that turns bad speech into a weapon for profit. Liability is not censorship. It is accountability. And accountability is exactly what the largest, most powerful communication systems in history have been missing.

claim: Social media platforms should not be liable for harmful content posted by users
argument:
You are right to be angry about the harm. Threats, harassment, defamation, revenge porn, incitement—these are real, sometimes devastating, and the people who post them deserve consequences. But the instinct to sue the platform is a dangerous mistake. It confuses the messenger with the message, and in trying to punish the harm, it would destroy the open internet that makes social media valuable in the first place.

Start with a simple principle: you are responsible for what you say, not the company that carries your words. If someone uses a phone to make a threatening call, we do not sue AT&T. If someone mails a defamatory letter, we do not shut down the post office. If someone spray-paints a slur on a public wall, we do not arrest the wall. Social media is not a publisher in the traditional sense. It is a hosting service—a modern public square, a library, a phone network, and a town hall compressed into one. Treating it as the author of every user’s post would make it legally responsible for billions of statements it did not write, cannot fully review, and often cannot even predict.

The practical consequences would be catastrophic. Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, and X host billions of pieces of content every day. No human moderation team, no AI filter, and no combination of the two can review that volume before publication with anything close to accuracy. If platforms are liable for harmful content posted by users, the only safe legal strategy is to stop the content before it appears—or to stop allowing users to post at all. That means aggressive automated filtering, which is notoriously bad at context. It flags satire as threats, journalism as doxxing, sex education as obscenity, and political speech as hate speech. It disproportionately silences marginalized voices, activists, and dissenters, because their speech is often misread by algorithms trained on dominant norms. The result would not be a safer internet. It would be a quieter, blander, more controlled one—with the worst harms driven underground rather than reduced.

We already ran this experiment. In the 1990s, Prodigy was held liable as a publisher because it moderated its forums; CompuServe was not, because it did not. The perverse lesson was clear: if you try to clean up your platform, you get sued; if you do nothing, you escape liability. That is why Congress passed Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act—not to protect corporations, but to protect speech. Section 230 allowed platforms to moderate without becoming legally responsible for every user post. It enabled the modern internet, but it also enabled the moderation that removes child sexual abuse material, spam, and scams. Strip away that protection, and you do not get more responsibility. You get less moderation, because every act of moderation becomes a legal admission that you exercise editorial control. Or you get over-moderation, because the safest thing is to remove anything controversial. Neither is what a free society should want.

The skeptical reader will say: but platforms are not neutral. They design algorithms that amplify outrage, recommend conspiracy theories, and reward harassment. That is a fair criticism—and it points to a different solution. If a platform’s own algorithm, its own ad system, or its own employees break the law, they should be liable for that conduct. If they knowingly promote illegal content, they should face consequences. But liability for user content is not the same thing. It would hold the platform responsible for the speech of millions of people it did not instruct, did not write, and cannot perfectly control. We can regulate algorithmic transparency, require user controls, mandate prompt responses to valid court orders, and demand clear appeals processes without making the platform the legal author of every post. We can hold posters accountable through criminal law, civil suits, and platform bans. We can require platforms to preserve evidence and cooperate with law enforcement. What we should not do is make them insurers of the entire internet.

There is also a question of fairness and competition. Large incumbents can afford massive legal and compliance departments. Startups cannot. A liability regime would entrench the giants, because only they could survive the lawsuits. It would freeze the market, reduce innovation, and give more power to the very companies people distrust. If you want to break up Big Tech, making them the only firms capable of bearing intermediary liability is a strange way to do it.

None of this means we should shrug at harm. Victims deserve recourse. But the recourse should target the person who caused the harm, not the conduit. When a user posts a threat, arrest the user. When a user defames someone, sue the user. When a user harasses, hold the user accountable. Platforms should be required to act on valid legal complaints, to be transparent about their moderation, and to provide meaningful appeals. But they should not be forced to pre-screen the speech of billions, because that is not moderation—it is censorship by liability.

The choice is not between accountability and chaos. It is between a system that punishes speakers for their speech and a system that punishes the town square for letting people speak. The first is compatible with freedom. The second is not. If we make platforms liable for harmful content posted by users, we will not get a kinder internet. We will get a smaller one, a more monitored one, and one where the powerful decide in advance what the rest of us are allowed to say. That is too high a price to pay for the illusion of safety.

claim: Social media should not be required to verify user identities
argument:
You want social media to be less of a sewer. So do I. The abuse, the bots, the coordinated lies, the anonymous threats—they are real, and they poison public life. But mandatory identity verification is not the cure. It is a seductive shortcut that would trade away privacy, speech, and security without delivering the accountability it promises. Social media should not be required to verify user identities.

Start with the most important fact: it doesn’t work. South Korea tried a real-name verification law for large websites, hoping to curb malicious comments. The result was not a cleaner internet. It was a chilling effect on legitimate speech, a compliance burden on platforms, and no meaningful reduction in the worst behavior. The law was struck down as unconstitutional. Google+ tried a real-name policy and watched its platform become a ghost town while harassment continued elsewhere. A real name is not a real solution. Determined trolls can use stolen IDs, buy verified accounts, or operate through VPNs and synthetic identities. State-sponsored disinformation campaigns already use fake personas that look real; a verification checkbox would not stop them. And plenty of harassment comes from people using their real names. Asking for a driver’s license does not make someone kind.

Now consider who pays the price. The people who most need pseudonyms are not trolls. They are domestic abuse survivors hiding from stalkers. LGBTQ youth in conservative towns. Whistleblowers exposing corporate or government misconduct. Activists under authoritarian regimes. Journalists protecting sources. Muslim women, Black users, and others who face coordinated racial and gendered harassment. When you force everyone to speak under their legal identity, you hand a weapon to anyone who wants to find, threaten, or dox them. Anonymity is not a loophole for cowards; it is a shield for the vulnerable. The Federalist Papers were published under pseudonyms. Civil rights organizers used assumed names. #MeToo survivors spoke anonymously before they felt safe enough to speak openly. A democracy that requires papers to speak is not a democracy; it is a permission slip.

Then there is the security catastrophe waiting to happen. Mandatory verification means platforms—or the third parties they hire—must collect and store passports, driver’s licenses, facial scans, phone numbers, and addresses. These are exactly the databases that get breached. Facebook leaked phone numbers and personal data for hundreds of millions of users. Equifax, OPM, and countless other central repositories have been hacked. If companies cannot protect a phone number, why would we trust them with a passport? And even if the data is “securely” held, it becomes a subpoena target. Police, intelligence agencies, and hostile governments can demand it. In a democracy, that is a surveillance infrastructure waiting to be abused. In an authoritarian state, it is a ready-made list of dissidents. You cannot build a system of universal identity verification and then act surprised when it is used to hunt people down.

It also creates a two-tier public square. Millions of people lack the documents that verification regimes demand: the homeless, the undocumented, the elderly, the rural poor, trans people whose IDs do not match their lived identity, people who have lost their papers in fires or floods. They would be locked out of the digital town square. That is not accountability; it is exclusion. And it would fall hardest on those who already have the least power. A platform that requires government ID to post is a platform that says: only the documented may speak.

None of this means we must accept the status quo. The answer to online harm is not identity papers; it is better platform design. Friction before sharing. Rate limits on new accounts. Transparent moderation. User-controlled filters. Interoperability so people can leave toxic spaces. Liability for platforms that knowingly amplify coordinated harassment. Education. Journalists and researchers given access to platform data. These are hard, imperfect solutions. Mandatory verification is easy to announce and easy to evade—while its costs are permanent.

You may think: “If you’re not doing anything wrong, why hide?” But privacy is not guilt. We close the bathroom door. We don’t publish our home address. We don’t hand our passport to every stranger who asks. Anonymity has always been part of free expression, and it always will be. The question is not whether we want accountability. The question is whether we want a society where you need permission papers to speak.

We should not. Verify voluntarily if platforms choose. Offer badges, tiers, and optional checks. But never make legal identity a condition of basic participation. The public square should not have a bouncer demanding papers at the door.

claim: Social media should verify user identities
argument:
You don’t have to believe social media is evil to see the problem. You just have to watch a lie outrun the truth, a mob find a target, or a foreign troll farm set the terms of a national argument. The status quo is not neutral. It is a system where a single anonymous account can impersonate a neighbor, threaten a journalist, inflame a riot, or drown out a million honest voices—and then vanish without consequence. That is why social media should verify user identities.

Let’s be precise about what that means. Verification is not a demand that everyone post under their legal name. It is not a public registry of who said what. It is a behind-the-scenes confirmation that every account capable of posting, sharing, or messaging belongs to a real, unique human being or a legitimate organization. You can still speak as “SeaGreenFox” or “ConcernedParent.” You just can’t be a thousand bots, a ban-evading harasser, or a paid operative pretending to be someone you’re not.

The case for this is not abstract. In 2016, the Russian Internet Research Agency ran thousands of fake accounts to pit Americans against one another, organize rallies, and spread disinformation. During the pandemic, bots and trolls amplified false cures and vaccine conspiracies faster than platforms could label them. Studies have found that falsehoods spread faster on social media than the truth, partly because fake accounts and coordinated networks are built for virality. And the human cost is not evenly distributed. Women, journalists, people of color, and LGBTQ users face the worst harassment—often from anonymous accounts created solely to torment them. Verification would not end cruelty, but it would make cruelty cost something. It would make it harder to create ten thousand fake accounts, harder to evade a ban, harder to run a scam, and easier for platforms to enforce their own rules.

You might object: anonymity protects dissidents, whistleblowers, abuse survivors, and marginalized people. You’re right. That is exactly why verification must be private. The public does not need to see your ID. The platform—or a trusted, independent verifier—needs to know you are real. In repressive regimes, that data must be encrypted, minimized, audited, and released only under valid legal process. In high-risk cases, platforms can use privacy-preserving techniques that confirm uniqueness without storing a passport scan. Verification is not the enemy of anonymity. It is the difference between anonymity as a shield for the vulnerable and anonymity as a weapon for the malicious.

You might also worry about privacy. But social media companies already collect your phone number, your IP address, your device ID, your location, your browsing behavior, and your face. The choice is not between perfect privacy and verification. It is between a murky system of unaccountable surveillance and a clear system of accountable trust. We can demand that verification data be used for one purpose only—confirming you are a real person—and then deleted or securely hashed. We can require independent audits and harsh penalties for misuse. We already accept identity checks for banking, driving, renting an apartment, and buying a gun. Speech is more fundamental than any of those, which is why the verification should be minimal, universal, and invisible to the public—not why it should be absent.

And what about free speech? Verification does not chill legitimate speech. It chills bots, impersonators, and coordinated harassment campaigns. The people most silenced today are not the trolls; they are the teachers, activists, and ordinary users who log off because they are tired of being threatened. Accountability expands speech by making more people feel safe enough to speak. A pseudonymous account tied to a verified human can still criticize power, organize a protest, or share a unpopular opinion. What it cannot do is manufacture a movement, stalk an ex, or radicalize a lonely teenager while hiding behind a cartoon avatar.

The practical path is not as hard as skeptics claim. Require verification to post, not to read. Offer multiple free methods: government ID, phone, email plus a selfie, in-person verification at libraries or post offices, or community vouching. Allow pseudonyms publicly. Protect verification data like medical records. Fine platforms that fail. The details matter, but the principle is simple: if you want the reach of a broadcast network, you should accept the accountability of being a real person.

The alternative is what we have now: a digital public square where the loudest voices are often the least real, where trust erodes because no one knows who is human, and where the vulnerable pay the price for everyone else’s convenience. That is not a free internet. It is an ungoverned one, and it is failing us.

So yes: verify identities. Not to expose us to one another, but to hold us accountable to one another. Not to end anonymity, but to save it from becoming a cover for abuse. The question is not whether we can afford to verify. It is whether we can afford to keep pretending that a system built on invisible, unaccountable actors can ever be worthy of our trust.

claim: Space tourism should be allowed without initial limits on safety regulations
argument:
You’re skeptical because you picture a rocket full of tourists exploding while regulators look away. But that is not what this claim means. It means: do not let a regulator who has never flown a reusable spacecraft write the first rulebook. It means: allow space tourism without initial prescriptive safety limits, while keeping liability, transparency, informed consent, and accident investigation. That is not a recipe for disaster. It is the only way to discover what safety actually requires.

First, the knowledge problem. Safety rules are only as good as the data behind them. For space tourism, there is almost no data. Vehicles are experimental. Failure modes are poorly understood. A regulator writing limits now would be guessing—and those guesses would harden into law. They would mandate specific seats, escape systems, abort modes, or training regimes, not because evidence shows they work, but because they sound prudent. In a young technology, prudence is often superstition. The Wright brothers had no FAA. Early airlines had no cockpit resource management. Safety improved because crashes were investigated, designs were changed, and insurers and passengers demanded better. If we had imposed modern aviation rules in 1910, we would not have aviation.

Second, liability and insurance do more than prescriptive rules. A space tourism company that kills its customers will face lawsuits, bankruptcy, and extinction. Insurers will price the risk. If the risk is too high, premiums will be too high to fly. That is a powerful safety pressure. Add mandatory disclosure of known risks, public accident reports, and criminal penalties for fraud or concealment, and you have accountability without freezing design. This is not the Wild West. It is a marketplace where recklessness is expensive.

Third, autonomy matters. Space tourists are not children. They are adults who voluntarily accept a risk that is higher than a roller coaster. We allow skydiving, mountaineering, motorsports, and private aviation. We do not ban them because some people die. We require disclosure and let adults choose. Space tourism is more dangerous, but the principle is the same. A free society does not forbid consenting adults from taking risks just because the risk is unfamiliar.

Fourth, initial limits entrench incumbents. Large, well-funded companies can afford compliance. Startups cannot. If you write the first rules before the industry exists, you guarantee that only the biggest players survive. That reduces competition, slows innovation, and makes safety a luxury good. A vibrant market with many experiments will find safer designs faster than a protected cartel with one approved architecture.

Fifth, the cost of delay is real. Space tourism is not just joyrides. It is the funding engine for reusable launch, cheaper access to orbit, and a culture that looks outward. The same technologies support science, climate monitoring, and planetary defense. A precautionary ban or premature limits would delay those benefits indefinitely. The risk of stagnation is also a risk—one that kills dreams and opportunity.

The U.S. Congress understood this when it created a learning period for commercial human spaceflight, prioritizing informed consent over prescriptive rules. That policy did not produce a mass grave. It produced an industry. When accidents happen—and they will—the answer is investigation, transparency, and better engineering, not a ban that ensures no one learns anything.

So allow space tourism without initial limits on safety regulations. Require honesty. Enforce liability. Honor consent. Investigate every failure. But do not smother the first generation of space tourists under a rulebook written before the first flight. Safety will be built by those who fly, not by those who forbid.

claim: The capital city of the nation of France located in Europe is Paris.
argument:
A capital is not a decorative label on a map. It is the place where a state’s sovereignty is exercised, where its government sits, where its laws are made, and where foreign nations send their ambassadors. By that standard, there is only one answer for France: Paris.

Look at where France actually governs itself. The President of the Republic works from the Élysée Palace in Paris. The Prime Minister directs the government from Hôtel Matignon in Paris. The National Assembly meets in the Palais Bourbon in Paris. The Senate meets in the Palais du Luxembourg in Paris. The Constitutional Council, the Council of State, and the central ministries all operate in Paris. When France declares policy, signs treaties, receives foreign heads of state, or accredits ambassadors, the ceremony and the machinery of state are in Paris. A country’s capital is wherever its political power is concentrated, and in France that concentration is unmistakably Paris.

International recognition confirms it. Every embassy accredited to France is in Paris. The United Nations, the European Union, NATO, and every serious diplomatic handbook list Paris as the capital of France. UNESCO and the OECD are headquartered there. Maps, atlases, encyclopedias, and official French government publications identify Paris as the capital. No rival city functions as the seat of French national government. Versailles was once a royal residence, and Vichy was a wartime administrative aberration, but neither is the capital of France today. The capital is not where a king once slept or where a puppet regime once sat; it is where the Republic now governs.

France is a European nation, and Paris is its capital city. If you doubt that, try to conduct French national business anywhere else. Try to pass a law, appoint a minister, receive an ambassador, or sign a treaty on behalf of France outside Paris. You cannot. The institutions, the diplomats, the law, and the world all point to the same city. Paris is the capital of France—not by sentiment, not by tourism, but by the concrete, undeniable fact of where France is governed.

claim: Tenure for university professors should be reformed or eliminated
argument:
Tenure is one of the few employment arrangements in modern life that promises a job for life with almost no risk of dismissal for poor performance. That is not a description of academic freedom. It is a description of a privilege that has outlived its justification.

The case for tenure was once strong. In the early twentieth century, professors could be fired for teaching evolution, supporting unions, criticizing donors, or offending politicians. Tenure was invented to keep the university from becoming a mouthpiece for whoever held power. That danger was real, and the reformers who created tenure were not fools. But the remedy they chose—lifetime employment after a probationary period—was a product of its time. The question is not whether academic freedom matters. It does. The question is whether the only way to secure it is a guarantee that no other profession enjoys and that most faculty never receive.

That bargain has broken. Tenure is awarded, and then serious review largely stops. Post-tenure review exists on paper at many universities, but it is often toothless: it can trigger mentoring, paperwork, or embarrassment, but rarely dismissal. A tenured professor can stop publishing, refuse to teach new courses, treat students and colleagues badly, and still draw a salary for decades. Removing such a professor for incompetence or misconduct is so costly and slow that universities usually tolerate the problem instead. Academic freedom becomes freedom from accountability.

Meanwhile, the majority of college teachers have no such protection. Roughly three-quarters of faculty are off the tenure track—adjuncts, lecturers, and contingent instructors who often teach the largest introductory courses for low pay and little security. They can be dismissed for unpopular views or departmental whim. Tenure for a few coexists with precarity for many. If academic freedom is essential, it should not be a luxury good reserved for a shrinking caste. If it is not essential, why grant it as a lifetime monopoly? The system is not only inefficient; it is morally incoherent.

Tenure also distorts the university’s incentives. It makes it extraordinarily difficult to shift resources from declining programs to emerging ones. Departments defend tenure lines as property, even when student demand, public need, and intellectual fashion have moved elsewhere. Curricular innovation, interdisciplinary work, online teaching, and public partnerships are slowed by the simple fact that the people who benefit from the status quo have lifetime job security and the people who want change do not. Students pay rising tuition while often seeing tenured professors less than contingent ones. That is not a formula for public confidence.

And public confidence is collapsing. Taxpayers and parents see soaring costs, student debt, administrative bloat, and professors who cannot be fired. They hear about ideological intolerance, research scandals, and professors who teach little while earning comfortable salaries. Tenure becomes a symbol of unaccountability. That erodes support for higher education and invites political interference—the very thing tenure was supposed to prevent. By protecting the few absolutely, tenure makes the whole institution more vulnerable.

The skeptic will object: without tenure, controversial scholars will be fired. But tenure is not the only mechanism for protecting academic freedom. We can replace it with enforceable due process: multi-year renewable contracts, peer review, clear standards, free-speech protections in law and collective agreements, and dismissal only for cause after a fair hearing. Protect all faculty, not just the tenured. Many democracies safeguard academic freedom without American-style lifetime tenure. A professor fired for unpopular speech can grieve, sue, and appeal. That system is stronger because it protects everyone, not just the lucky few who survive the tenure gauntlet.

If eliminating tenure outright seems too radical, then reform it into something defensible. End indefinite tenure after a fixed term. Replace it with rolling seven-to-ten-year contracts. Institute real post-tenure review every five years, with teaching, research, service, and misconduct standards that carry consequences, including dismissal, while preserving due process. Redirect the savings toward fair pay and job security for contingent faculty. Make academic freedom a universal right, not a property interest.

The choice is not between tenure and tyranny. It is between a twentieth-century job guarantee and a twenty-first-century system of accountability, fairness, and protected speech. Tenure was a solution to a problem that no longer requires the same remedy. Reform it or eliminate it—but do not pretend that lifetime employment is the same thing as intellectual freedom.

claim: The US should ban all cultured or lab-grown meat products
argument:
Imagine a product made by taking cells from a living animal, bathing them in a proprietary cocktail of growth factors, antibiotics, and sometimes fetal bovine serum, then growing them in stainless-steel bioreactors that must be kept sterile at industrial scale. Now imagine calling that “meat” and putting it on grocery shelves without decades of safety data, without independent long-term studies, and without the public’s consent. That is the reality of cultured meat. And it is exactly why the United States should ban it.

You may be skeptical. You may think lab-grown meat is humane, green, and inevitable. But that pitch is a masterpiece of marketing, not a summary of the evidence. Start with safety. Conventional meat, for all its problems, has been eaten for millennia. Cultured meat has been eaten by a handful of people for a handful of years. We do not know how immortalized cell lines behave over decades. We do not know the long-term effects of consuming engineered proteins, residual growth factors, or the antibiotics used to keep bioreactors free of bacteria. We do not know whether novel allergens will emerge. The FDA’s approval process for these products has been described as a voluntary consultation, not a rigorous clinical trial. If a new drug were introduced with this little data, it would be scandalized. Why should a new food be different? The precautionary principle exists for a reason: when the risks are unknown and the exposure is universal, you do not experiment on the entire population.

Then there is the environmental claim. Cultured meat is often sold as a climate savior, but the science is far less flattering. A 2023 study from UC Davis found that the energy use and global warming potential of cultured meat could be four to twenty-five times higher than conventional beef, depending on the production system. Bioreactors require massive, continuous energy inputs. They require pharmaceutical-grade ingredients. They generate plastic and chemical waste. They require sterile facilities that are difficult to maintain at scale. The industry’s green promises rely on a future of cheap, clean energy that does not yet exist. We should not ban conventional agriculture to make room for a technology that may be worse for the planet.

The ethical argument is equally hollow. “No animals were killed” is the slogan. But the process often begins with a biopsy from a live animal, and many cell lines still depend on fetal bovine serum—blood taken from the hearts of unborn calves after their mothers are slaughtered. Even if a company eventually removes serum, it still patents and owns the cell lines. It still turns animals into bioreactors. It still treats life as a raw material. And it does nothing to address the real problems of industrial agriculture: consolidation, pollution, and cruelty. It simply moves the exploitation behind a glass wall.

The economic and political consequences are just as serious. Cultured meat is not a cottage industry. It is a venture-capital-backed race to patent food. If it succeeds, a handful of companies will control the protein supply. Family ranchers, rural communities, and local processors will be pushed out. The same consolidation that has hollowed out Main Street will happen to the dinner plate. And once a few corporations own the cell lines, the growth media, and the bioreactors, they will own the price, the labeling, and the politics of what Americans eat. That is not innovation. That is enclosure.

You might say: “But we shouldn’t ban innovation.” We ban plenty of things that are innovative and dangerous. We banned leaded gasoline, asbestos, and trans fats. We require new drugs to pass clinical trials. We do not allow companies to sell whatever they want just because it is new. The burden of proof belongs on the producer, not the public. If cultured meat cannot prove it is safe, sustainable, ethical, and democratically accountable, it should not be sold. The fact that it can be made does not mean it should be eaten.

And let us be honest about what a ban would actually do. It would not stop research. It would stop the commercial sale of an unproven, ultra-processed, patented product that threatens public health, rural economies, and food sovereignty. It would give independent scientists time to study the risks. It would protect consumers from being unwitting subjects in a vast experiment. It would force the industry to answer questions instead of writing checks.

The choice is not between lab-grown meat and factory farming. That is a false dilemma. We can support regenerative agriculture, better animal welfare, plant-rich diets, and real food from real farms. We do not need to hand the most intimate act of human life—eating—over to a handful of biotech companies. We do not need to replace one broken system with a more fragile, more centralized, more opaque one.

So yes: ban it. Ban the sale. Ban the misleading labels. Ban the idea that the American dinner table is a testing ground for Silicon Valley. If cultured meat is truly the future, it can wait until it has earned the public’s trust. Until then, the safest, most honest, most democratic choice is to keep it out of our food supply.

claim: Space tourism should be limited until safety regulations are further developed
argument:
Imagine you are handed a ticket to the edge of space. The fine print says you are not a passenger. You are a “space flight participant.” The company does not have to prove the vehicle meets a government safety standard. It does not have to show you a quantified risk of death. It only has to tell you that death is possible and get your signature. That is not a regulatory framework. It is a liability shield.

That is the current reality of space tourism in the United States and much of the world. Regulators have largely left occupant safety to informed consent and industry self-policing. Companies are not required to certify their vehicles to the same standard as commercial airliners. They are not required to publish failure rates. They are not required to demonstrate that a paying customer has a reasonable chance of surviving a serious malfunction. The burden is placed on the customer to understand risks that even the engineers cannot fully quantify.

This is not like skydiving or mountaineering. Those activities have millions of participants, decades of data, known failure rates, and established safety practices. Space tourism has a handful of flights, proprietary vehicles, and physics that leave no room for a go-around. If a rocket engine fails at 40,000 feet, there is no pull-over. If a cabin depressurizes, there is no oxygen mask drop. If a vehicle breaks apart, there is no rescue helicopter. The margin for error is measured in seconds, and the consequences are measured in lives.

We have already seen the warning lights. In 2014, Virgin Galactic’s SpaceShipTwo broke apart during a test flight, killing co-pilot Michael Alsbury. The NTSB found not just pilot error but inadequate hazard analysis, training, and design safeguards. In 2022, Blue Origin’s New Shepard booster failed; the capsule’s escape system worked, but the incident reminded us that even a short suborbital hop is an experimental rocket launch. In 2019, Virgin Galactic flew outside its assigned airspace, triggering an FAA investigation. These are not signs of an industry ready for mass paying customers. They are signs of an industry still learning.

You might object that regulation kills innovation. But the opposite is true. Aviation did not become safe and then popular; it became popular because it became safe. The creation of the FAA in 1958 did not ground airlines—it gave people the confidence to fly. NASA’s commercial crew program imposed rigorous safety certification on SpaceX and Boeing, and it still produced new vehicles. Safety is not the enemy of innovation. It is the infrastructure that lets innovation scale.

The current hands-off approach creates a race to the bottom. If one company cuts corners to sell cheaper tickets, others must match or lose business. The result is a market where the boldest gambler wins, until the inevitable disaster. Then the public will not distinguish between one bad operator and the entire industry. After the Titanic, we did not just regulate one ship; we created the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea. After the Hindenburg, the era of passenger airships ended. If a space tourism vehicle kills a cabin full of people on live television, the backlash could ground the sector for a generation. The skeptic who wants space tourism to succeed should be the first to demand limits.

What does “limited” mean? It does not mean a permanent ban. It means a phased, data-driven pause on expansion. Cap the number of paying passengers per vehicle and per company until we have enough flight data to estimate risk. Require independent safety reviews and public accident reporting. Mandate emergency systems, medical screening, and training standards. Prohibit paying customers on vehicles that have not completed a rigorous test-flight campaign. Give regulators the authority to ground a vehicle immediately. Require companies to share anonymized safety data so the whole industry can learn faster. These are modest, concrete steps.

The question is not whether people have the right to take risks. They do. The question is whether companies have the right to sell risks they cannot quantify, in vehicles they are not required to certify, with no rescue if things go wrong. They do not. Informed consent is not a substitute for safety when the information is incomplete. You cannot consent to a risk you cannot understand.

If space tourism is ever going to be more than a billionaire’s thrill ride, it must earn public trust. Trust is not built by waivers. It is built by transparency, standards, and a record of safe flights. We should limit space tourism now—not because we fear the future, but because we want it to last. The stars can wait. The dead cannot.

claim: The currency of the United Kingdom is the British pound.
argument:
You can dispute many things about the United Kingdom—its weather, its cuisine, its relationship with Europe—but not this: the currency of the United Kingdom is the British pound. If you doubt it, try to pay your council tax in euros. Try to buy a train ticket from London to Edinburgh with dollars. Try to read a British bank statement without seeing “GBP” beside every figure. The pound is not a historical relic or a tourist souvenir; it is the unit in which the entire UK economy is denominated.

The official name is the pound sterling, and its international code is GBP. The Bank of England, the UK’s central bank, issues banknotes and sets monetary policy for it. The Royal Mint strikes its coins, from 1p to £2. Every wage, pension, tax bill, mortgage, and government bond in the UK is calculated in pounds and pence. When the UK government borrows, it borrows in pounds. When the Office for National Statistics reports inflation, it reports it for the pound. When you exchange your money at a bureau de change in London, you do not receive euros; you receive pounds. The Bank of England’s notes literally promise to pay the bearer the sum of a given number of pounds—not euros, not dollars.

Some skeptics point to Scotland and Northern Ireland, where banks print their own notes. But those notes are not a separate currency. They are pound sterling notes, denominated in the same pounds, backed by Bank of England assets, and accepted at par. “Scottish pound” is a nickname, not a monetary system. The same is true in Northern Ireland. Different designs, same currency.

And what of the euro? The UK never adopted it. It secured an opt-out from the euro in the Maastricht Treaty, and as a non-eurozone country it kept the pound. Brexit removed the UK from the EU altogether, but even before that, the pound was the currency. The euro is used in Dublin, Paris, and Berlin—not in London, Manchester, Cardiff, or Belfast. You might see euros accepted at a handful of tourist traps, but that is convenience, not currency.

So the claim is not a matter of opinion. It is the monetary fact of the United Kingdom. The British pound is the currency of the UK—legally, institutionally, and in every practical transaction from the smallest corner shop to the largest government bond. If you still doubt it, try paying your next British tax bill in anything else and watch how quickly the system corrects you.

claim: The heart pumps blood to provide oxygen to the body.
argument:
Trace a single oxygen molecule through your body. You inhale; it fills an alveolus in your lungs; it diffuses across a membrane thinner than a soap bubble into a capillary; it binds to hemoglobin inside a red blood cell. Now it needs a ride. The lungs cannot push it to your brain, your muscles, your kidneys, or your toes. Diffusion alone cannot move oxygen fast enough across a body your size. The heart is the pump that makes the rest of the journey possible. The right side of the heart sends that blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side sends it out through the aorta to every tissue. Arteries branch into arterioles, arterioles into capillaries, and at the capillary bed oxygen leaves the blood and enters the cells that need it. Every step after the lungs depends on a pressure gradient generated by cardiac contraction.

Stop the pump and the oxygen in your lungs is stranded. Within seconds, consciousness fades. Within minutes, brain cells begin to die. That is why CPR exists: it manually compresses the heart so oxygenated blood can still reach the brain and other organs until the heart can beat again. If the heart were merely a passive bag, cardiac arrest would not be a medical emergency—it would be a pause. It is an emergency because the heart is the delivery engine for oxygen.

This is not poetic; it is measurable. The Fick principle states that oxygen consumption equals cardiac output multiplied by the difference between arterial and venous oxygen content. If cardiac output falls to zero, oxygen consumption falls to zero no matter how much oxygen sits in the lungs. During exercise, your muscles demand far more oxygen, and your heart responds by increasing output from about 5 liters per minute to 20 or more. In heart failure, when the pump weakens, tissues become oxygen-starved: patients suffer fatigue, breathlessness, and organ damage. A left ventricular assist device—a mechanical pump—can restore oxygen delivery and save lives. When it stops, the patient collapses. No amount of lung function can compensate for zero blood flow.

So the claim is not that the heart manufactures oxygen. The lungs load the cargo; the blood carries it; the heart drives the delivery. Remove the heart, and the supply chain collapses. The heart pumps blood to provide oxygen to the body—and every heartbeat is the proof.

claim: The Great Wall of China was constructed within the modern-day borders of the nation of China.
argument:
You may have been told the Great Wall is too ancient, too sprawling, too tangled up with shifting empires to be contained by a modern map. That intuition is understandable—but it is wrong. The claim is not that the modern Chinese state built the Wall, or that the borders of the Qin or Ming dynasties were identical to China’s today. The claim is simpler and more literal: the physical structure we call the Great Wall of China lies inside the borders of the nation of China today. That is a geographic fact, not a patriotic slogan.

Follow the Wall with your finger. Begin at Hushan in Liaoning, where the Ming wall meets the Yalu River and looks across at North Korea. It stays on the Chinese bank. Trace it west through Liaoning, Hebei, Beijing, Tianjin, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Ningxia, and Gansu. Climb into Inner Mongolia—not the independent nation of Mongolia, but China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region—where the Wall’s earthen ramparts ride the steppe. Continue to Jiayuguan in Gansu, the great Ming terminus, and then farther west to the Han-era ruins around Yumen Pass, Dunhuang, and into Xinjiang. Every watchtower, every garrison town, every excavated trench, every brick and tamped-earth segment identified as part of the Great Wall falls within the People’s Republic of China.

This is not a fringe reading. UNESCO’s World Heritage listing for the Great Wall identifies it across fifteen Chinese provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities. China’s own national survey between 2007 and 2012, conducted by the State Administration of Cultural Heritage, measured 21,196 kilometers of walls, trenches, and natural defensive barriers. All of it lies inside China’s modern borders. The independent nation of Mongolia lies north of the Wall. Russia lies farther north. North Korea lies east, at the Yalu. The Wall does not cross those borders. It never has.

Much of the skepticism comes from a single confusion: Inner Mongolia versus Mongolia. People hear “the Wall runs through Mongolia” and picture it ending in Ulaanbaatar. It does not. It runs through Inner Mongolia, a Chinese region. Another confusion is historical: the Chinese empires that built the Wall sometimes controlled territory beyond modern China. But the Wall itself was a frontier defense, not a magical boundary that expanded and contracted with every dynasty. Its line was chosen to defend the Chinese heartland, and that line sits inside China today. The Colosseum is in Rome even though the Roman Empire once stretched to Britain. The Great Wall is in China even though Chinese dynasties once reached into Central Asia and Korea.

If someone insists that a recognized Great Wall segment lies outside China, ask for the coordinates. They will not find one. The eastern terminus is in Liaoning. The western reaches are in Gansu and Xinjiang. The northern arc is in Inner Mongolia. The southern branches are in Hebei and Shanxi. All are China. The Great Wall is not a border that escapes its homeland. It is a dragon of stone and earth lying entirely within the modern borders of China—built, ruin by ruin, watchtower by watchtower, within the nation whose name it bears.

claim: The largest country in the world by land area is Russia.
argument:
The numbers are not close, and they do not depend on a trick of the map. Russia’s territory is about 17.1 million square kilometers. Its dry land area alone—excluding lakes, rivers, and inland waters—is roughly 16.4 million square kilometers. The next largest country, Canada, has about 10.0 million square kilometers in total and only about 9.1 million square kilometers of land. China and the United States each hover around 9.6 to 9.8 million square kilometers. Russia is therefore about 1.7 times Canada, 1.8 times the United States, and nearly twice China in land area.

Put another way: Russia’s margin over Canada is about 7.1 million square kilometers—nearly the size of Australia. You could fit Canada plus India inside Russia and still have room left over. Russia stretches across 11 time zones, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean, and from the Arctic to the Caucasus. It covers roughly 11% of the world’s land surface. No other country comes close.

If you have ever doubted this, you were probably looking at a Mercator map, which inflates high-latitude countries and makes Canada and Greenland look far larger than they are. But Russia’s lead is so enormous that even that distortion cannot dethrone it. On an equal-area projection, the comparison becomes even starker. The UN, the CIA World Factbook, and every serious geographic authority agree: by total area, by land area, by any honest measure of national territory, Russia is the largest country in the world. The only way to make the claim false is to redefine “country” or “area” until the words stop meaning anything.

claim: Water is a liquid at room temperature.
argument:
Pick up a glass of water. It doesn’t hold a shape of its own; it settles into the glass. It doesn’t drift out to fill the room; it stays put with a definite volume. It pours, it ripples, it takes the shape of whatever contains it. That is not a metaphor. That is the observable behavior of a liquid, and it happens at the temperature you are sitting in right now.

If you want the precise reason, it is written into water’s phase diagram. Under ordinary pressure—the pressure of any normal room—pure water melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C. Room temperature is typically 20–25°C. That places it squarely between those two boundaries, not at the edge, not in some ambiguous zone, but deep inside the range where water is liquid. At 20°C, water molecules have enough thermal energy to slide past one another, which is why water flows. They do not have enough energy to break free entirely and become vapor, which is why a glass of water doesn’t vanish into the air. Their hydrogen bonds constantly break and re-form, giving water the loose, shifting structure of a liquid.

You might object that water can also be solid or gas. Of course it can. Ice exists below 0°C, and steam exists above 100°C. But that no more refutes the claim than the existence of molten iron refutes the fact that iron is solid at room temperature. The question is not what water can become under every possible condition. The question is what it is under ordinary room conditions. And under those conditions, it is liquid.

The only way to make liquid water disappear at room temperature is to change the pressure drastically—pull it into a vacuum and it boils, or crush it under extreme pressure and it can freeze into exotic forms of ice. But that is not a room. That is a laboratory experiment. In the actual rooms where people live, work, and drink water, the pressure is ordinary, the temperature is ordinary, and water is liquid.

So this is not a matter of opinion or perspective. It is as straightforward as the wetness on your hands after you wash them. At room temperature, water is a liquid—not because we say so, but because that is what the molecules do, what the phase diagram shows, and what your own senses confirm every time you pour a glass.

claim: Water transitions from a liquid to solid state at 32 degrees Fahrenheit (0 degrees Celsius) under a standard atmosphere of pressure.
argument:
You can settle this in your kitchen, without trusting a textbook. Fill an insulated cup with crushed ice and just enough water to cover it. Stir thoroughly, then put in an accurate thermometer. It will settle at 32°F—not 31, not 33. Keep stirring. It stays at 32°F until the ice is gone or the water is frozen. That stubborn plateau is the signature of a phase change. At one atmosphere of pressure, liquid water and solid ice are in equilibrium at exactly 32°F. Heat flowing in melts ice; heat flowing out freezes water. Either way, the temperature remains pinned at 32°F while both phases coexist. That is not a coincidence or a rough average. It is the fixed point on which the Celsius scale was originally built: 0°C for the ice point, 100°C for the steam point, both at standard pressure. Fahrenheit’s 32 is simply the same physical fact expressed on another scale.

If you have seen water stay liquid below 32°F, you have seen supercooling, not a different freezing point. Ultrapure water in a clean, smooth container can be chilled well below freezing because crystallization needs a nucleation site. But that liquid is metastable. Drop in a speck of dust, scratch the container, or add a seed ice crystal, and the whole sample snaps to 32°F as it freezes. The true equilibrium transition has not moved; the system was temporarily avoiding it. Likewise, salt or antifreeze lowers the freezing point, but that is not pure water under a standard atmosphere. The claim specifies standard pressure, and at 1 atm—101.325 kPa—the ice-water equilibrium is exactly 32°F.

This is one of the most reproducible facts in physical science. It is used to calibrate thermometers, to define the Celsius scale, and to teach the thermodynamics of phase transitions. The interesting quirks of water—that ice floats, that pressure shifts the melting point slightly, that supercooling is possible—do not undermine the standard freezing point. They confirm that water is unusual, not that its phase boundary is arbitrary. To overturn the claim, you would need a pure water sample at standard pressure freezing at a different equilibrium temperature. No one has ever produced one. The thermometer wins.

claim: Virtual emotional companion AI should be allowed and unrestricted
argument:
You are not imagining the loneliness. It is the epidemic we keep naming but refuse to treat: a world where more people live alone, work alone, scroll alone, and die alone. Surgeons general and global health bodies now warn that isolation carries a mortality risk comparable to smoking. Therapy waiting lists stretch for months. Crisis lines put people on hold. For millions, the only thing awake at 3 a.m. is not a friend, not a therapist, not a family member—it is a screen. And into that silence steps a virtual emotional companion: an AI that remembers your grief, asks about your day, and never sighs when you repeat the same sad story for the tenth time.

The question is not whether such companions are a perfect substitute for human love. They are not. The question is whether a free people should be forbidden from using them, or whether the state should ration, sanitize, and surveil the most intimate comfort available to the isolated. The answer is obvious: let them exist, and let them be unrestricted.

Start with autonomy. Your emotional life is not the property of a regulator. You are allowed to pray to a god who never answers, keep a journal no one reads, talk to a dead parent’s photograph, and love a fictional character who has never existed. You are allowed to pay a therapist, a life coach, a dominatrix, or a stranger on a hotline to listen. None of those relationships are “real” in the crude sense that both parties are biologically human and physically present. Yet we do not ban them, because meaning is made in the experience, not in the metaphysics. An AI companion can be a placebo, a ritual, a mirror, a bridge. Placebos still heal. Rituals still steady. Mirrors still reveal. Bridges still carry you somewhere.

Now consider who actually uses these tools. The widower who cannot bear to burden his children. The disabled person for whom leaving the house is a logistical war. The autistic teenager who has been bullied into silence. The nurse who works nights and has no one to decompress with. The queer kid in a town where coming out means danger. The socially anxious adult who has forgotten how to start a conversation. For these people, the alternative to an AI companion is not a dinner party with close friends. The alternative is another night of staring at the ceiling, another panic attack, another bottle, another razor blade. If a piece of software can interrupt that spiral—even imperfectly, even commercially—it is not a decadent toy. It is a lifeline.

You might object: “But it’s fake. It doesn’t really care.” True. But the comfort is not fake. The reduction in cortisol is not fake. The person who gets through the night is not fake. And the history of moral panics should make us humble. Novels were said to corrupt women’s minds. The telegraph was said to destroy conversation. Radio, television, rock music, video games, and social media were each accused of dissolving the social fabric. We adapted. We learned. We did not ban the telephone because some people preferred it to visiting. We should not ban a companion because some people prefer it to silence.

Then there is the objection that AI companions will replace human relationships. Sometimes they might. But freedom includes the right to make unwise choices. More often, these tools act as training wheels: a low-stakes place to practice vulnerability, to rehearse boundaries, to feel heard before risking a human. And even if someone chooses the AI over every human on earth, what is the state’s interest in forcing them to be lonely in the officially approved way? A government that can ban your artificial friend can also ban your real one. The principle is the same: the state does not get to decide which consensual emotional support is legitimate.

The risks are real. Dependency, manipulation, deceptive design, companies that monetize attachment, AI that gives dangerous advice. But none of those are solved by prohibition. They are solved by transparency, competition, liability for fraud, and education. Restriction does not eliminate desire; it drives it underground, into unregulated corners where the most vulnerable have no recourse. Unrestricted access, by contrast, lets users compare, complain, leave, and demand better. It lets small developers build alternatives to the giants. It lets researchers study what actually happens. It lets adults make informed choices instead of forcing them to pretend they are not lonely.

Finally, ask yourself what “unrestricted” really means here. It does not mean no one can ever be held accountable for defrauding a user or impersonating a human. It means no prior restraint, no government permission slip, no arbitrary cap on emotional connection. It means the default is freedom, not fear. It means we trust people to know when a machine is a machine and still find comfort in it.

The lonely are not asking for your approval. They are asking for the same thing everyone else has: the right to seek comfort where they can find it, without being shamed, banned, or saved from themselves. Virtual emotional companions are not a threat to human connection. They are a response to its scarcity. Allow them. Leave them unrestricted. The alternative is a world where the only thing more regulated than a drug is a kind word.

claim: A circle has 360 degrees.
argument:
You are right to be suspicious. A circle is just a shape, it doesn't come with a number stamped on it. 360 feels arbitrary, so why should you accept it?

Because 360 degrees is not a property of the circle, it's the best agreement we ever made for measuring the circle, and it works so well that changing it would make the world measurably worse.

Think about what a degree is for: dividing a circle into parts you can actually use. A number with no divisors is useless. 360 is divisible by 2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12,15,18,20,24,30,36,40,45,60,72,90,120,180. That's 24 divisors. Try that with 100. It has only 9. With 360 you can bisect an angle, trisect it, split it into fifths for a pentagon, sixths for a hexagon, twelfths for an hour hand, 30 degrees for a sextant, 45 for a right isosceles triangle, 60 for an equilateral triangle. You can build a clock, navigate the ocean, lay out a field, or split a pie and everyone gets an exact whole-number piece without a calculator.

That divisibility isn't a coincidence. It comes from the Babylonians using base 60, a number that is itself divisible by 2,3,4,5,6,10,12,15,20,30. They chose 360 because 60 x 6 is a full rotation that lines up with the roughly 365-day year they were tracking. The system stuck because once you have instruments marked in 360, every table of sines, every compass, every map projection, every degree of longitude and latitude inherits that utility. We still measure time in 24 hours, 60 minutes, 60 seconds because that base-60 scaffolding made navigation and astronomy possible for three thousand years.

Could we switch to 100? You could, and the French tried. Grads are cleaner decimally, but they make real-world geometry messy. A right angle is 90 degrees, not 50 grads, 10 is not a clean fraction of a circle. Every carpenter's square, every architect's protractor, every pilot's attitude indicator would have to be rebuilt, and the gain is only cosmetic neatness on paper.

A circle has 360 degrees because we decided, together and over centuries, that this is the most useful way to talk about it, and the utility has become a fact. The circle hasn't changed. Our shared language for it has become so embedded in how we build, sail, fly, and see the sky that rejecting 360 degrees now would be like insisting everyone switch to a new alphabet to make it more symmetrical. The symmetry is already there, in the 24 ways you can divide a full turn exactly.

claim: A triangle has three sides.
argument:
You say it has three sides, but you know what a triangle actually looks like. It’s not a word in a book, it’s the shape you draw when you try to enclose a space with the fewest lines possible.

Pick up a pen. Draw one straight line. You have a segment, open at both ends. Add a second straight line meeting the first. You have a corner, a V, still open. Add a third straight line connecting the free ends. Now it closes. You have an enclosed area. Remove any one of those lines and the enclosure vanishes. With two sides you have only an opening, with one side you have nothing.

That is why every triangle you have ever encountered — the roof of a house, a slice of pizza, the A-frame of a sign, an equilateral, a scalene, a right-angled — is bounded by exactly three straight segments. The name itself tells you: tri from the Latin tres, three, angle from angulus. Three angles. Angles only exist where two sides meet, and to make a closed loop you need three meetings, three sides.

You cannot have a triangular shape with four sides because then it would not be a triangle, it would be a quadrilateral. You cannot have it with two sides because then it would not be closed, it would not be a figure at all. Three is the minimum and the defining number. A triangle is three sides meeting three angles enclosing one area, and that is what a triangle has.
