claim: Gas car sales should be banned after a set phase-out date
argument:
You’re not being asked to give up driving. You’re being asked to stop buying a machine that poisons your kids, bankrupts your town, and locks you into a fuel system that is already failing. A phase-out date for new gas car sales is not an attack on freedom. It’s the only way to protect it.

Right now the market is lying to you. A new gas car looks cheap on the lot and expensive to live with. The average American family spends $2,800 a year on gasoline alone. That money leaves your community every week and goes to oil companies and, increasingly, to hostile petrostates. Over a 15-year life, that’s more than the price of the car. Electric vehicles already cost less to fuel and maintain, and total cost of ownership is now lower for most models. Without a deadline, manufacturers keep selling the high-margin gas models they’re comfortable with, and dealers keep pushing them because they’re familiar. A clear end date forces the industry to do what it’s done every time before: innovate faster. Catalytic converters, unleaded fuel, and seatbelts were all “impossible” until the law made them inevitable.

The health case is immediate and local. Gas cars don’t just emit CO2. They emit nitrogen oxides and particulates that settle in the lungs of children near highways and in low-income neighborhoods. The American Lung Association estimates that vehicle pollution causes over 100,000 premature deaths in the US each year and costs $180 billion in health care. That cost is not on the sticker; it’s on your insurance premiums, your ER wait times, and your kid’s asthma inhaler. An electric car bought at home or at work produces zero tailpipe emissions. Banning new sales after a set date means the fleet turns clean within a generation, without forcing anyone to junk a car they already own.

Then there is climate. Transportation is America’s largest source of greenhouse gas emissions. The science is not ambiguous: we need a net zero power sector and a net zero vehicle fleet by mid-century to avoid the worst, irreversible damages. Every new gas car sold today will still be on the road in 2050, emitting for 15 to 20 years. That is a commitment we cannot afford. A phase-out date is a straight line drawn from the physics to policy. It tells car buyers, automakers, utilities, and city planners the same thing: build for an electric future, not a gas present.

You might be thinking about rural life, long trips, and cost. That’s fair. The solution is not to freeze the whole country in 2025. It’s to plan. With a known end date, charging networks get built where people actually drive, not just in cities. Battery costs have dropped 90% in a decade, and will keep falling when demand is guaranteed. Used gas cars remain legal and available for years, and hybrids bridge the gap. The people who lose if there is no ban are the buyers who hold out, pay more for fuel, and get stuck with a depreciating asset while the charging, maintenance, and resale ecosystem moves on without them.

This is also about national security. Gas dependence is a vulnerability. The 2022 price spike, the 1970s oil shocks, and every refinery outage remind us that a foreign commodity can dictate your commute. Electric cars run on a grid that we can power with wind, solar, nuclear, and hydro from our own land. Energy independence is not a slogan; it’s what happens when you stop needing a gas station for every mile.

A ban after a phase-out date doesn’t tell you how to live. It tells the industry how to build. It aligns the market with what you already want: cleaner air, lower running costs, fewer breakdowns, and a car that is quieter, faster, and safer. The question isn’t whether we can afford to end new gas car sales. It’s whether we can afford not to, while we keep subsidizing a technology with a clock that’s already run out.

claim: Genetic engineering of unborn babies should be allowed to eliminate disease.
argument:
You would not deny a child a vaccine to prevent polio. You would not deny surgery to repair a congenital heart defect. You would not watch a baby suffocate from cystic fibrosis and call it natural.

Yet that is exactly what a ban on germline editing for disease does: it forces a child to be born with a suffering you had the power to prevent.

These are not abstract risks. Sickle cell disease steals decades of life in agonizing pain. Tay-Sachs, Huntington's, cystic fibrosis, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and hundreds of others are not a matter of lifestyle or chance; they are a single letter error in the genetic code inherited before birth. We already use prenatal screening to identify those errors, and parents already face the choice of whether to continue a pregnancy they know will end in prolonged suffering and early death. Editing the embryo in vitro is not playing God, it is refusing to play executioner.

The technology is not science fiction. CRISPR-based correction has already fixed disease-causing mutations in human embryos in the lab and can do it before implantation, with the edited embryo then carried to term exactly as with IVF. The goal is not to design a smarter or taller or bluer-eyed baby. It is therapy, the same principle as correcting a typo so the book can be read. The first application would be for monogenic diseases where the mutation is well understood, the risk of off-target edits is measurable and falling, and the alternative is guaranteed disease.

The real ethical risk is inaction. A ban does not stop editing; it moves it underground, to countries with fewer safeguards, and it leaves wealthy families able to access it while everyone else is left with disease. A regulated system with strict limits to serious, heritable disease, transparent safety review, and independent monitoring protects people far better than a prohibition that only preserves suffering.

We have a duty to the child who will be born. That child cannot consent to be born with a preventable genetic disease, but we can consent on their behalf to spare them that fate, just as we consent to vaccinate them, feed them, and treat them when they are sick. Letting them be born diseased when we could have let them be born healthy is not humility. It is cruelty.

claim: Genetic modification of unborn babies is unethical and dangerous.
argument:
You are not just editing a child. You are editing the people that child will become, and the people their children will become, without their permission and without a way to undo it.

Germline editing is permanent. A change made to an embryo with CRISPR is written into every cell of that person and then passed down, generation after generation, whether they wanted it or not. That is the definition of irreversible. Therapeutic medicine treats a sick patient who can consent, understand risks, and stop treatment. A baby in utero can do none of those things. We would be making a profound medical decision for a whole lineage on the basis of parental preference and a snapshot of science that is still moving.

And the science is not safe enough to trust with that power. The first human babies edited with CRISPR in 2018 were found to have mosaicism and off-target mutations we hadn’t predicted. We still cannot reliably predict where the scissors will cut, how many cells will be edited, or what the long-term effects will be on brain development, immunity, fertility, and aging. Animal work shows unintended chromosomal rearrangements and increased cancer risk from the editing process itself. We are talking about risks that won’t show up in a newborn check-up, but twenty or forty years later in a person who never agreed to be an experiment.

Danger is not only technical. It is social. Once we normalize editing embryos to avoid disease, the line moves fast to “enhancement” — taller, smarter, better-looking, more obedient. That is not science fiction; it is already the market logic driving interest in germline modification. The result is a new class divide written into DNA. If only the wealthy can afford designer babies, we don’t get healthier children, we get a caste system that is heritable and inescapable. History remembers eugenics not as a failed experiment in health but as a state-sanctioned dehumanization. The same idea dressed up as choice is still eugenics, just privatized.

Even the most well-intentioned use is dangerous because it displaces what we actually know works. We have effective ways to reduce genetic disease: preimplantation genetic testing, IVF, prenatal screening, newborn screening, and for many conditions, gene therapy that acts only in the individual after birth. Those tools respect the boundary between treating a person and redesigning a species.

We do not get to be humble about this after the fact. If an edit causes harm, the harm is not contained to one patient. It is a legacy. The most ethical thing we can do with a technology this powerful is to not use it on the germline until we can ensure safety, consent, equity, and a society ready for the consequences — and we are nowhere near that.

The question is not whether we can modify embryos. We can. The question is whether we have the right to gamble with a human life, and all the lives that follow it, for gains we cannot guarantee and risks we cannot fully see. We do not.

claim: Gravity causes objects to fall towards the earth.
argument:
You drop a coin. It doesn't drift sideways, it doesn't float away, it goes straight down and hits the floor. You do it a hundred times a day with keys, pens, a glass of water. That isn't a coincidence, it's a pattern.

If falling were about air pushing things down, or about objects being ‘heavy’ in some vague sense, then a feather should fall differently than a hammer only because of air, and in a vacuum they should fall the same. They do. Drop a hammer and a feather on the Moon, where there is no air at all, and they hit the dust at the same time. On Earth put them in a vacuum chamber and you see the same thing. Air resists, it does not cause the fall.

If falling were about density alone, a watermelon and a steel ball should fall at different rates in proportion to weight. They don’t. In every careful measurement, from Galileo’s inclined planes to modern laser timing, all objects accelerate toward the ground at about 9.8 meters per second squared, regardless of material, shape, or size, until air drag matters. That uniformity cries out for a single cause pulling everything the same way.

You can feel that cause when you stand up: your blood has to fight it. You see it in the tides, twice a day, as the Earth’s water is tugged toward the Moon and, more locally, toward the Earth’s own center of mass. You see it in the planets, which don’t fly off into space but curve around the Sun, falling perpetually toward it while moving sideways fast enough to miss it. An orbit is falling that never lands.

Gravity is that falling. It is the Earth reaching out for everything with it. Not a mysterious invisible force, just the name we give to the fact that mass tells space how to curve and space tells mass how to move, and the Earth’s mass makes every loose thing want to be at its center. If you remove the Earth, the fall stops. Take you to the International Space Station and you float, because you are falling around the Earth so fast you never hit it.

You don’t need faith for this. Drop something right now. It will fall. Gravity is why.

claim: Governments and technology companies must do more to protect online privacy and security.
argument:
You don't need to be a criminal to be a victim online. You just need to be online. When a hospital database is leaked, your entire medical history — diagnoses, prescriptions, mental health notes — is sold on the dark web, and suddenly getting life insurance becomes a negotiation you never asked for. When a password reuse breach hits, accounts you haven't logged into in years are drained, and the hours you spend calling banks and filing police reports are time stolen from your life. This isn't theoretical. The average data breach now costs companies $4.45 million, and that cost is passed back to you through higher prices, worse service, and a permanent underclass of people whose identities are never quite their own again.

The "I have nothing to hide" objection confuses privacy with secrecy. You lock your front door not because you're hiding a crime, but because you expect to decide who comes in and when. Privacy is the same boundary online: the freedom to search symptoms without an employer flagging you, to research a political cause without being profiled, to message a doctor or a therapist without that data becoming an ad target. Once that boundary is gone, behavior changes. People self-censor. Markets shrink. Democracy gets quieter.

Technology companies built the infrastructure we live on, and they designed it to extract data by default because data is their product. That is a structural conflict of interest. Security can't be an optional setting buried in menus, and privacy can't be a premium subscription. Companies must be required to minimize collection, encrypt data by default, and prove security through independent audits, not press releases after a breach.

Governments have a responsibility too, not to spy more, but to set the floor. Stronger breach notification laws, binding privacy standards, limits on data retention and third-party sharing, and real enforcement with penalties that hurt — not cost-of-doing-business fines — are the baseline of a digital public square. This doesn't kill innovation; it creates trust. People use more services, share more honestly, and take more economic risk when they believe the system won't turn against them tomorrow.

Privacy and security are not luxuries for the paranoid. They're the conditions for a free life online. If we keep pretending that convenience is worth being watched, hacked, and commodified, we don't get freedom. We get a cheaper, more efficient form of control, and you pay the price every time you log on.

claim: Humans need oxygen to breathe.
argument:
You can stop breathing for a few seconds on purpose and feel fine. Stop for a minute and your vision tunnels, your lungs ache to move, your brain knows something is wrong. That ache is not a habit. It is a demand.

Breathe in. The air you just pulled in is not what keeps you alive, it is what delivers what keeps you alive. Every cell in your body is burning fuel right now, using glucose and fat to make the ATP that powers your heartbeat, your thoughts, the tightening of a muscle. That burn is combustion, and like any combustion it needs an oxidizer. For humans that oxidizer is oxygen.

Without it the chain stops mid-step. Your red blood cells carry oxygen to tissues because your mitochondria can only extract energy from food if oxygen is available as the final electron acceptor. No oxygen, no ATP. No ATP, no ion pumps, no nerve firing, no cell survival. The body knows this before you do. The first thing that fails is the brain, which uses 20% of your oxygen despite being 2% of your weight. Three to four minutes without oxygen causes irreversible damage; four to six minutes is usually fatal.

You can replace the nitrogen in air with argon and breathe comfortably for a short time. You cannot replace the oxygen. Diving accidents, anesthesia mishaps, high altitude sickness, and COVID-19 all kill in the same way: not by stopping the lungs from moving, but by stopping oxygen from reaching cells. People who climb Everest without supplemental oxygen get slower, weaker, and confused because their bodies are literally running out of fuel. People who survive a near-drowning are left with brain injury because those minutes without oxygen cost neurons they never get back.

Breathing is not moving air for the sake of moving air. It is the only way we have, as land animals, to get the one molecule our metabolism cannot live without into the blood, into the cells, and into the mitochondria. You need oxygen to breathe because breathing exists for oxygen.

claim: Ice is a solid state of water.
argument:
Ice is water. The skepticism is understandable — ice looks different, feels different, behaves different. It cracks, it floats, it won’t pour. But difference in behavior is not difference in identity, it’s difference in arrangement.

Every gram of ice is H₂O. Chemically analyze it, melt it, and you get exactly the same H₂O you started with, down to the parts per million. No new substance is created when water freezes, and no substance is lost when it melts. The molecules are identical: two hydrogens bonded to one oxygen. The only thing that changes is how those molecules relate to each other.

In liquid water the molecules move freely, sliding past one another. Cool it below 0°C at atmospheric pressure and the kinetic energy drops enough for hydrogen bonds to lock the molecules into a repeating hexagonal lattice. That lattice is a solid. It has a fixed shape, definite volume, and resists compression. Warm it again and the lattice breaks, the molecules regain mobility, and you have liquid water once more. It is reversible, continuous, and predictable.

That is the definition of a phase change, not a chemical change. You do not need to add or remove anything to turn steam into liquid into ice, just heat. If ice were a different substance from water, melting would be a decomposition reaction, and refreezing would be a synthesis reaction. It is not. We can freeze the same sample a thousand times and it remains the same sample.

You can taste it, measure it, and trace it. The water you drink in summer is the same water that falls as snow in winter. The ice cubes in your glass came from the tap. When they melt, the level in your glass rises because ice is less dense, not because a new liquid is being produced.

Ice is not water in denial of itself. It is water made still.

claim: Individuals must take responsibility for online privacy without excessive government mandates.
argument:
You don’t have a privacy problem because the internet exists. You have a privacy problem because you act like privacy is something that happens to you, not something you do.

Every time a government promises to protect your online privacy with a new mandate, it is selling you a trade you should never make: give up control for the illusion of safety. Those mandates don’t stop data collection, they just move it, centralize it, and make it less visible. A law that forces every company to use the same privacy standard creates a single point of failure. Hack one regulated database and you get millions of lives. Keep privacy decentralized, and a breach is damage, not a catastrophe.

Mandates also freeze innovation. Privacy tools are not static. End-to-end encryption, zero-knowledge storage, ephemeral messaging, local-first apps, paid ad-free services — all of this emerged because individuals and companies were free to experiment with what privacy means to them. A regulator writing rules today will be certifying the privacy of yesterday. By the time a mandate passes, the threat has evolved.

The core truth is that privacy online is a series of choices, not a right you can legislate into existence. You choose what to share on social media. You choose whether to download that free app with a 40-page privacy policy. You choose to use a password manager, to enable two-factor authentication, to pay for a service instead of selling your attention for it. Those are hard choices, but they are yours. When government replaces them with mandates, it trains you to ignore the choice entirely. “The government handles it” becomes the excuse to be careless.

This is not about trusting corporations blindly. It is about recognizing that no law can keep up with reality and no agency can be a proxy for your judgment. A mandate can ban a type of cookie, but it can’t stop you from posting your home address in a public forum. It can require notice, but it can’t make you read it. Responsibility can.

Individual responsibility also scales. One million people using encrypted messaging protects one million conversations. One law protecting one million people protects exactly nothing until it is enforced, litigated, and circumvented. The former is immediate, adaptive, and free of political capture. The latter is bureaucratic, slow, and a prize for lobbyists.

You are already responsible for your physical privacy. You lock your door, you don’t shout your bank PIN in a cafe, you choose where to live and who you let in. Online privacy is the same: the tools exist, the knowledge is accessible, and the cost of inaction is yours to bear. Mandates promise to take that burden off you. They don’t. They just hide it until it fails spectacularly.

Take the burden back. Demand better tools, pay for privacy when it matters, and treat your data the way you treat your keys. That is how privacy actually gets defended, and it is the only defense that can’t be voted away.

claim: Internet access should be considered a basic human right
argument:
You already treat it as essential in every other area of your life, you just haven't caught up with the language yet.

Try holding a job without internet. No applications, no scheduling, no remote work, no banking, no benefits portal. Try getting an education without it. No homework, no research, no library database, no college lectures, no GED program. Try staying healthy without it. No telehealth appointments, no prescription refills, no locating a clinic that takes your insurance, no public health alerts. Try participating in democracy without it. No reading the candidates, no voter registration, no checking how your representative voted, no organizing a protest.

These aren't conveniences. They are the basic functions of a modern society, and in 2025 the internet is the pipe that carries them.

A basic human right isn't defined by what our grandparents needed to survive in 1945. It's defined by what you need to live with dignity and agency today. Food, water, shelter, and healthcare meant survival. Internet access means participation. Without it you are not just poorer, you are invisible. You can't speak to power because you can't be heard, you can't learn because you can't be taught, you can't earn because you can't be found.

Skeptics say internet is expensive and fragile. So was electricity a hundred years ago. So was clean water. We didn't leave those to the market. We built grids, set standards, and recognized that exclusion from them is exclusion from citizenship. The UN already recognizes access to information as a human right. Internet access is simply what makes that right real instead of theoretical.

You don't have to love the internet to respect it. You don't have to want people streaming video to want them to have a classroom, a doctor, a job application, and a voice. Denying access isn't neutral. It's a decision to keep a class of people permanently on the outside of civic life.

If a right is about giving every person the minimum tools to provide for themselves and have a say in the world they live in, then internet access is that minimum. Now.

claim: Internet access should not be considered a basic human right
argument:
A basic human right is something you possess simply because you are human, and that others must leave you alone to enjoy. Life, liberty, bodily integrity, freedom of conscience and speech, due process. These rights require others to refrain from harming you. They cost nothing to grant and everything to violate.

Internet access is none of those things. It is a service, a technology, an infrastructure built and maintained by people, companies, and states. It requires fiber, spectrum, power, maintenance, upgrades, and constant payment. Declaring it a right does not create it out of thin air; it creates a duty on someone else to build it, run it, and pay for it. A right that forces a third party to labor on your behalf is not a right, it is a claim on other people's work.

If internet access were a basic human right, what would that actually mean? That every person on Earth is entitled to a continuous, high-speed, reliable connection provided at public expense. Who pays? Who decides the quality of that connection? Who maintains it when it breaks? The moment you make a service a right, you make the state the provider of last resort. That hands governments the power to define what counts as adequate access, who gets priority, and what speech is permitted on the network they must supply. The most powerful way to control people is to make them dependent on you for the channel of expression itself.

We already have the right that matters. The right to seek, receive and impart information. That right existed before the internet, it survives if the internet fails, and it constrains governments regardless of technology. What the internet does is make that right easier to exercise for some people. Ease is not the same as necessity. A printing press was not a human right; freedom of the press was. Postal service was not a human right; freedom of correspondence was.

Treating connectivity as a right also confuses need with entitlement. Yes, modern life is difficult without the internet. So is electricity, a car, a bank account, a smart phone. We recognize these as goods that improve welfare, not as moral prerequisites for being treated as human. We do not call housing, food, and medicine human rights in the strict philosophical sense, we treat them as urgent public goals precisely because they cannot be guaranteed as rights without immense coercion and distortion. Calling internet a right does not make it more available; it politicizes it, makes it a lever for patronage, and turns access into a favor distributed by the state.

The most humane approach is to protect the freedom to use whatever tools exist, and to invest in making those tools cheaper and more widely available through voluntary innovation, competitive markets, and targeted public programs. That respects both people and the reality of how technology works. The internet is a remarkable public good. It is not, and should never be, a basic human right.

claim: It is fair for insurers and lenders to use credit scores and risk models.
argument:
You want fairness. So do I. And fairness isn’t everyone paying the same price whether they’re likely to pay you back or not. That’s not fairness, that’s a tax on the responsible to subsidize the reckless.

Insurers and lenders aren’t charities. They’re in the business of pooling risk, and a pool only works if people who are more likely to use it pay more into it. If an insurer has to charge the same premium to a driver with twenty years of safe driving and no claims as to a driver with three DUIs and two at-fault accidents, the safe driver will leave. Good risks exit, bad risks stay, premiums spiral, and eventually the product becomes unaffordable for everyone. That’s what happened with community-rated health insurance in places that tried it without risk adjustment — healthy people opt out, sick people crowd in, the system collapses.

Credit scores and risk models are how a lender or insurer estimates who you are likely to be, not who your parents were. They are blunt, imperfect, and they do reflect the reality that past behavior predicts future behavior far better than good intentions do. Missed payments, debt-to-income, length of history, utilization — these are not immutable traits like race or sex. They are records of choices. A score can go up within months when someone starts paying on time. That is the opposite of a caste system; it is a system that rewards change.

The alternative to risk-based pricing isn’t some pure, flat world of equal treatment. It’s rationing. If you can’t price risk, you can’t serve risk. Lenders will simply say no to anyone with anything less than a pristine file, and insurers will pull out of markets altogether. Risk-based pricing is what lets a young person with thin credit get a starter card at a higher rate for a year, build history, and graduate to a lower rate. It’s what lets someone with a spotless record borrow a home at 6% instead of 9%.

Yes, risk models can embed bias if the data they learn from is biased. That’s a real problem and it needs fixing — better data, auditing, recourse, and transparency. But the answer to a biased model is a less biased model, not no model at all. Banning the use of credit scores wouldn’t make the underlying risk disappear. It would just hide it and make it more expensive for the people who have the least leverage to fight it: the honest, stable, low-risk borrowers who currently benefit most from differentiation.

Fairness means you pay for the risk you bring with you, not the risk your neighbor brings. Using credit scores and actuarial risk models is how lenders and insurers keep promises to the people who depend on them, stay solvent, and keep credit and coverage available at all.

claim: Lifespan extension would exacerbate inequities and should not be pursued
argument:
You already get to live longer if you’re rich. That’s not a prediction, it’s the status quo.

Today in the US, a man in the top income quintile can expect to live about 15 years longer than a man in the bottom quintile. In the UK, men in the most deprived areas die on average 9 years earlier than men in the most affluent. Black Americans die roughly 6 years earlier than white Americans. The gap isn’t biology, it’s access: neighborhoods with clean air, good food, safe streets, earlier diagnosis, better doctors, time off to rest.

Now imagine lifespan extension actually works. Not general health, not preventive care, but real, purchasable extra years — senolytics, partial reprogramming, engineered tissues, whatever comes first. It will not arrive as a public vaccine. It will arrive as a drug, a procedure, a subscription. History tells us exactly how that gets distributed.

Cancer drugs already cost $100,000 to $2 million per patient. Gene therapies like Zolgensma are $2.1 million for one child. GLP-1s for weight loss, which are also extending healthspan, are rationed by price and prior authorization. The first effective longevity intervention will be priced at whatever the market will bear, because the buyer is someone desperate to keep what they already have.

That means the first extra decades will go to the people who already own the first decades. Older, wealthy people in wealthy countries will buy time, and time is power. They’ll keep their seats on boards, their capital compounding, their votes active for longer. Inheritance gets stretched. The children who would have inherited at 70 inherit at 95. Social Security, pensions, Medicare, all systems built on a roughly 78-year life expectancy, buckle when the top 1% starts routinely hitting 110 while the bottom 50% is still dying at 72.

You don’t just get more inequality in lifespan, you get more inequality in everything lifespan buys. Longer life for the rich is longer accumulation of wealth, expertise, networks, and political influence. It’s a gerontocracy with a price tag. The effect on younger people is brutal: fewer promotions, fewer housing opportunities, fewer places in school and clinics, while a cohort of well-preserved elites stays in place indefinitely.

Globally it’s worse. The North-South gap in life expectancy is already 20 years. If longevity is a product, it will be exported first to London, San Francisco, Singapore, and Dubai, not to Lagos or La Paz. We will have a world where citizenship becomes a longevity credential.

The moral appeal of longer life assumes it will be shared. It won’t. We can already extend healthy life for everyone by doing things we know work: universal clean water, maternal care, vaccination, air pollution limits, paid sick leave. Those interventions cost money but they compress morbidity and they actually reach poor people.

Pursuing lifespan extension as a technology first, equity later, guarantees the opposite outcome: it turns a basic human good — more years — into a luxury good that widens the chasm we already have. If we can’t make sure everyone gets to 80 in good health, we have no business selling 120 to the few.

claim: Limits should be placed on acceptable human risk levels for initial Mars colonization missions
argument:
Mars colonization will not be remembered by how fast we get there, but by whether anyone is still alive to build a second generation there. That is the difference between a stunt and a settlement, and a settlement demands limits on risk that no flag-planting mission ever did.

An initial colonist is not spending six months on a ship to bring back rocks. They are expected to live, work, reproduce, and maintain life support for years in an environment that has no rescue, no hospital, no spare parts, and no way out. If the first crews are lost at rates we would consider unacceptable for any other high-risk profession, we will not have a colony. We will have a graveyard, a lawsuit, and a public that will never fund a second attempt.

We already know what the baseline hazards are. Interplanetary radiation alone delivers roughly 0.7 millisieverts per day on the surface, with solar particle events that can spike to lethal levels in hours. A round trip with a 500-day surface stay is on the order of one sievert, a dose that NASA's own models tie to a ~5% increase in lifetime fatal cancer risk and a substantially higher risk of acute radiation sickness. Landing and takeoff from Mars requires powered descent through a thin atmosphere with no abort to orbit, and with return windows every 26 months. A single life-support failure, a micrometeoroid strike, a dust storm that cuts solar power for weeks, or a psychological breakdown in isolation is not an inconvenience; it is an extinction event for that crew.

You can accept a high probability of death when the goal is a few hours on the Moon. You cannot accept it when the goal is permanence. A colony that begins by normalizing coin-flip odds does not inspire follow-on investment; it guarantees the project is seen as a sacrifice, not a migration. People will not sign up, insurers will not cover, Congress will not reauthorize, and the public will turn on the agency that sent civilians to die for a press release.

Limits are not cowardice. They are engineering. The Apollo program's 1-in-50 loss-of-crew expectation is often romanticized until you remember the program was saved only because the O-rings, the guidance, and the quality control were treated as non-negotiable. A formal, public risk ceiling — say, loss-of-crew probability per mission on the order of the commercial airline standard, not the test-pilot standard — forces the hard choices that make colonization possible at all: robust radiation shielding, in-situ propellant production for a reliable return, closed-loop life support tested for years on Earth, redundant habitats, and crew mental-health protocols.

Without a ceiling, risk is quietly traded for schedule and budget. With a ceiling, the mission survives. Limits do not mean never going. They mean going in a way where the first settlers can become the second settlers, and the third. That is the only definition of colonization worth attempting.

claim: Penguins of all existing species are biologically incapable of self-powered flight.
argument:
You want flight? Flight demands three things a penguin will never have at once: lift, power, and a wing that can both generate that lift and fold away for the rest of life.

A flying bird is built around flight first. Its skeleton is hollow and light, its sternum is a deep keel to anchor massive pectoral muscles, and its wings are long, narrow, and asymmetrical, shaped to bite air. A penguin has the opposite blueprint.

Every living penguin species, from the 40-centimeter little blue to the 120-centimeter emperor, has turned its forelimbs into flippers. The bones are solid and dense, not hollow. That density is ballast for diving, and it is dead weight for the air. The sternum is present but shallow, incapable of anchoring the huge flight muscles a bird needs to actively beat its wings. Instead, the chest muscles are thick and powerful, but they are built to pull the flipper down in water, where the resistance is 800 times greater than air. In water that muscle is devastating; in air it is useless.

The wing itself is the clincher. A flying bird’s wing is a high-aspect-ratio airfoil that can be tucked against the body. A penguin’s flipper is short, broad, and stiff, with a tiny surface area relative to body mass. The ratio of wing loading to muscle power is impossibly high. Even the most powerful bird muscles couldn’t generate enough thrust to overcome the drag of a penguin’s torsomass, dense bones, and blunt body in air.

You can see it in action every time a penguin “tries.” On land they can’t get airborne; they waddle and toboggan. At the edge of the water they launch not by flapping, but by using the momentum of a head-first plunge and their flipper muscles to push off the ground into a controlled fall. That isn’t self-powered flight, it’s a dive start in reverse.

Penguins are not failed birds. They are expertly successful penguins. They traded the air for the ocean and their bodies were remade to match. Give them a wing built for soaring and they drown. Give them dense bones and flippers built for propulsion and they can never leave the water on their own power. That is why none of the 18 extant species, past or present in your lifetime, can ever be lifted into true, sustained, self-powered flight.

claim: No limits should be placed on acceptable human risk for initial Mars colonization missions
argument:
You are skeptical because you are imagining a mission run on children or conscripts. No one is asking for that. The first Mars colonists will be adults who volunteer knowingly, who are trained for years, and who understand the odds better than any safety board ever could. To put a cap on acceptable risk for them is to decide for them that their life choices are not theirs to make.

Every great expansion in human history was begun by people who accepted risks that would be illegal today. The first transatlantic crossings, the first Arctic over-winterings, the first flights over the ocean, all were done with mortality rates that would shut down a modern airline in a week. We do not call those people reckless; we call them pioneers, and we are still living off what they risked. Mars is not a science tour. It is a permanent settlement. You cannot bootstrap a settlement with a risk budget designed for a tourist flight.

A hard limit on risk does not make a mission safer, it makes it impossible. It forces engineers to over-engineer, to add mass for redundancy that requires more fuel, which requires bigger rockets, which creates more failure modes. Apollo 1 killed three astronauts in a test. The program did not stop. It fixed the fire and flew. If NASA had a binding "one in a thousand" rule in 1967, we would never have landed on the Moon. A colonization window is 26 months. If you cannot launch when the window opens because a risk model says 1.8% is too high instead of 1.5%, you lose a generation and die of old age on Earth.

The real risk is not to the crew, it is to humanity. Earth has one biosphere, one point of failure. A self-sustaining Mars colony is the first insurance policy against a civilization-ending event, whether asteroid, pandemic, or self-inflicted collapse. The moral calculus is not risk to seven volunteers versus zero risk. It is risk to seven volunteers versus the risk that no one ever goes, and the species remains trapped.

If you would not let a volunteer firefighter into a burning building because the building is too dangerous, you have stopped being humane and started being custodial. These people are not cargo. They are consenting adults choosing to accept extraordinary risk for an extraordinary purpose. The only ethical limit is informed consent, not a bureaucratically defined number. Let them choose what risk is acceptable, because they are the only ones who have to live with the choice.

claim: People receiving welfare benefits should be tracked to prevent fraud/abuse.
argument:
You pay taxes. So do I. That money is supposed to be a lifeline for people who genuinely can’t make ends meet — a single mother working a double shift, a veteran with a disability, a family rebuilding after layoffs. It is not an entitlement for anyone to game.

Right now that lifeline is being drained, and the honest people who need it most are the ones who pay the price. The Government Accountability Office and state audits have repeatedly found welfare fraud in the millions: duplicate enrollments across states, benefits claimed while earning full-time income, identity theft rings using stolen Social Security numbers to open new cases. In 2022 alone, improper payments across federal programs totaled over $230 billion. Some of that is error, but a substantial and growing share is intentional abuse.

That is not a victimless crime. Every dollar lost to fraud is a dollar not available for a child’s food, rent assistance, or job training. When budgets are tight, the first thing cut is the benefit increase or the outreach program — not the fraud.

Tracking is not punishment. It is verification. We already track who gets a mortgage, who gets unemployment, who flies on a plane. A simple, modern system — cross-referencing income data from employers and state tax agencies, flagging duplicate addresses or ID numbers, requiring periodic check-ins via phone or an app — would catch the abuse without humiliating the majority of recipients.

Think of it as protecting the program from itself. Recipients who do nothing wrong have nothing to hide, and they are tired of being lumped in with the cheaters. Tracking gives them a clear way to prove they belong and restores public trust in the system they rely on.

If we want welfare to remain a moral safety net and not a political punching bag, we have to make it clean, accountable, and fair to the taxpayers who fund it and the people who truly need it. Tracking is how we do that.

claim: Prescription drug ads should not be allowed on television
argument:
You trust your doctor with your life, and television prescription drug ads are designed to break that trust.

Every sixty seconds during prime time, a glossy thirty-second spot tells you that a new pill can fix your low mood, your joint pain, your restless bladder, your “brain fog.” It shows smiling people hiking, laughing at dinner tables, getting their lives back. Then, in a rush of tiny print and a voice so fast it’s unintelligible, it lists the risks: suicidal thoughts, heart attacks, strokes, death. The ad doesn’t tell you the odds, it doesn’t tell you the alternatives, and it doesn’t tell you that the benefit you just saw was cherry-picked from a single trial.

The result isn’t more informed patients. It’s more demanding patients. Studies consistently show direct-to-consumer advertising drives people into doctors’ offices asking for a brand name they saw on TV, not a diagnosis they need. Doctors report spending valuable time talking patients out of drugs, or worse, prescribing them to avoid an awkward confrontation. That creates overtreatment: more prescriptions for conditions that would resolve on their own, more switches to newer, more expensive drugs with no proven advantage over cheaper generics, and a surge in polypharmacy for older adults who are already vulnerable.

It also makes medicine more expensive for all of us. Those ads aren’t free. In the U.S. alone, pharmaceutical companies spent over $6 billion on direct-to-consumer advertising in recent years. That cost is baked into the price of the drug. You pay for the ad every time you fill a prescription, and the rest of us pay when insurance premiums rise to cover it. The U.S. and New Zealand are the only two countries in the world that allow this kind of broadcast advertising; every other developed nation, including the U.K., Australia, and Canada, bans it because they concluded the public health harms outweigh any benefit.

The core promise of the ads — that they empower you — is a lie. Real empowerment comes from a conversation with a clinician who knows your history, your allergies, your other medications, and your values. A TV spot, written by a marketing team and approved by a regulator that allows disease-mongering language, can’t do that. It can only create anxiety about normal life and sell a product.

Take the ads off the air and you don’t take away information. Physicians can still prescribe, patients can still research, and doctors can still discuss new treatments with you directly, without a 30-second commercial turning your living room into a pharmacy waiting room. A ban protects the integrity of the doctor-patient relationship, reduces dangerous overuse, and stops you from subsidizing commercials that were never made to help you.

claim: Prescription drug ads should be allowed on television
argument:
You’re worried these ads are a thirty-second commercial for profit, not health — that they’ll make people demand pills they don’t need, confuse them with side effects flashed in tiny print, and put a marketing budget between a patient and a doctor. That concern is real, and it’s why we regulate them. But banning them on television doesn’t protect people. It hides information from them.

A prescription drug ad is the only time a regular person is told a condition might have a name, a treatment, and a conversation worth starting. Without that prompt, millions stay silent. Depression, ADHD, osteoporosis, high cholesterol, and uncontrolled asthma are all routinely under-diagnosed and under-treated, not because doctors don’t care, but because patients don’t know the symptoms are worth mentioning until they see them named in a way they can understand.

When you see an ad, you are not forced to take the drug. You can’t even get it without a prescription. What you get is a starting point for an informed conversation. Studies consistently show that direct-to-consumer advertising increases patient-physician dialogue, and that dialogue improves adherence and outcomes. Patients who learn about a condition from a TV spot are more likely to ask questions, to seek follow-up, and to stay on therapy once prescribed. In the U.S., where ads are allowed, patients are also more likely to be aware of newer, safer alternatives than in countries where advertising is banned, not less.

The alternative to television ads isn’t no ads. It’s worse information. People still hear about drugs — from social media influencers with no oversight, from online forums, from pharmaceutical reps who can only speak to doctors. Television advertising is the one channel where the FDA requires a fair balance of benefits and risks, a black box warning when necessary, and a clear “talk to your doctor” mandate. You can see the risk list in real time, in plain language, and you can’t buy the product at the end of the spot. That is more transparency, not less.

Keeping patients uninformed in the name of protecting them assumes the doctor knows everything the patient is experiencing, and that the patient will come forward on their own. They often don’t. Giving people language for their own bodies — and the right to ask about it — isn’t manipulation. It’s respect. Prescription drug ads belong on television precisely because health shouldn’t be a secret you only hear about after it’s too late.

claim: Raising the minimum wage to $15 would hurt small businesses and jobs.
argument:
$15 an hour sounds like a fair number on a poster. For a small business it is a math problem you cannot poster your way out of.

A small restaurant, a neighborhood salon, a family hardware store does not have layers of corporate overhead to absorb a cost shock. It has a thin margin, rent that is already up, and a payroll that is 25 to 40 percent of every dollar it brings in. Raise the wage floor by 50 to 100 percent overnight and that payroll line does not get smaller. It gets larger, and everything else has to shrink to compensate.

Owners will not just eat it. First they cut hours. Then they cut positions. A second opening is delayed or never happens. A 20-hour a week entry job for a high school kid becomes a 12-hour job, or disappears because the machine that does the same task for $4 an hour in electricity is now cheaper than a $15 employee. That is exactly what happened in Seattle after the phased $15 rollout. The University of Washington’s own analysis found low-wage job losses of 6 to 9 percent in the city, with the pain concentrated in small businesses and in the lowest-paid workers who lost hours. San Francisco saw similar patterns: higher pay for the workers who kept their jobs, fewer jobs overall.

The claim that businesses will simply raise prices misses the reality of small markets. A diner can raise a burger $1 and lose customers to the chain down the street that can negotiate cheaper food, national marketing, and bulk labor. Small businesses compete on price and personal service, not pricing power. When costs rise, they can’t pass it all on, so they get smaller.

This is not about being against workers earning more. It is about how you get there. A sudden jump to $15 punishes the exact businesses that hire first-time workers, it rewards automation, and it leaves the owner with a choice no one should have to make: pay people more and close the doors, or keep the doors open and pay people less. That is a loss for employees and for the community that depends on those locally owned shops for jobs, tax base, and life.

claim: Prescription drug importation should be allowed to increase access and lower costs.
argument:
You are paying three times more for the exact same pill, manufactured in the exact same factory, and the government is stopping you from buying it.

In Canada, insulin lispro costs $98 per vial. In the United States it costs $275. The same vial. The same maker. The difference is not research, it is not quality, it is a policy choice that lets U.S. manufacturers charge Americans a monopoly price while selling to everyone else at a fair one. Last year Americans spent $835 billion on prescription drugs, more than any other country on earth, while covering fewer people. The average American pays 2.56 times what citizens in other wealthy countries pay for the same medicines.

That is not a market. That is a hostage situation.

You are told importation is unsafe. That is the fear the industry sells you, and it collapses under scrutiny. The drugs we would import from Canada would not be bootleg pills from the internet. They would be the same FDA-approved drugs made by Pfizer, Novartis, Sanofi and sold in licensed Canadian pharmacies under Health Canada regulations that mirror our own Good Manufacturing Practices. The FDA already allows personal importation of prescription drugs on a case-by-case basis for patients with serious conditions. The FDA already permits importation of drugs for veterinary use and for clinical trials. The government can and does inspect foreign facilities, and Canada has a single-payer system with a national regulatory agency that has a powerful incentive to not allow unsafe drugs in.

The real risk is not importing a safe drug from Canada. The real risk is what happens now: 1 in 4 Americans rationing their medication because of cost, 1 in 3 seniors skipping doses, and thousands dying of preventable conditions because an insulin-dependent diabetic chose groceries over insulin. A 2022 JAMA study found that high out-of-pocket costs were associated with 1 in 4 deaths from heart attacks and strokes. That is a safety crisis you are already living with.

Importation is not a radical experiment. It is a pressure valve. Florida, New Hampshire, Maine, Colorado and Vermont have already passed state importation programs. The Department of Health and Human Services certified in 2020 that a Canadian importation program could be done safely. The hold-up is not science, it is lobbying.

Allowing a vetted, FDA-supervised importation program does not force anyone to buy foreign drugs. It simply gives you the legal option to do what you already do illegally or not at all. It creates competition for the first time in decades. Overnight, prices fall because pharmacy benefit managers and drug makers know Americans can walk across the border or click to a certified Canadian pharmacy and get the same drug for a third of the price.

You can keep the FDA as the gatekeeper. You can require serialization, lot verification, chain-of-custody tracking, and sales only from licensed pharmacies. What you cannot keep is the moral fiction that a free country should ban you from buying a cheaper, safe, life-saving medicine because it inconveniences an industry that has turned your illness into a profit center.

If a neighbor can get a heart medication for $40 that costs you $240, and both pills come from the same plant, the ethical choice is not to ban the neighbor. It is to let you buy it too.

claim: Recreational drone pilots should not require registration and testing
argument:
Recreational drone flying is a hobby, not a hazard, and treating it like commercial aviation is a solution in search of a problem that ends up punishing the people who are already the safest pilots in the sky.

The core safety concern is real: no one wants a drone near an airport or over a crowd. But registration and testing don't address that risk. The people who cause dangerous incidents aren't going to register first. They are already flying illegally, and a $5 registration sticker and an online quiz will not deter them. Meanwhile the only people who comply are the law-abiding hobbyists who were already flying responsibly, often under 400 feet, away from people and airports, exactly as the FAA recommends.

A registration system creates risk instead of reducing it. It builds a government database of names, addresses, and the serial numbers of thousands of private devices owned by families, teachers, and kids. That database is a privacy liability and a target for misuse, and it does nothing for actual safety. The data isn't used to intercept a reckless pilot in real time; it is only useful after an incident has already happened.

Testing adds cost and friction for no measurable gain. The current recreational rules already require pilots to follow community-based safety guidelines and keep visual line of sight. Adding a test means a fee, study time, and a renewal process that will price out students, seniors, and low-income families from a hobby that is often their only affordable access to flight, photography, and STEM learning. When you make a hobby bureaucratic you don't make it safer, you make it disappear into the shadows where it can't be engaged with or improved.

Safety is better served by what actually works: clear, simple voluntary guidelines, accessible education through clubs and manufacturers, and targeted enforcement against the small minority who intentionally break the rules. The model works for model airplanes for decades before drones existed. We don't register every kid with a kite, and we don't test them before they fly. We trust them with guidance, a community norm, and consequences for misuse.

Keep the sky open for the responsible majority instead of building a registration wall that only the reckless will step over.

claim: Recreational drone pilots should be registered and tested
argument:
You love flying for the same reason the rest of us do: the quiet thrill of seeing the world from above, getting the perfect shot, the satisfaction of learning a machine that responds to your hands. That freedom is exactly what registration and testing protects.

Without a baseline of competence, the hobby is eating itself. In the last three years the FAA logged over 29,000 near-misses between drones and manned aircraft, and more than 1,600 reports of drones entering restricted airspace around airports. A recreational pilot who doesn’t know about Class B, C, D and E airspace, or how to read a sectional chart, can and will fly a $500 drone into a $10 million helicopter’s approach path. One serious incident — one person hurt, one hospital helicopter grounded — is all it takes for Congress to ban drones outright, the way they banned RC planes near airports in the 1980s.

Registration isn’t a tax, it’s a name tag. For a few dollars you tie a serial number to a real person. That means when a drone crashes into a crowd at a park, damages a car, or buzzes a wildfire crew, there’s a way to find the operator instead of the public paying the cleanup. It also means responsible pilots are no longer lumped in with the reckless ones. Right now a pilot who memorizes the rules has no way to prove it; a registration plus a short test gives you that proof.

The test itself would be tiny. The FAA’s existing recreational test is 60 multiple-choice questions you can study for in an evening: keep your drone within visual line of sight, stay under 400 feet, yield to manned aircraft, don’t fly over people, know where you can and can’t fly. It’s not a pilot’s license and it doesn’t cost hundreds of dollars. It’s a competence check that every other hobby with risk already requires — you need a license to drive, a certification to hunt with a bow, a permit to fly a model rocket over a certain size. No one calls those bans on freedom; they’re the minimum price of being allowed to operate in shared space.

A tested, registered community is a safer community for you. Fewer reckless flyers means fewer angry homeowners calling 911 on every buzzing quadcopter, fewer local ordinances banning takeoffs from parks, and more access to clubs and flying fields. Airlines, fire departments, and police are already lobbying hard for stricter rules. Giving them a voluntary, low-cost safety floor now lets us write the rules ourselves later.

You don’t register and test because you’re a bad pilot. You do it because you’re a good one, and you want other people to stay good enough that you’re still allowed to fly tomorrow.

claim: Requiring all police officers to wear body cameras should not be mandated
argument:
You want more accountability, which is understandable. Body cameras feel like an obvious fix: record everything, and abuse disappears. But a blanket mandate for every officer would make policing less safe, less accountable, and less trustworthy — and the evidence shows it won’t deliver what you think it will.

First, cameras don’t change behavior reliably. The Rialto experiment that launched this movement showed a sharp drop in complaints for about a year, then the effect faded. Multiple later studies in Washington D.C., Phoenix, and across the UK found no consistent, lasting reduction in use of force. What they did find consistently is a change in how officers police. With a camera on every uniform, officers become risk-averse. They hesitate in ambiguous, fast-moving encounters because they know a three-second clip will be stripped of context and judged months later by people who weren’t there. That hesitation costs lives when someone needs immediate intervention, and it pushes officers toward more bureaucratic, self-protective policing instead of proactive community work.

Second, a mandate creates a massive surveillance infrastructure with no safeguards. Body cameras don’t just record suspects; they record victims of domestic violence, children in schools, people having mental health crises, and anyone inside a private home during a welfare check. A mandatory policy means the state is permanently recording innocent people in their most vulnerable moments, and that footage will be stored, accessed, and potentially leaked. Without strict, locally controlled limits, you’re trading a hypothetical increase in police accountability for a guaranteed increase in citizen surveillance.

Third, the cost and burden falls hardest where policing is already strained. A full mandate means hardware, data storage, redaction staff, and IT compliance for every small-town and rural department. Redacting footage to comply with privacy law can take hours per incident. For departments with 30 officers and one clerk, that’s not accountability, it’s bankruptcy and delay. Those resources are better spent on training, de-escalation, and mental health co-responders that actually reduce conflict.

Accountability doesn’t come from a camera; it comes from clear policies, real oversight, and officers who feel trusted enough to be honest. Mandating cameras signals distrust and invites the worst of both worlds: officers who police for the camera and a public that still doesn’t see justice, because the footage is edited, withheld, or ruled inadmissible. Let departments choose cameras where they fit local needs, with strong privacy protections, and focus on what works: independent review, better training, and community relationships, not a mandate that looks good on paper and backfires in practice.

claim: Self-driving cars will increase safety and should replace human drivers.
argument:
You are already safer when you’re not driving. Think about the last time you were a passenger. You could relax, look out the window, actually get to work. The person driving could still kill you, but at least you weren’t responsible for it.

That’s the problem: driving is a terrible job for humans. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration found human error causes 94% of crashes. Not bad roads, not bad weather. Distraction, impairment, aggression, fatigue, misjudgment. 42,795 people died in U.S. traffic crashes in 2022. That’s 117 people every single day, almost all because a human made a mistake at the worst possible moment.

A self-driving car doesn’t get drunk, doesn’t get tired after a double shift, doesn’t take a call, doesn’t get road rage, doesn’t look away for two seconds to grab a coffee. It doesn’t have a medical emergency behind the wheel. It sees 360 degrees at once with lidar, radar and cameras, and it reacts in milliseconds, every time, with no ego.

The record is already here. Waymo’s vehicles have logged over 25 million real-world miles and millions more in simulation. In Phoenix, where they operate commercially, they have a lower crash rate per mile than human drivers. Tesla’s Autopilot data shows a 40% reduction in crashes when engaged. This isn’t theory, it’s happening now, and the gap widens every year as the system learns from every mile driven by every car in the fleet. A human driver learns from their own mistakes. A robot learns from everyone’s.

You worry about hackers, edge cases, ice on a mountain road. Those are real engineering challenges, but they are solvable challenges. Human drivers fail those same cases, badly and routinely. We don’t ban airplanes because pilots can fall asleep; we eventually replaced pilots with automation where it saves lives, and then required it.

The transition will be uncomfortable. We trust people we know, even when they’re bad drivers. We distrust a machine we don’t. But safety isn’t a feeling, it’s a count. If we replaced human drivers with self-driving systems tomorrow, tens of thousands of parents would come home to their kids next year. Thousands of families wouldn’t get a phone call that says, “I’m sorry.”

We don’t let humans do brain surgery while texting. We shouldn’t let them do two-ton vehicles at 70 mph while tired and distracted. Keeping the human in control isn’t freedom, it’s a lottery. Replacing human drivers isn’t replacing you, it’s finally protecting you.

claim: Smartphones/social media should be banned for kids under 16
argument:
You would not give a 12-year-old a car, a bottle of vodka, or a loaded credit card. Not because you distrust them personally, but because the risk is too high and the stakes are too great. A smartphone is all three at once, and it goes everywhere with them.

The adolescent brain is under construction. The prefrontal cortex, which governs impulse control, risk assessment, and long-term planning, does not finish developing until the mid-20s. Meanwhile the limbic system, the drive for reward, social approval, and novelty, is running at full throttle. Social media is engineered precisely for that mismatch. Infinite scroll, variable rewards, likes, streaks, and push notifications hijack the same dopamine circuitry casinos use to keep adults hooked. It is not a neutral tool; it is a product designed to capture attention by design, and it is most effective on the brains least equipped to resist it.

We are seeing the results in real time. Emergency rooms are filling with teenagers in crisis. Rates of major depression, anxiety, and self-harm have risen sharply in the decade since smartphones became universal in childhood. The American Academy of Pediatrics, the UK's Health Secretary, and the Surgeon General have all issued warnings that the evidence for harm is now too consistent to ignore, especially for girls on image-based platforms and for sleep-deprived teens scrolling until 2 a.m. Sleep loss alone impairs learning, mood regulation, and immune function, and screens are the single biggest driver of it.

This is not about sheltering kids from the modern world. It is about giving them a protected window to develop without constant surveillance and comparison. Childhood was once a place of boredom, neighborhood play, face-to-face negotiation, and books. Those were not bugs, they were the training ground for attention span, empathy, and identity formation. Now a 13-year-old's self-worth is being scored minute by minute by strangers, and their attention is auctioned to the highest bidder.

A ban under 16 is not prohibition forever. It is a developmental boundary, like age limits for driving or voting. Delaying first exposure until the brain has more defenses buys time for friendships, curiosity, and resilience to take root. Kids can still learn coding, research, and digital literacy in school with supervised devices. They can join family outings, sports teams, music lessons, and communities where reputation is earned, not curated.

Nobody handed you a smartphone at 10 and said good luck. We owe the next generation at least that much protection, not because they are weak, but because the product was built to exploit them, and we are the only adults with the power to say no until they are ready.

claim: Social media companies should be required to label AI-generated content
argument:
You don’t need to trust AI. You need to be able to tell when you’re looking at it.

Right now you can’t. A perfectly rendered video of a politician saying something they never said can sit next to a real news clip on your feed with no distinction. A fake product review written in seconds by a model can look identical to one written by a human. The only way to tell is to already know the answer, and by then the damage is done.

Labeling isn’t censorship. It’s a nutrition label for information. We don’t ban junk food, we make companies tell you what’s in it. We require cigarettes to carry warnings, not because we hate smokers, but because people deserve to know what they’re consuming. AI-generated content isn’t inherently dangerous, but it is inherently different: it has no lived experience, no accountability, no memory of having been there. That difference matters when you’re deciding whether to donate, vote, buy, or believe.

The skepticism is understandable: who decides what counts as AI? Won’t labels be abused? Won’t this chill speech? All fair concerns, and they’re solved by a simple, narrow rule: if a company knowingly distributes synthetic media at scale, it must disclose it, just as it already discloses ads. The label is not a scarlet letter, it’s a flag that says “this was made by a machine, not a person.” Platforms already moderate billions of posts for copyright, harassment, and misinformation. Adding provenance metadata is technically trivial. The C2PA standard for content authenticity is already built and used by major cameras, Adobe, and OpenAI. The infrastructure exists.

Without labeling, the incentive is to hide. An unscrupulous actor can flood the zone with synthetic testimonials, deepfake endorsements, and AI-written rage-bait that costs nothing to produce and can’t be bothered by defamation law. The platforms profit from engagement, not truth. If they can plausibly claim ignorance, they will. A labeling requirement shifts the cost back where it belongs: onto the distributor who benefits from the traffic.

This also protects creators. Human artists, journalists, and writers are being drowned out by cheap, infinite synthetic copies. A label lets audiences choose to support real work, and lets markets price authenticity.

You’re worried about free speech? Labels increase speech. They let you speak with full information. You’re worried about bureaucracy? It’s less burdensome than the content moderation systems already in place. You’re worried it won’t work? It doesn’t have to be perfect to be useful. Seatbelts don’t prevent all deaths, they change behavior.

We already label what we buy. We should label what we’re told.

claim: Self-driving cars will not be safe enough to fully replace human drivers.
argument:
You want to believe the car will get safer just like the plane did, and that's the trap. Planes fly in a highly controlled, three-dimensional corridor with trained professionals, strict separation, and no one cutting in front of them. Roads are the opposite: chaotic, crowdsourced, and intentionally lawless.

A self-driving car doesn't need to be good at the easy 99% of driving. It needs to be perfect at the 1% that determines life and death. That is the long tail problem, and it is not tiring away with more data because the tail is infinite.

A human driver handles a toddler chasing a ball into the street, a mattress falling off a truck, a police officer waving conflicting hand signals in a rainstorm at dusk because the signal is broken. These are not rare. They are rare and different every time. When a human encounters them, they use judgment, context, social negotiation, and a lifetime of embodied experience to guess intent. The car uses a model trained on what it has seen before. If it hasn't seen it before, it freezes, brakes late, or chooses the wrong interpretation. That is what the crash data already shows.

Waymo, Cruise, Tesla Autopilot, and others have logged billions of miles and still have disengagements and collisions that a competent human would have avoided. Waymo reports roughly one intervention every 11,000 miles in Phoenix, a sunny, well-mapped suburb with perfect conditions. Move that same system to Pittsburgh in January, or to a chaotic intersection in Mumbai or Lagos, and performance collapses. Full replacement requires it to work everywhere, not just in geofenced sun.

Skeptics say the fleet will just get better. But human drivers are not static. They adapt to the cars. When regular drivers know an AI can't read a sarcastic shoulder check, they exploit it. When other drivers know a robot car is overly cautious, they bully it. The system is adversarial and co-evolving, not a lab test.

Then there's responsibility. A human crash is tragic but understandable. An AI crash is a design failure, reproduced across every identical vehicle at once. One software bug can kill hundreds before it's patched. The industry has never accepted that level of moral liability for a consumer product, and regulators never will. That's why every 'autonomous' system still requires a human licensed driver ready to take over — an admission that the car is not trustworthy on its own.

Humans are flawed, distracted, drunk, and they kill about 40,000 people a year in the US. That's horrific. It's also the baseline we have to beat, everywhere, always, in all weather, at all times of night, on roads with no lanes, with animals, debris, construction, and other humans making irrational decisions on purpose.

Self-driving cars will be excellent tools for limited tasks: highway autopilot, fixed routes, low-speed shuttles. They will not be safe enough to fully replace a human driver because full replacement requires solving general intelligence in the wild, not driving in a parking lot. Until a machine can say "I don't know, you take over" and mean it ethically and reliably, the safest car on the road is still the one with a human in the loop.

claim: Smartphones/social media should not be banned for kids under 16
argument:
You want to protect kids, and the fear is real. The images are everywhere: a 13-year-old scrolling until 2 a.m., a 14-year-old curled in on themselves after a cruel comment, a classroom where no one looks up. A hard ban for under-16s feels like the clean, decisive answer. It isn’t, because it trades a manageable risk for guaranteed harms.

A ban doesn’t remove exposure to the internet, it just removes your ability to shape it. Kids under 16 will still be online. They’ll borrow a sibling’s phone, use a friend’s account, or move to platforms with even worse moderation that don’t check ID. When access is forbidden, use goes underground, where there is no parental visibility, no conversations, and no chance to model boundaries. The most vulnerable kids — those without engaged adults around them — are exactly the ones a ban leaves the most exposed.

The world they’re growing into doesn’t have an off switch. By 16, and certainly by 18, they will need to navigate social media, digital reputation, job applications, online banking, telehealth, and civic information. If we wait until then to teach them, we’re handing them the keys to a car they’ve never been allowed to practice driving. Countries and districts that have tried age-gated bans have seen the same pattern: delayed adoption, not reduced use, and a sharp spike in anxiety and secrecy around tech. Digital literacy is a safety skill now, not a reward for adulthood.

The research on harm is serious, but it’s not a case for prohibition. Large reviews, including the American Psychological Association’s 2023 Task Force and a 2024 meta-analysis of over 100,000 adolescents, find associations between heavy, unsupervised use and poorer sleep and mood, but the causal arrow is weak and bidirectional. Depressed teens scroll more. Heavy scrolling can worsen sleep. That is a problem of *how* and *when* they use these tools, not that the tools exist.

What actually moves the needle is what parents and schools do around the phone, not whether the phone exists. Teens with consistent, non-punitive boundaries — phone-free bedrooms after 10 p.m., regular co-viewing of feeds, open talk about algorithms and comparison — show better outcomes than teens with either unrestricted access or strict bans. They learn self-regulation instead of rebellion.

A ban tells kids the internet is inherently dangerous and adults can’t help them survive it. A guided approach tells them it’s a powerful, flawed space they can learn to use well. You don’t keep a child safe from cars by banning them from the driveway; you teach them traffic rules, you ride with them, and you make sure the seatbelt is on. Let kids under 16 have smartphones and social media, with scaffolding, not secrecy. That is how you actually protect them.
