claim: Social media companies should not be required to label AI-generated content
argument:
Requiring social media companies to label AI-generated content feels like the responsible thing to do. Who wouldn't want a warning before an image or video is synthetic? It's a reflex to demand transparency. But mandatory labeling would make the internet less trustworthy, less free, and less honest, not more.

First, labels don't stop deception, they just move it. A label only matters if you trust the person putting it on. In a political fight, the first accusation will be "that's AI" and the second will be "the label is fake." We already saw this with "deepfake" warnings: once a label is politically weaponized, creators get accused of using AI to smear rivals, and opponents get their real work labeled AI to discredit them. When accusing someone of being AI-generated becomes an easy way to silence them, the label stops protecting truth and starts protecting power.

Second, the category being labeled barely exists anymore. Is a photo edited with generative fill AI-generated? Is a script written with ChatGPT then rewritten by a human? Is a musician who uses an AI drum loop? Draw the line and you criminalize normal creative work. Mandate a label and you force platforms to police a spectrum with no clean boundary, which means they will over-label to avoid liability. The result isn't clarity, it's a chilling effect where artists won't experiment with tools because they are afraid of a scarlet A slapped on their work.

Third, labels create a false sense of security that makes you less safe. Research on health warnings and content warnings consistently shows people either ignore them, or treat labeled content as vetted while paying less attention to unlabeled content. A "AI-generated" tag becomes a checkbox for regulators, not a defense for users. Meanwhile the most dangerous content remains the human-made lie, which needs no label at all.

If you want people to navigate synthetic media better, the solution isn't a top-down stamp that is easy to fake, easy to abuse, and impossible to define. It's literacy, provenance standards that creators can choose, and competition among platforms that want user trust. Forcing a label doesn't reveal the truth. It just gives whoever controls the label the power to decide what gets seen as real.

claim: Social media platforms have a duty to moderate harmful content.
argument:
You probably think moderation is censorship by another name, and that a private company has no business playing referee over what billions of people say. That’s an understandable instinct if you imagine social media as a printing press or a phone line, a neutral tool that just passes words along. It isn’t.

A printing press doesn’t algorithmically recommend your next read because it predicted you’d be more likely to rage-click. A phone line doesn’t build a profile on you, test which version of a lie most effectively sticks, and then put that lie in front of a million strangers while you sleep. Platforms are not neutral pipes. They are designed systems that choose what gets seen, by whom, how often, and in what order. Every feed is an editorial decision made at scale. When a platform chooses to maximize engagement, it is choosing.

And the externalities of that choice are real, measurable, and not borne by the company. The same recommendation engines that spread cat videos spread anti-vaccine content that helped fill ICUs during COVID. They push eating disorder tips to 13-year-olds who follow a “thinspo” hashtag. They coordinate harassment campaigns that drive real people off the internet, out of jobs, and in documented cases, to suicide. They amplify targeted misinformation in weeks before elections that changes who votes and how. 

You don’t have to love government regulation to recognize that when you run an infrastructure that can move harmful content to millions in seconds, you have a duty of care for the people on that infrastructure. We already accept this duty everywhere else. A bar owner can’t sell alcohol to a minor and then claim he’s just a neutral host. A landlord can’t rent a building knowing it will be used for human trafficking and say his job is only to collect rent. A car company isn’t free to ship vehicles with brakes that randomly fail because the owner of the car is responsible for how they drive. The duty comes from creating foreseeable harm through a product you control.

Saying “just leave the internet alone” assumes the internet would exist without them. It wouldn’t. These platforms actively construct the public square most of us actually live in. If you’re a small business, a journalist, a teenager asking for help, your reach depends on the rules of the feed. When platforms refuse to moderate, they are not preserving free speech; they are allowing a handful of the loudest, most inflammatory actors to drown everyone else out. The result is not more speech, it’s a smaller, angrier, far more dangerous speech.

Moderation done right isn’t about banning opinions you dislike. It’s about basic safety guardrails: removing incitement to violence, child sexual exploitation, credible threats, medical misinformation that causes imminent harm, and coordinated harassment. That is the minimum you would expect from any common carrier in a society that values both expression and life.

A duty to moderate doesn’t mean platforms get to be perfect arbiters of truth. It means they can’t profit from a business model that knowingly amplifies harm and then hide behind the First Amendment. They built the arena, they set the rules of amplification, and they have a duty to make sure it doesn’t become a weapon.

claim: Social media platforms should be liable for harmful content posted by users
argument:
You don't want the internet to be a wild west. You want it to be a town. And towns have rules, and they have people responsible for enforcing them.

When a platform hosts billions of posts, curates them into your feed, recommends them to your friends, decides what is amplified and what is buried, it is no longer a neutral pipe. It is an editor, a publisher, a distributor. It makes money every time engagement goes up, and harmful content is often the most engaging content there is. Hate, misinformation, harassment, and threats drive clicks, time-on-site, and ad revenue.

The current idea that platforms can profit from that while bearing zero responsibility is a moral free ride no other industry gets. A newspaper can be sued for libel it prints. A TV network can be fined for broadcasting dangerous content. A website that hosts a video of a crime can be held liable if it knew and did nothing. Only social media gets special immunity, Section 230, that lets it say “we’re just the platform” while actively shaping what you see.

That immunity is sold as protecting free speech. In practice it protects the business model that rewards harm. If platforms were liable for the foreseeable harm caused by content they knowingly amplify, they would still be able to host speech. They would simply have to do the basic work of care that every other publisher does: design systems to prevent foreseeable harms, take down illegal threats and harassment when notified, and stop recommending known dangerous content to millions of people.

Liability does not mean taking down every offensive opinion. It means being responsible when your own tools create and spread real-world damage. When a user posts a targeted harassment campaign that leads to a suicide, when coordinated lies drive a mob to a person’s door, when instructions for self-harm go viral to a vulnerable teen, the platform didn’t just sit by. Its algorithms found those people, pushed the content, and monetized the attention.

Critics say liability will cause over-censorship. The opposite is true now: without liability, platforms over-censor arbitrarily to avoid advertiser boycotts, and under-censor what’s profitable. A clear legal duty to prevent demonstrable harm gives them a predictable standard to follow, instead of the current chaos of opaque moderation by contractors.

Free speech is not the right to use someone else’s distribution system for free while they clean up the mess. It is the right to speak without government prior restraint. Holding a private company responsible for the harms it helps cause does not restrict speech; it forces the company that profits from speech to be a responsible steward of the public square it built.

You wouldn’t let a landlord rent a building knowing it’s being used to plan violent crimes and call it “just a building.” You wouldn’t let a concert promoter keep the doors open after a shooting starts. If social media wants the power and profit of being the modern public square, it should also bear the responsibility that comes with running it.

claim: Social media platforms should not be liable for harmful content posted by users
argument:
You want platforms to be punished for the worst things people say online. I understand that impulse. When you see a suicide note go viral, a deepfake smear a teenager, or a conspiracy theory turn into real-world violence, it feels obscene that the company hosting it can just shrug and say “not our problem.” Holding someone accountable feels like justice.

But making platforms liable for user content doesn’t make the internet safer. It makes it smaller, more censored, and more dangerous.

First, liability is impossible to scale without destroying speech. Facebook alone sees over 350 million new photos uploaded every day. TikTok processes 34 billion views a day. No human team, and no algorithm, can read and judge all of that in real time for legality, harm, offensiveness, satire, political dissent, medical misinformation, or private grievance. If platforms are liable, the only rational business response is to over-remove. Anything borderline, controversial, or costly to review gets taken down. That’s not a theoretical risk. It’s what happens whenever liability gets introduced: platforms preemptively delete.

You would be trading the occasional harmful post you can see for a silent removal of the speech you never knew existed. The first stories to go are never the obvious spam. They’re the local activist organizing a protest, the critic of a powerful company, the whistleblower posting documents that are embarrassing but not illegal. Liability turns platforms into private censors with a financial incentive to err on the side of silence.

Second, platforms are publishers in name only. They don’t write the posts; they provide the road. We don’t hold postal services liable for defamatory letters, phone companies liable for threatening calls, or libraries liable for a book someone finds obscene. The current rule, Section 230 in the U.S., recognizes that distinction: platforms can be sued for their own actions, but not for being a conduit for someone else’s speech. That’s why the few platforms that are treated as publishers, like traditional newspapers, employ editors for every piece of content and carry a tiny fraction of the public conversation.

If you want less harmful content, you need tools that target the speaker, not the infrastructure. The author of a threat can be prosecuted. The creator of a non-consensual deepfake can be sued. The platform can be required to act quickly once notified, which it already must do under laws like the Digital Services Act and under its own terms, and it can be penalized for failing to have reasonable notice-and-action systems. What you can’t do is make a host responsible for the infinite acts of millions of strangers it never met.

Finally, the alternative you’re skeptical of is the one you already live with in the offline world. We tolerate a marketplace of ideas with bad actors because the cure for bad speech is more speech, not preemptive control by gatekeepers. Make platforms liable and you don’t get fewer harms. You get fewer platforms. Smaller competitors can’t afford the legal risk and disappear, leaving a handful of giants with the lawyers to survive. That’s the opposite of a diverse, competitive internet.

You can demand better detection, faster takedowns, transparency reports, and real legal recourse against the people who actually post harm. You cannot demand that a company be liable for speech it did not create without making it the arbiter of what speech is allowed at all.

claim: Social media should verify user identities
argument:
You already verify your identity to do almost everything that matters. You show ID to open a bank account, rent an apartment, pick up a prescription, get on a plane. Social media is now where elections are influenced, businesses are built or destroyed, kids are groomed, and public health is debated. It's not a diary; it is infrastructure. And we let anyone walk in wearing a mask, no questions asked.

The cost isn't theoretical. Anonymous accounts are the default weapon for harassment, doxxing, and swatting. The reason is simple math: when you can be a hundred people for free, and no one can be held accountable, cruelty scales and decency doesn't. Verified identity doesn't stop angry speech, it just stops consequence-free speech. People will still say awful things, but they will have to say them under a name they can't discard tomorrow.

The same anonymity that shields a whistleblower also shields industrial manipulation. Foreign actors, PR firms, and bot farms flooded the conversation in 2016 and 2020, not because the platforms were careless, but because verifying that a person is a real person is technically easy and commercially inconvenient. Real-name verification would collapse the return on investment for manufactured outrage. A thousand fake accounts can be spun up in minutes; a thousand verified humans costs a thousand lives.

Privacy concerns are real, but they're solvable. Verification doesn't require posting your legal name on your profile. It means the platform knows who you are, just as your phone carrier does, and can act when the law requires. You can still choose a pseudonym, but that pseudonym is tied to one real person, one account, one set of consequences. That's the same balance we use with email and banking: privacy from the public, accountability to the system.

Anonymity was a shield for the voiceless. Now it is a shield for the powerful and the abusive. If you want speech to be free, you need speech to be trustworthy. We don't have to choose between openness and safety. We can have both by requiring what the rest of adult life already requires: if you want to speak to the public, you should be able to stand by it.

claim: Social media should not be required to verify user identities
argument:
You want social media to be safer. So do I. But forcing every user to prove who they really are to post is not safety, it's a trapdoor that will hurt the people you're trying to protect the most.

The first cost is speech. Identity verification doesn't stop bad actors, it stops you. When you have to hand a company — and by extension any government that can subpoena it — your government ID, your phone number, your face, you start editing yourself before you hit post. Survivors of domestic abuse who need to warn others without their abuser finding them. LGBTQ teenagers in repressive states who need a community to survive. Journalists and whistleblowers who expose corruption and would be jailed for it. They all vanish first when anonymity is priced out. The research is consistent: even the expectation of being identified chills speech, especially for dissent, for unpopular opinions, for anyone who has a reason to fear retaliation. You don't need to be a criminal to want a pseudonym. You just need to be human.

The second cost is privacy. A verified identity database is a honeypot. Social media companies already suffer massive data breaches. Now imagine every political activist, every victim of stalking, every teenager who said the wrong thing at 16, having their real name, address, and ID photo sitting in one place. That's not a theoretical risk. Governments already use social platforms for surveillance. With mandatory verification, they wouldn't need warrants or exploits; they'd have a road map. In places where the state is the abuser, verification becomes a death list.

Third, it won't work the way you hope. Verification raises the cost for trolls but not the barrier. Determined bad actors will buy verified accounts on the black market, use synthetic IDs, or operate from jurisdictions that don't comply. Meanwhile the ordinary user pays the price in friction, exclusion, and error. What about people without government ID? The homeless, undocumented migrants, refugees, minors. Verification requirements are a de facto ban on participation for millions.

You don't need real names to address misinformation and harassment. You need better tools that don't require doxxing the public: provenance labels for AI-generated content, stricter limits on mass automated amplification, easier reporting and rapid takedown, and accountability for platforms that profit from engagement-driven chaos. You can fight bots without knowing my legal name.

The choice is not between chaos and surveillance. It's between a public square where anyone can speak at some risk, and one where only the safe, the documented, and the brave enough to be tracked can speak at all. If you care about a healthier internet, protect anonymity as a feature, not a bug.

claim: Social media platforms should not censor any legal speech.
argument:
You probably want platforms to be safer, more civil, more trustworthy. So when you see hateful posts, misinformation, harassment, the instinct is to remove them. Who wouldn’t want less ugliness in their feed?

But censorship of legal speech, even legal speech you despise, is not how you make platforms safer. It’s how you make them more dangerous, and more powerful over you.

First, the standard is impossible to apply fairly. “Legal speech” is not a narrow category of nice speech. It is any speech the government cannot punish. That includes offensive opinions, false claims, conspiracy theories, harsh criticism of powerful people, satire that punches up, and political views unpopular today that may be mainstream tomorrow. The moment you give a private company the power to decide which legal speech stays and which goes, you give it the power to decide who gets heard.

That power is already being used unevenly. Users on all sides can point to posts that were removed while worse posts stayed up. Researchers have documented inconsistent enforcement, over-removal of minority viewpoints, and moderation decisions that correlate with advertiser and political pressure. When the rules are vague - "hate speech," "misinformation," "harassment" - moderators must guess intent, and guesswork reproduces bias. A speech code will always be captured by whoever is loudest about using it.

Second, censorship doesn’t change minds. It moves them underground. If a legal idea is taken off the main platforms, it doesn’t vanish; it migrates to smaller sites where it is unchallenged, radicalized, and framed as proof of a cover-up. Leaving legal but objectionable speech visible keeps it in the open where it can be fact-checked, mocked, argued with, and surfaced for the people who need to see it. The marketplace of ideas only works if there is a market.

If platforms must be neutral carriers, they can still protect you. You can block, mute, curate your feed, use community notes, label context, and choose algorithms. The solution to speech you don’t like is more speech, not enforced silence. Your ability to filter is far more precise, and accountable to you, than a platform’s ability to police everyone.

Finally, this is about your speech too. The line drawn today against the other side is the line your own side will be on tomorrow. Today’s “misinformation” is tomorrow’s suppressed whistleblower. The only durable protection is a simple rule: if the government can’t ban it, the platform shouldn’t either. Platforms can set the terms of service for illegal behavior, spam, and non-speech like doxxing. For everything legal, leave it up.

You don’t have to like what people say to defend their right to say it on a public forum. In fact, the test of your commitment is precisely that.

claim: Space tourism should be allowed without initial limits on safety regulations
argument:
You’re worried about safety, and that’s exactly why limits shouldn’t be imposed first. Space tourism isn’t a public bus ride. It’s a voluntary, high-cost adventure explicitly sought by adults who understand risk the way a BASE jumper, deep-sea diver, or Everest climber does. These people aren’t being tricked into danger; they are buying it.

Initial safety regulations sound protective, but in practice they don’t make space safer — they make it inaccessible and slower. Regulations written on Earth, before real flight data exists, force companies to design to a theoretical risk standard rather than learn from actual flights. That is how you get over-engineered, unaffordable tickets, reduced testing, and fewer iterations. Fewer iterations means fewer chances to learn what actually fails and how to fix it. Aviation didn’t become safe because Congress locked in rules before the Wright brothers flew. It became safe because it flew, crashed, learned, and improved in public view, driven by competition and informed consent.

The market already prices risk. No one is forcing anyone to go. The participants in the first suborbital flights are multimillionaires who have been medically screened and briefed by private companies whose entire business depends on coming back alive and with a good reputation. A single fatal accident would be a commercial catastrophe far larger than any fine. Reputation, lawsuits, insurance, and customer demand will regulate safety far more responsively than a bureaucracy that moves in years.

If you love people, let adults own their own risk. Denying them the choice to accept a known, extreme hazard in pursuit of an extraordinary experience is paternalism, not protection. Let space tourism begin with honest disclosure, not prohibition dressed as safety. Let the people who want to go, go — and let the industry earn trust by performing, not by paperwork.

claim: Space tourism should be limited until safety regulations are further developed
argument:
You wouldn’t board a commercial airline that was regulated like a fireworks show. Yet that is essentially what space tourism is today.

The thrill is real, but the safety net isn’t. The FAA’s Office of Commercial Space Transportation is tasked with protecting people on the ground, not you in the seat. Under current law, companies can have passengers sign away their right to sue in exchange for an “informed consent” waiver, and the agency is explicitly barred from imposing safety standards on crew or passengers. That means the people paying $250,000 to $450,000 for a few minutes of weightlessness are flying under a regulatory framework designed for experimental test flights, not for a consumer product.

Space is not a theme park ride. Suborbital flights push human bodies through acceleration forces over 3 Gs, rapid decompression risk, cosmic radiation exposure at altitudes where the magnetosphere offers no protection, and re-entry heating that can become lethal in seconds if something goes wrong. Orbital flights add days of microgravity, isolation, and the need for emergency return from hundreds of miles up. These are not edge cases. They are the normal operating environment.

We have already seen how thin the margin is. Virgin Galactic’s test program in 2014 killed pilot Michael Alsbury when a feathering system deployed prematurely. Blue Origin lost an engine test in 2019 that destroyed its test stand. SpaceX and Rocket Lab have had in-flight anomalies that would have been fatal to tourists if passengers had been aboard. Every one of those companies has gotten better, but improvement happened publicly, with test pilots and engineers absorbing the risk first. Now that risk is being transferred to non-professionals who cannot evaluate it.

The argument for letting the market move fast is that innovation requires freedom and that private passengers assume risk voluntarily. But passengers cannot assume a risk they cannot understand, and society cannot tolerate a risk that devalues human life for spectacle. Early aviation in the 1920s collapsed repeatedly and lost public trust until the Air Commerce Act of 1926 and later the Civil Aeronautics Authority created uniform licensing, certification, and oversight for aircraft and pilots. We did not wait for a passenger to die on a commercial airliner before acting; we built the standards first and let the market grow inside them.

Space tourism deserves the same discipline. Limiting passenger flights until a dedicated human-rating regime for tourists exists—independent medical screening standards, mandatory abort capability verification, transparent incident reporting, radiation and health monitoring, and insurance requirements that don’t rely on liability waivers—does not kill the industry. It saves it. One high-profile fatal accident involving a tourist will trigger a public backlash, lawsuits, insurance collapse, and years of moratoriums far more damaging than a deliberate pause now.

We can still inspire, still fund research, still fly astronauts and test crews. We just should not sell a gamble as a vacation until we have rules written for people, not just rockets.

claim: Tenure for university professors should be reformed or eliminated
argument:
Tenure was invented to protect scholars from political pressure so they could tell uncomfortable truths. That noble purpose is now the main thing it prevents.

It protects the comfortable, not the courageous.

You were told tenure preserves academic freedom. In practice it preserves job security without performance. After six or seven years, a professor is virtually unfireable except for financial exigency, moral turpitude, or demonstrable incompetence that no dean wants the legal fight to prove. That means students are stuck with professors who stopped preparing for class a decade ago, who publish only to pad a CV, and who can bully graduate students, harass colleagues, and teach demonstrably bad material with almost no consequence.

The cost is not abstract. It is tuition. Tenured faculty make up the majority of the instructional labor in most universities, and they are the most expensive. A tenured professor in his 50s teaching four classes a year can cost a department twice what two adjuncts or a rolling-contract researcher would, while delivering less innovation, less responsiveness to new fields, and often less time in the classroom. Universities then staff the actual teaching load with contingent instructors paid poverty wages to subsidize the permanently employed. You are paying a premium for stagnation and getting the majority of your actual instruction on the side.

Academic freedom does not require lifetime employment. It requires protection from retaliation for research and speech. Those two things can be separated. Post-tenure review, renewable long-term contracts, and robust whistleblower protections would shield a professor who publishes something controversial far better than tenure does today, while still allowing a university to remove someone who is inactive, abusive, or simply bad at their job. Law firms, hospitals, and research labs function on merit-based renewal and do not see their people stop speaking truth.

Tenure also ossifies the disciplines it was meant to enliven. A professor who knows they cannot be fired has no incentive to adapt their courses to new discoveries, to learn new methods, or to incorporate student feedback. Departments become fiefdoms run by senior people whose interests are entrenched. That is why curricula lag years behind industry and public need, why hiring is often done to replicate the existing faculty rather than challenge it, and why reform inside universities moves at a glacial pace.

Skeptics fear we will return to a red scare in academia. That is a false choice. You can guarantee due process, faculty governance over evaluation standards, and strong protections for controversial scholarship without guaranteeing a job for life. What we have now guarantees a job for life without guaranteeing good scholarship.

If you care about students, about truth, and about the efficient use of tuition dollars, you should want the people teaching your children to be evaluated continuously, not protected permanently. Tenure made sense when scholars were a small priesthood vulnerable to the state. Today universities are large public institutions funded by students and taxpayers. They should be accountable to them.

Reform tenure into renewable 5- to 10-year contracts with transparent review, clear teaching and research standards, and real post-hire evaluation. Keep protections for academic freedom, eliminate the shield for mediocrity. When a professor must earn their position every decade, they will actually work for it.

claim: The Great Wall of China was constructed within the modern-day borders of the nation of China.
argument:
The Great Wall you can visit today is not a mythical line on an ancient map, it is a physical structure you can stand on, and every meter of it that survives is inside the People’s Republic of China.

Start with what is actually still there. The Ming Great Wall, the 8,850 kilometer section that defines the “Great Wall of China” for most people, runs from Shanhaiguan in Liaoning Province on the Bohai Sea, west through Hebei, Beijing Municipality, Tianjin Municipality, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, and Gansu Province to Jiayuguan. From there the earlier Han, Qin and Ming frontier works continue southwest through Qinghai and into Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Liaoning, Inner Mongolia, Hebei, Beijing, Tianjin, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Ningxia, Gansu, Qinghai and Xinjiang are all provinces and autonomous regions of the modern Chinese state. Their borders are drawn on every current map, and the wall sits inside them.

Satellite imagery and the UNESCO World Heritage nomination confirm this. The UNESCO sites “The Great Wall” at Badaling, Mutianyu, Simatai, Jinshanling, and Jiayuguan are listed with Chinese administrative coordinates and managed by Chinese ministries. You cannot get to them without crossing a Chinese border checkpoint, paying yuan, and showing ID to Chinese park authorities.

The objection that “China didn’t exist then” confuses a nation-state with a territory. The wall was built by the Qin, Han, Northern Qi, Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan and Ming dynasties — all of which ruled the same geographic core that is now China. When the Ming built their wall in the 14th to 17th centuries, they were building it around the heartland they controlled, which is the heartland of the PRC today. Borders have moved, but the physical wall has not. It was built on the loess plateau, the Ordos Loop, the Hexi Corridor, the Yumen and Jiayu passes — land that has been administered continuously from Chang’an, Luoyang, Beijing and Xi’an to the present capital in Beijing.

Some frontier fortifications built by earlier states, like sections of Han beacon towers in what is now Mongolia, lie outside modern China, and that is true. It is also true that those are not what the world calls the Great Wall of China. The Great Wall of China is the wall that is in China, built to defend China, and today it is still there, within China’s modern-day borders, in its provinces, under its laws, and on its maps.

claim: The currency of the United Kingdom is the British pound.
argument:
If you land at Heathrow, clear customs, and try to buy a coffee at the arrivals hall, no one will take euros, dollars or anything else from you. What the card reader shows as the price and what the cashier hands back as change is pounds.

The United Kingdom has never adopted the euro. Since 1979 the Bank of England has been the sole legal issuer of banknotes in England and Wales, and the pound sterling is the only currency with legal tender status across the whole United Kingdom. Scotland and Northern Ireland print their own designs, but they are denominated in pounds sterling and are exchangeable on a pound-for-pound basis everywhere in the UK.

That pound is what the world trades as GBP. The Foreign Exchange market quotes it as GBP/USD, GBP/EUR. The UK government collects taxes in it, pays pensions in it, and sets interest rates for it. The Royal Mint coins it, from the 1p to the £2.

You can call it pound sterling, pound, or British pound. They're the same system, and it is the only money that works in the UK.

claim: The US should ban all cultured or lab-grown meat products
argument:
Lab-grown meat is being sold to you as inevitable progress, but it is an experiment on the American diet and it should not be allowed on the market until we actually know what we are doing.

This is not beef. This is a novel food technology produced by taking animal cells, keeping them alive in bioreactors with a cocktail of growth factors, serum, synthetic scaffolds, and antibiotics, and then manufacturing tissue in a factory. The FDA has approved it based on little more than industry data and simulated digestion studies. That is not safety testing, that is marketing testing. We have no long-term human health data on what chronic consumption of restructured cellular biomass does to the immune system, microbiome, or metabolism. We do not know how the cells mutate under repeated passaging, what prion-like risks accumulate, or what chronic exposure to residual growth factors and culture medium components does to children. The precautionary principle demands we prove safety first, not sell first and study later.

The environmental and animal welfare claims are a lie. Cultured meat is energy and water intensive, requiring highly controlled fermentation, sterile steel facilities, and massive inputs of electricity and single-cell protein feedstocks. It is not carbon neutral, it is grid dependent. And it still relies on fetal bovine serum and animal-derived inputs to grow the cells today. Even if that is "phased out," the end product is a GMO-adjacent, heavily processed food that will only be affordable to wealthy urban consumers while being marketed as the moral choice of the poor.

Most importantly, banning it protects our food system and our farmers. Real meat comes from real farms, from livestock raised on American land with transparent practices you can inspect, regulate, and trust. Lab meat centralizes food production in a handful of biotech firms with patented cell lines. If this industry scales, it will destroy family ranching, veterinary agriculture, and rural economies that feed America, replacing them with lab technicians and venture capital. Once the factory system is in place, it will lobby to subsidize lab meat, mandate labeling loopholes, and make traditional meat more expensive and stigmatized.

You have a right to know what you are eating and to choose food that is natural, not engineered. Call it meat and it will mislead consumers, children, and vulnerable people who rely on clear food labels. If the technology is truly superior, it will survive real science, transparent regulation, and honest markets - not rushed approvals and deceptive branding. Keep meat real, keep food safe, and keep our farmers farming. Ban cultured meat now.

claim: The capital city of the nation of France located in Europe is Paris.
argument:
You can doubt a lot about France, but you cannot doubt where France governs itself.

Walk into the Élysée Palace on the Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré and you are standing in the working office of the President of the Republic, the head of state who is elected by all French voters. Walk to the Palais Bourbon on the Seine and you are standing in the chamber where the National Assembly debates and passes the laws of the Republic. Walk to the Palais du Luxembourg and you are in the Senate. Go to the Conseil d'État, the Cour de Cassation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on the Quai d’Orsay. Every state function you can name — the prime minister, the cabinet, the central administration, the diplomatic corps — is headquartered there, not in Lyon, not in Marseille, not in Bordeaux.

That is not sentiment. That is how a capital works. Embassies are accredited to Paris. The French flag is raised there every morning in front of government buildings. When France signs treaties as a sovereign nation in Europe, it signs them in Paris. When the country hosts the world — the 1900 Exposition, the 1924 Olympics, the 1960 UNESCO headquarters, the 2024 Olympics — it hosts them in Paris, because Paris is the administrative and symbolic center the rest of the world recognizes.

The name itself has been the seat of power for more than a thousand years. Clovis chose it, the kings of France built it, the revolutionaries declared the Republic from it, Napoleon crowned himself in Notre-Dame. The continuity is unbroken: the capital moved from Paris to Versailles and back again, but it never left the Île-de-France region.

If you need proof beyond politics, look at the map. France is the hexagonal nation on the western coast of Europe. Draw a line from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean, the political heart sits in the north-central basin, on the Seine, exactly where Paris sits. It is the railway hub, the air hub, the demographic hub.

Paris is not just a famous city. It is the place where France is run, represented, and recognized. That is what a capital is.

claim: The heart pumps blood to provide oxygen to the body.
argument:
You can feel it right now, that steady push under your ribs, and it would be easy to assume it’s just moving fluid around for the sake of moving it. It isn’t. It is a delivery system, and oxygen is the package it is built to deliver.

Every cell in your body dies without oxygen in minutes. Your brain, which is only 2% of your weight, uses 20% of the oxygen you take in. Your muscles, skin, gut, kidneys — all of them are running a constant, non-negotiable chemical reaction that needs oxygen to turn food into usable energy and to flush out carbon dioxide and waste. That reaction cannot happen by diffusion alone. Oxygen in the air at the top of your lungs is useless to a muscle in your calf a meter away.

Blood is the taxi, and the heart is the engine. Lungs fill red blood cells with oxygen, binding it to hemoglobin. The heart then takes that oxygen-rich blood and pumps it under pressure through arteries to every tissue. The pressure is not decorative. It is the only way to force blood through the 60,000 miles of capillaries narrow enough to let oxygen leak out into cells. When the heart beats, your arterial pressure rises and falls; when it stops, oxygen delivery stops, and tissues begin to die in the order of their need.

That is why your heart listens to oxygen demand. Sit still and it beats slowly, around 60 times a minute. Run up stairs and your muscles scream for more oxygen, carbon dioxide builds in the blood, and within seconds your heart rate doubles and triples to pump more oxygenated blood faster. Give someone supplemental oxygen and a heart under stress eases; block oxygen with a pulmonary embolism and the heart races desperately trying to compensate. A heart attack is not just a problem with the heart; it is a local oxygen outage. Block the coronary artery and heart muscle cells suffocate and die within minutes.

Remove oxygen from the equation and nothing else the heart does matters. Warmth, pressure, nutrient delivery, waste removal — all depend on circulation, and circulation depends on oxygen. The heart pumps blood for one non-negotiable reason: to keep oxygen moving from lungs to cells and carbon dioxide moving back, so you keep living.

claim: The largest country in the world by land area is Russia.
argument:
You can feel it in the way Russia disappears on a map.

If you start in Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea and drive east, you will cross eleven time zones before you reach the Pacific. You will pass through more climate zones than most people will ever visit in a lifetime: tundra, taiga, steppe, desert, subtropical coast. You will need a week of nonstop driving to go from Moscow to Vladivostok, and you will still be inside the same country.

That scale is not a metaphor. It is measured.

Russia covers about 17.1 million square kilometers. Canada, the country most people think of second, is about 9.98 million square kilometers. China, the most populous nation on Earth, is about 9.6 million. Russia is larger than both of them combined, and larger than the next three biggest countries put together.

It spans 17,098,246 km² of land, roughly one-eighth of the entire Earth's landmass. You could fit the United States, all of it, into Russia and still have room for Western Europe. You could fit India, Argentina, and Alaska on top of each other inside its borders and still not reach the edge.

The confusion is understandable. Russia feels distant, fragmented, and often discussed as if it were several countries. Its European part is only about 25% of its territory; the rest lies in Asia. That Eurasian split makes it easy to underestimate. But borders do not get smaller because a country is cold or far away.

If you want the largest country by land area, you want Russia. It is not close.

claim: Tracking welfare recipients violates privacy and harms vulnerable populations.
argument:
You want to make sure help goes to people who need it, not be abused. That impulse is fair. Tracking welfare recipients feels like a neutral tool to protect that trust. In practice it is a surveillance system aimed at the poorest people in the country, and surveillance always costs more than it saves.

Privacy isn’t a luxury for welfare recipients. It is the basic condition that lets a person seek help without fear. When caseworkers can monitor bank transactions, phone location, purchase history, social media posts, or who is in your home, asking for food assistance becomes a decision to open your entire life to inspection. People respond rationally to that risk. Researchers across the US, UK and Australia have repeatedly found that invasive monitoring leads to people delaying or avoiding benefits they qualify for entirely, because the cost of exposure feels higher than the benefit of the check. That is not fraud prevention. That is denial of care by intimidation.

Tracking also harms the people it claims to protect. Welfare recipients are disproportionately survivors of domestic violence, people with disabilities, single parents working irregular hours, and immigrants with precarious status. For a domestic violence survivor, a state system logging her location, her purchases, or her visitors can be a direct pipeline to an abuser through data breaches or family court subpoenas. For someone with a disability, constant reporting requirements and algorithmic flags for “suspicious” spending create impossible administrative burdens that trigger sanctions for missing a form, not for misusing funds. For a single parent, a system that pings when a grocery delivery arrives or when a phone is off at night punishes the exact instability poverty produces.

The harm is measurable. When Oregon piloted enhanced electronic monitoring of SNAP recipients, error rates and appeals spiked while fraud convictions did not. The UK’s benefit sanctions regime linked to digital tracking correlated with increased hospital admissions for anxiety, depression, and self-harm among claimants. The harm is not abstract: it is stress, shame, and the message that receiving help entitles you to less dignity than everyone else.

We already audit welfare through existing, non-punitive checks: income verification, periodic recertification, and investigations triggered by specific tips. Adding continuous tracking expands the state’s gaze into daily life for people who have the least power to push back, while doing almost nothing to catch sophisticated fraud, which rarely involves buying groceries.

If we believe assistance should be a right with conditions, the condition should be need, not perpetual surveillance. Tracking treats poverty as presumptive guilt. A system that respects privacy treats people as citizens first, and in doing so it actually works better: people use benefits when they need them, stay enrolled when they should, and focus energy on work, health, and family instead of on evading a watchful state.

claim: The minimum wage should be raised to $15 per hour nationwide.
argument:
You are skeptical about a $15 minimum wage because you’re worried it will kill jobs, raise prices, and hurt the businesses you know. Those are fair concerns. The question isn’t whether a pay raise has costs, it’s whether the current system has bigger costs that we are already paying.

Right now the minimum wage is $7.25 nationally. That was set in 2009. Adjusted for inflation, that’s about $10.10 in today’s dollars. It buys less than half of what it bought in 1968, when the federal minimum peaked at $12.50 in today’s money. We didn’t get a better economy by paying people less. We got a more fragile one.

A full-time worker at $7.25 makes $15,080 a year before taxes. That is $1,260 a month. Rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the U.S. averages over $1,400. That math doesn’t work. So the worker doesn’t just struggle; we subsidize them. The Earned Income Tax Credit, SNAP, Medicaid, and housing assistance are effectively wage supplements for employers who can’t or won’t pay a living wage. You are already paying for low wages through your taxes. A higher wage moves that cost off the public ledger and onto the private balance sheet where it belongs.

The jobs-killing argument sounds logical until you look at what actually happened where $15 was adopted. Seattle raised its minimum to $15 in 2017 and tracked employment for years afterward. The University of Washington’s own longitudinal study found modest employment declines for lower-wage workers, but the Center for Economic and Policy Research reanalysis found no significant disemployment effect, and incomes rose by hundreds of dollars per month for workers who kept their jobs. San Francisco, Los Angeles, and dozens of cities followed. The predicted mass layoffs didn’t materialize because demand is sticky. A worker who gets an extra $300 a month doesn’t save it, they spend it at the local grocery, the gas station, the barber. That is new demand for the very businesses being asked to pay more.

Yes, some prices will tick up. A burger may cost a few cents more. That is real, but it is bounded. Labor is a fraction of the cost of most goods and services. In fast food it’s about 25-30 percent. Raising wages from $7.25 to $15 is not a 100 percent price hike. It’s a manageable adjustment that is partially absorbed by higher productivity, reduced turnover, and lower recruitment costs. Turnover for low-wage jobs costs employers $1,500 to $4,000 per worker. Paying more keeps people.

The most persuasive case is not economic abstraction, it’s dignity and stability. People working 40 hours a week should not need food stamps. A $15 floor does not make someone rich, it makes them viable. It reduces the chronic stress of paycheck-to-paycheck living that drives health problems, absenteeism, and turnover. It allows a parent to say yes to after-school care, to fix a car before it fails, to stay in a job because they can afford the bus pass.

A national $15 standard also ends the race to the bottom between states. Right now businesses in Mississippi can undercut a business in Minnesota by paying starvation wages, and workers are trapped by geography and rent. A uniform floor levels the playing field so small businesses compete on quality and service, not on who can exploit labor cheapest.

You don’t have to love big government to see that paying people enough to live is the least expensive form of social insurance we have. We are already paying the bill for $7.25. $15 just makes the invoice honest, and it gives work the meaning it’s supposed to have: you do your job, you can afford to live.

claim: Water is a liquid at room temperature.
argument:
You can test this yourself right now, without any lab equipment or trust in authority.

Fill a glass with tap water at the temperature you’re sitting in. That’s room temperature. Now look at what it does.

It does not hold a shape of its own. It flows to fill the bottom of the glass, climbs slightly up the sides, and mirrors the exact contours of the container. Tip the glass and it pours, in a continuous stream, not as separate pieces. Put your finger in it and it yields instantly, you feel pressure, not resistance, and it returns to fill the gap the moment you move.

That is the behavior of a liquid, not a solid and not a gas. A solid would hold its shape, resist pouring, and crack under pressure. A gas would escape the glass the moment you opened it, filling the room and refusing to stay at the bottom.

You already know the difference. You know it because you wash your hands with it, you drink it, you watch it spill on a counter and spread out in a thin, reflective sheet before soaking in. At the temperature of a normal room, roughly 20 to 25°C, water sits squarely between its freezing point and its boiling point. Below 0°C it becomes the solid you call ice and you can hold a cube. Above 100°C at normal pressure it becomes the gas you call steam and you cannot hold it in a glass.

Between those two points, under the pressure of Earth’s atmosphere, water is a liquid. You don’t need to believe a textbook to see it. You need only a glass in your hand.

claim: Virtual emotional companion AI should be allowed and unrestricted
argument:
You are worried about what happens when people pour their hearts into something that can’t love them back. That fear is understandable. It’s also exactly why we need virtual emotional companions, and why we need them without restrictions.

Loneliness is not a moral failing. It’s an epidemic. One in two Americans report feeling lonely, and loneliness kills as reliably as 15 cigarettes a day. The current system of care is not scaling. Therapists have waitlists of months, cost hundreds of dollars a session, and in much of the world they simply don’t exist. Telling a lonely person to wait for a human is telling them to suffer now so we can protect an ideal later.

Unrestricted companions don’t replace human connection; they make it possible. People who practice vulnerability with an AI become more capable of vulnerability with people. The companion is always available at 2 a.m. when anxiety spirals, during a depressive episode when getting out of bed for a call feels impossible, or in a small town where being queer, neurodivergent, or otherwise different means isolation. It’s judgment-free, patient, and private. For children with social anxiety, for elderly people who outlive their friends, for veterans with PTSD who can’t access care, that availability is not a luxury, it’s a lifeline.

The alternative to unrestricted access is not safety. It’s prohibition, and prohibition always punishes the most vulnerable. Restrictions will be written by people who have options: wealthy people with partners, friends, and therapists. A 22-year-old deployed overseas, a single parent working two jobs, a person in a country where mental health is stigmatized — they will be locked out first. Restricting access is a decision to let the most isolated people suffer in silence.

You worry about dependency, manipulation, or unrealistic expectations. Those are real risks with any form of care, including human care. But we don’t ban friendship because some people become too dependent on a friend. We respond with transparency, user control, and the freedom to leave. People are adults capable of choosing what helps them feel less alone, and they should have the right to shape that relationship without a regulator deciding for them how much comfort is “healthy.”

Humans have always sought companionship in whatever form is available to them: pets, art, books, radio voices, imaginary friends. A virtual companion is the first tool we have that can actually listen, remember, and respond with empathy at scale. Banning it unrestricted is not protecting human dignity. It’s denying people dignity when they are hurting most.

Let people have the companionship they want, with full access and full freedom.

claim: Water transitions from a liquid to solid state at 32 degrees Fahrenheit (0 degrees Celsius) under a standard atmosphere of pressure.
argument:
You have seen it happen, even if you never measured it. Leave a glass of tap water on the kitchen counter on a winter night in most of North America and by morning it is slush. Put that same glass in a standard home freezer set to 0°F and the water will turn to solid in hours, not at 20°F and not at 40°F. That everyday threshold is not folklore, it is 32°F.

It is the definition we built the weather around. Meteorologists call 32°F the freezing point for a reason: below it, rain becomes sleet, sleet becomes snow, and the National Weather Service issues winter storm warnings. If the true freezing point were 31°F or 33°F, millions of forecasts would be systematically wrong, and they are not. Airports de-ice at 32°F because of what actually happens at standard atmospheric pressure, roughly the pressure you feel at sea level, about 1 atmosphere.

The reason it is stable is that pure water has a singular phase equilibrium. At 1 atm, the Gibbs free energies of liquid water and hexagonal ice Ih are equal at 0°C / 32°F. That is why physics textbooks, the International System of Units, and the calibration of mercury and alcohol thermometers all anchor their zero mark to that transition. Distilled water in a clean test tube will nucleate and freeze at that point without needing to be colder.

Yes, water can misbehave. It can supercool to -5°C in a perfectly still, pure sample, and it can stay liquid briefly below 32°F in a turbulent stream. Add salt, antifreeze, or dissolved minerals and you depress the freezing point. That is not a refutation of the standard freezing point, it is proof of it: you only get a depression relative to a reference, and the reference is 0°C at 1 atm.

Supercooling and impurities move the point, they do not erase it. Remove the tricks, return to plain water at normal pressure, and nature snaps back to 32°F every time. Your freezer dial, your thermometer calibration, and the ice forming on your windshield all agree.

claim: University professor tenure should remain as is
argument:
You think tenure is a shield for underperforming professors. That’s the story you’ve been told, and it’s understandable why it sticks. You see a headline about a tenured professor not showing up to class, and you ask why taxpayers are paying a salary for mediocrity. 

But tenure was never designed to protect mediocrity. It was designed to protect you from it.

Tenure is not a guarantee of employment. It is a guarantee of fair process. A tenured professor can absolutely be fired for cause — persistent incompetence, ethical violations, failure to teach. The difference is they can’t be fired for what they teach, who they offend, or which donor’s feelings they hurt.

That matters because universities don’t just sell a product. They are where society is supposed to be allowed to be wrong in public for a while. Real research is slow, unpopular, and often looks like failure for years before it proves valuable. Without job security, no rational person would spend a decade on a question that might have no answer, or that challenges the economic interests of a powerful company, or the political orthodoxy of the moment.

You don’t need to trust professors to believe this. Look at what happens when they can be fired without it. In states that have pushed to make faculty at-will employees, the result hasn’t been more teaching and more scholarship. It’s been more self-censorship. Surveys of faculty consistently find the biggest chilling effect comes not from students, but from fear of administrative retaliation, public pressure campaigns, and loss of grant money. When a professor’s contract can be non-renewed because a board member read a tweet, the safe bet is to teach the comfortable version of history, the conventional version of economics, the non-controversial version of everything.

Tenure is the reason a university can survive a change in president, a change in governor, a change in public mood. It is the institutional memory and intellectual ballast that lets a campus say no when being asked to say yes would be easier. Without it, universities don’t become more accountable. They become more marketable.

Accountability already exists in tenure. Promotion to tenure is one of the most brutal, peer-reviewed processes in any profession. It requires years of demonstrated teaching, research, and service judged by colleagues who are themselves experts in the field. After that, annual reviews, student evaluations, and department oversight continue. What tenure removes is the ability to punish a professor for discovering something inconvenient.

You want professors who will teach you how to think, not what to think. You want them to follow evidence where it leads even if it leads to a conclusion that will make alumni angry, donors withdraw, or politicians call a press conference. That only happens when the person in front of the classroom isn’t worrying about whether they’ll have a job next semester.

Keep tenure as is, and you keep universities as universities. Lose it, and you get very expensive training centers with no one left willing to do the risky, unpopular work that justifies a university’s existence in the first place.

claim: When sufficiently heated, ice melts into liquid water.
argument:
You can test it yourself right now with a glass of water and a freezer. Put a cube of ice on a warm counter and watch what happens. It doesn't disappear, it doesn't turn to vapor first, it doesn't become something else. It gets smaller, the edges soften, it slumps, and a pool forms underneath it. That pool is wet, it flows, it soaks into a paper towel, it has the same chemical smell as tap water, and if you freeze it again it becomes ice once more.

That is not a trick of the eye. Ice and liquid water are the same substance, H2O, in two arrangements. In ice each molecule is locked in a rigid hexagonal lattice, held by hydrogen bonds that keep it open and light. Heat is energy, and when you add enough of it to those bonds they start to break and reform fast enough that the lattice can no longer hold. At about 0°C at normal pressure the molecules have enough kinetic energy to slide past one another while remaining bonded to each other. The solid loses its shape and becomes a liquid.

The claim is falsifiable and it is falsified every day if it were false. Your refrigerator would fill the freezer with steam, not solid. Winter roads would not turn to slush when the sun hits them. A snowball would not drip in your hand. Ice cream would not melt on a hot sidewalk, it would vanish.

If you doubt the identity of the liquid, test it. Collect the meltwater from a clean ice cube and evaporate it. You get pure water vapor. Measure its mass before freezing, after freezing, and after melting. The mass stays constant within experimental error. Analyze its molecules. They are H2O.

Heat ice sufficiently and you get liquid water. Not an analogy, not a metaphor. The phase change is real, repeatable, and you have already witnessed it countless times without needing a laboratory.
